lessons.title: What Digital Image Processing Is
lessons.content:
Take out your phone and open any photo. To you it is your friend laughing at a tea stall in Old Dhaka. To the phone it is something much more boring and much more useful: a giant table of numbers. A 12 megapixel photo is a table with about 4000 columns and 3000 rows, and every cell says how bright and what colour that tiny spot is. Digital image processing (DIP) is the study of doing clever maths on that table so the picture becomes clearer, smaller, safer, or easier for a computer to understand. In this first lesson we build the big picture: what an image really is to a computer, what kinds of jobs image processing does, where images come from, and the map of the whole course.

An image as a function: Scientists write an image as f(x, y). Here x and y are a position, and f(x, y) is the intensity (brightness) at that position. In the real world x, y and f can take any value, so the image is continuous, like a painting. A digital image is what you get when x and y are only allowed whole-number positions and f is only allowed a fixed set of values. Each position with its value is called a pixel, short for picture element. So a digital image is a matrix: row number, column number, and a number inside. For a gray (black-and-white) image with 8 bits per pixel, the value runs from 0 (black) to 255 (white), and 128 is middle gray.

A tiny example: Here is a 3 x 3 gray image written as rows: [10, 10, 200], [10, 10, 200], [10, 10, 200]. The left two columns are almost black and the right column is almost white. If you blew this up on a screen you would see a dark block with a bright stripe on its right side. Everything in this course, blurring, sharpening, finding edges, cutting out objects, is just rules for changing or reading numbers like these. A colour image usually keeps three such matrices, one for red, one for green and one for blue, stacked like three sheets of paper.

Why we need it: Raw images are rarely perfect. Photos taken at night are dark and grainy. A scanned exam paper has shadows. An X-ray may be too low in contrast for a doctor to see a hairline fracture. A satellite photo of the Sundarbans may be hazy. Also, images are huge: a raw 12 megapixel colour photo is about 36 million bytes, which is why we must compress it before sending it on WhatsApp. And finally, more and more machines must understand images on their own: a toll booth reading number plates, a factory checking biscuits, a phone unlocking with your face. Image processing is the toolbox for all of these.

Three levels of processing: Experts often split the work into three levels. Low-level processing takes an image in and gives an image out: removing noise, improving contrast, sharpening. Mid-level processing takes an image in and gives out pieces of information about it: cutting it into regions (segmentation), finding edges, measuring the size and shape of objects. High-level processing tries to make sense of what was found: this region is a car, that one is a person, the person is crossing the road. Most of this course lives in the low and mid levels. The high level, true understanding, is the job of Computer Vision (deep-cse-8-3) and Deep Learning (deep-cse-8-1), which stand on top of what you learn here.

DIP, graphics and vision: These three are cousins that people often mix up. Computer Graphics (deep-cse-5-2) goes from a description to an image: you give it a triangle and a light, it draws the picture. Image processing goes from an image to a better image or to measurements. Computer Vision goes from an image to a description: it looks at a picture and says there are three cows in a field. A simple rule: graphics makes pictures, image processing fixes and measures pictures, vision understands pictures. Real systems mix all three, for example an augmented reality filter on Snapchat finds your face (vision), smooths your skin (processing) and draws cat ears (graphics).

A short history: One of the earliest uses of digital images was in newspapers in the early 1920s. The Bartlane cable picture system sent photos across the Atlantic by undersea cable between London and New York, cutting the time from more than a week by ship to less than three hours. Early systems coded only 5 gray levels; later ones used 15. Real computer-based processing began in the 1960s, when space programs needed to clean up pictures sent back by probes. Pictures of the Moon from the American Ranger 7 probe in 1964 were processed by computer to correct camera distortions. In the early 1970s computerized tomography (CT) was invented, which builds a slice image of the body from many X-ray measurements; Godfrey Hounsfield and Allan Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in medicine for it. Since then, cheap sensors, fast processors and phones have put image processing in billions of pockets.

Images beyond what eyes see: Light that we see is only a small slice of the electromagnetic (EM) spectrum. Image processing works on images made from many other parts of it. Gamma rays: nuclear medicine scans (like PET) and astronomy. X-rays: medical X-rays, CT, airport baggage scanners, checking welds and circuit boards. Ultraviolet: microscopy with fluorescent dyes, checking currency notes for hidden marks. Visible light: ordinary photos, microscopes, fingerprints, number plates. Infrared: night vision, thermal cameras that found people with fever at airports, crop health from satellites. Microwaves: radar, which can see through clouds, very useful in Bangladesh during monsoon floods when optical satellites see only clouds. Radio waves: MRI scanners in hospitals and radio telescopes. Not every image even comes from EM waves: ultrasound (sound waves) shows a baby before birth, and electron microscopes use electron beams.

The fundamental steps: A typical image processing system is a pipeline. Step 1, image acquisition: getting the picture from a camera or scanner, maybe with some first fixes. Step 2, image enhancement: making it look better for a particular purpose, which is a bit subjective. Step 3, image restoration: undoing damage such as blur or noise using a model of what went wrong, which is more objective. Step 4, colour image processing. Step 5, wavelets and multiresolution processing: looking at the image at several scales. Step 6, compression: making it smaller to store or send. Step 7, morphological processing: tools for extracting shapes. Step 8, segmentation: cutting the image into meaningful parts. Step 9, representation and description: turning regions into numbers (area, perimeter, texture) called features. Step 10, recognition: giving a label to an object based on its features. Behind all of these sits a knowledge base, what we already know about the problem, such as "number plates are rectangles about 2 to 4 times wider than tall".

Components of a system: The hardware side has a sensor (a camera chip that turns light into voltage), a digitizer (turns voltage into numbers), a computer (from a phone chip to a server), specialised hardware such as a GPU for heavy, parallel pixel work, storage (images are big, so this matters), displays and printers for output, and a network to move images around. The software side today is mostly libraries: OpenCV, scikit-image and NumPy in Python, MATLAB's image toolbox, and phone camera software stacks. A key idea: most image operations do the same small job on millions of pixels, so they run very well in parallel on a GPU.

How to look at an image as numbers: A great habit for this course is to open an image in Python and print a small corner. With OpenCV you can write img = cv2.imread("photo.jpg", 0) to load it as gray, and then print(img[0:3, 0:3]) to see a 3 x 3 block of numbers. Notice that OpenCV uses [row, column], so the first index goes down and the second goes across, and the origin (0, 0) is the top-left corner, not the bottom-left as in school graphs. We will come back to this coordinate convention in lesson 04.

Enhancement vs restoration: These two words come up all the time, so fix them early. Enhancement means "make it look better for this job", with no promise of truth. Increasing contrast in a dark selfie is enhancement; there is no correct answer, only nicer or worse. Restoration means "get back the original as closely as possible" using a model of the damage. If we know a photo was blurred by the camera moving 10 pixels to the right, we can try to undo exactly that. Lessons 06 to 12 are mainly enhancement; lessons 13 to 15 are restoration.

Course map: Here is how our 26 lessons fit together. Lessons 02 to 05 are foundations: how the eye and camera form images, sampling and quantization, relations between pixels, and moving pixels around geometrically. Lessons 06 to 10 are enhancement in the spatial domain: changing intensities, histograms and filters. Lessons 11 and 12 move to the frequency domain with the 2D Fourier transform. Lessons 13 to 15 cover noise and restoration. Lessons 16 and 17 handle colour. Lessons 18 and 19 are morphology. Lessons 20 to 22 are segmentation: edges, thresholding and regions. Lesson 23 is wavelets, lesson 24 is compression, lesson 25 turns regions into features, and lesson 26 builds a full number plate reader.

Real-life example 1, a document scanner app: Imagine you use a scanning app to send your HSC admit card to your college office. Acquisition: your phone camera takes a colour photo, tilted and with your hand's shadow on one corner. Enhancement: the app converts to gray and boosts contrast. Segmentation: it finds the four edges of the paper. Geometric correction: it warps the tilted quadrilateral into a neat rectangle. Thresholding: it makes text pure black and paper pure white, even under uneven light. Compression: it saves a small PDF instead of a 4 MB photo. Every step is a lesson in this course.

Real-life example 2, flood mapping: During the 2024 floods in eastern Bangladesh, clouds blocked optical satellites for days. Radar satellites, however, see through clouds. Calm flood water reflects radar away from the satellite, so it looks dark in the radar image, while land looks brighter. Analysts take the radar image, reduce its grainy speckle noise with filters, apply a threshold to mark dark pixels as water, clean up the result with morphology, and compare it with a dry-season image by subtraction to see which villages are newly under water. The map then guides rescue boats and relief.

Real-life example 3, hospitals: A CT scan at a hospital in Dhaka is itself an image processing result: the machine never takes a direct photo of a slice of your body; it measures X-rays from hundreds of angles and a computer reconstructs the slice. After that, doctors use windowing (a contrast trick from lesson 06) to show bone or soft tissue more clearly.

Common mistakes: First, thinking an image is a picture rather than numbers; once you see the matrix, everything becomes maths. Second, mixing up the three fields: if the output is a better image, it is processing; if it is a label like "cat", it is vision. Third, forgetting that 0 is black and 255 is white in an 8-bit gray image, not the other way round. Fourth, assuming enhancement is objective; a filter that makes a picture prettier may destroy details that a doctor needs. Fifth, mixing up rows and columns: in most libraries the first index is the row (going down).

What exams ask: Define a digital image and a pixel. Explain the fundamental steps of DIP with a block diagram. Name application areas by EM band with one example each. Differentiate image processing, computer graphics and computer vision. List the components of an image processing system. Distinguish enhancement and restoration.

Recap: A digital image is a matrix of numbers f(x, y), each cell a pixel. Image processing changes or measures those numbers at low, mid and high levels. It grew from newspaper pictures and space probes to every phone and hospital. Images come from the whole EM spectrum and beyond. The standard pipeline runs from acquisition through enhancement, restoration, colour, wavelets, compression, morphology, segmentation, description and recognition. Next lesson, we go back to the very start of that pipeline: how your eye and a camera actually form an image.
key_points: A digital image is a function f(x, y) sampled on a grid: a matrix whose cells (pixels) hold intensity values.
In an 8-bit gray image values go from 0 (black) to 255 (white); colour images usually hold three such matrices (R, G, B).
Low-level processing outputs images, mid-level outputs regions and measurements, high-level tries to understand the scene.
Graphics makes images from descriptions, image processing improves and measures images, vision describes images.
Images come from the whole EM spectrum (gamma, X-ray, UV, visible, infrared, microwave, radio) and also from ultrasound and electrons.
The fundamental steps: acquisition, enhancement, restoration, colour, wavelets, compression, morphology, segmentation, description, recognition.
Enhancement is subjective (make it look better); restoration is objective (undo a known damage).
lessons.tip: Whenever you learn a new operation, print a tiny 3 x 3 or 5 x 5 corner of the image before and after. Seeing the numbers change is the fastest way to understand what a formula really does.
lessons.task: Draw a 6 x 6 grid on paper. Fill it with numbers from 0 to 255 so that it shows a bright plus sign on a dark background. Then write next to it which EM band would be used to image: a broken bone, a cloudy flood area, a person with fever, and a printed book.

quiz.q: In an 8-bit grayscale image, which pixel value is white?
quiz.explain: 8 bits give 256 values, 0 to 255; 0 is black and 255 is white.

quiz.q: Taking a photo and producing the label 'three cows in a field' is mainly...
quiz.explain: Going from an image to a description of what is in it is computer vision (high-level processing).

quiz.q: Why are radar (microwave) images useful for mapping floods in monsoon?
quiz.explain: Optical satellites cannot see through thick cloud, but radar can, and calm water looks dark in radar images.

quiz.q: Removing a known camera-shake blur using a model of the motion is an example of...
quiz.explain: Restoration uses a model of the degradation to get back the original; enhancement only aims to look better.

quiz.q: Which step turns regions into numbers like area, perimeter and texture?
quiz.explain: Representation and description computes features from segmented regions so they can be recognised.

lessons.title: Human Vision, Light and Image Formation
lessons.content:
Stand at the door of a dark room on a sunny afternoon and step inside. For a few seconds you see nothing, then slowly the chair, the bed and the clock appear. Your eye just changed its sensitivity by a huge amount without you noticing. The final judge of most processed images is a human eye, so before we touch a single pixel we should understand how that judge works, and how a camera turns a scene into numbers in the first place. That is this lesson: the eye, a few famous tricks it plays on us, light itself, camera sensors, and a simple model of how an image is formed.

Structure of the eye: The eye is nearly a ball, about 20 mm across. Light first passes the cornea, a clear tough window at the front, which does much of the bending. Then it passes the pupil, the hole in the coloured iris, which grows and shrinks to control how much light enters. Next is the lens, which muscles squeeze thinner or fatter to focus on far or near objects. Finally light lands on the retina, the thin inner lining at the back, which is covered with light receptors. The retina is the eye's sensor, just like the chip in a phone camera.

Cones and rods: The retina has two kinds of receptors. Cones are about 6 to 7 million in each eye, packed mostly in a small central spot called the fovea. They work in bright light, see colour, and give sharp detail; each cone has its own nerve connection, which is why you read text by looking straight at it. Rods are far more numerous, about 75 to 150 million, spread across the retina. Many rods share one nerve, so they give a rough overall picture, they do not see colour, and they are very sensitive to dim light. This is why at night under a weak street light in your mohalla, objects look grayish: only rods are working. Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no receptors at all, which creates the blind spot.

The eye as a camera, with differences: A camera lens has a fixed focal length and moves to focus; the eye's lens changes its shape instead. The distance from the lens to the retina is about 17 mm, and the image formed on the retina is upside down and tiny; the brain flips and interprets it. Also, the eye is not a uniform sensor: it is sharp only in the fovea and blurry elsewhere, so your eyes constantly jump around a scene and your brain stitches the views. A camera chip, in contrast, has the same pixel spacing everywhere.

Brightness adaptation: The eye can handle light levels from a starry night to a sunny beach, a range of roughly 10 to the power 10, ten billion to one. But it cannot see that whole range at once. At any moment it is set to a smaller window around the current brightness level, called the brightness adaptation level. Walking into a dark room forces it to slide the window down, which takes time. A camera has the same problem, which is why a photo of a bright window from inside a room shows either a white window or a black room. The perceived brightness (what you feel) is roughly a logarithmic function of the actual light intensity, which is one reason the log transform in lesson 06 looks natural to us.

Weber ratio: How small a change can you notice? Experiments put a small bright spot of extra intensity delta I on a background of intensity I, and increase delta I until the observer just notices it half the time. The smallest noticeable increase is delta Ic, and the Weber ratio is delta Ic divided by I. A small Weber ratio means good discrimination. Worked numbers: if the Weber ratio is about 0.02 at a moderate brightness, then on a background of 50 units you notice a change of 0.02 x 50 = 1 unit, but on a background of 200 units you need 0.02 x 200 = 4 units. The same change of 2 units is visible on a dark background but invisible on a bright one. Brightness discrimination is poor at low light (rods) and better at high light (cones).

How many gray levels can we tell apart? An ordinary person can tell apart only about one to two dozen gray levels at one spot at a time. Yet we store 256 levels in an 8-bit image. Why? Because the eye's window moves as it looks around different parts of a scene, and because when gray levels change smoothly across a large area, too few levels create visible steps (false contours, lesson 03). So 256 levels is a safe number for smooth display, not the number we can name one by one.

Mach bands: Look at a series of flat gray stripes, each a bit brighter than the one before. Each stripe has a constant intensity, yet near each border you see a slightly darker line on the dark side and a slightly brighter line on the bright side. These are Mach bands, named after the physicist Ernst Mach. The eye's own processing exaggerates edges, which helps us see object borders. It is a lesson for image processing: what we perceive is not always what the numbers say, and our visual system already does some sharpening of its own.

Simultaneous contrast: Put three identical gray squares on three backgrounds: black, mid-gray and white. The square on black looks lightest and the one on white looks darkest, though all three have the same pixel value. Perceived brightness depends on surroundings. There are many such optical illusions, and they warn us that judging a processed image only by eye can mislead. When it matters, measure the numbers.

Light and the EM spectrum: Light is electromagnetic energy that travels as waves, and also comes in packets called photons. Wavelength lambda and frequency nu are linked by c = lambda x nu, where c is about 3 x 10^8 m/s. Photon energy is E = h x nu, where h is Planck's constant. Visible light runs from about 400 nm (violet) to about 700 nm (red). Worked: green light of 550 nm has frequency 3 x 10^8 divided by 550 x 10^-9, which is about 5.45 x 10^14 Hz. A handy shortcut: energy in electron-volts is about 1240 divided by wavelength in nm, so 550 nm gives about 2.25 eV, violet 400 nm gives about 3.1 eV and red 700 nm about 1.77 eV. Shorter wavelength means more energy, which is why X-rays and gamma rays can pass through flesh and can damage cells.

Describing light: Light without colour is achromatic or monochromatic, and its only attribute is intensity, which in images we call the gray level. Chromatic light (colour) is described by three quantities. Radiance is the total energy flowing from the source, in watts. Luminance, in lumens, is how much of that energy an observer actually perceives; a source emitting strong infrared has high radiance but almost zero luminance, because we cannot see infrared. Brightness is the subjective feeling of intensity and cannot really be measured. We will return to colour properly in lesson 16.

Sensors that make images: A sensor turns incoming energy into a voltage. A single sensor (like a photodiode) can make a whole image if either the sensor or the object moves in two directions, which is how some old drum scanners and laser-based microscopes work. A sensor strip, a line of sensors, captures one row at a time while the object or the strip moves: flatbed scanners and many satellites build images this way, line by line, as they move. A sensor array, a 2D grid, captures the whole image at once: this is the chip in every phone and digital camera. CT machines use a ring of sensors around the patient.

CCD and CMOS: The two main types of array chips are CCD (charge-coupled device) and CMOS. In a CCD, the charge collected at each pixel is passed along, bucket-brigade style, to a single output where it is converted, which historically gave low noise. In CMOS, each pixel has its own amplifier circuit, which makes it cheaper, faster and less power-hungry. Today almost all phone cameras use CMOS sensors. Each pixel collects photons during the exposure time; more photons mean a stronger signal, which is why long exposure helps in low light but blurs moving things.

Bayer filter: A sensor pixel measures only how much light arrives, not its colour. To get colour, most cameras put a tiny coloured filter over each pixel in a repeating 2 x 2 pattern called the Bayer pattern: one red, one blue and two green. Green gets double because our eyes are most sensitive to green and it carries most of the brightness detail. So a 12 megapixel sensor actually measures 6 million green, 3 million red and 3 million blue values. The camera then guesses the missing two colours at every pixel from its neighbours, a step called demosaicing. Poor demosaicing creates colour fringes on fine patterns like a striped shirt.

The image formation model: A simple but powerful model says the light reaching the camera from a point is the product of two things: f(x, y) = i(x, y) x r(x, y). Here i is illumination, how much light falls on the scene from sources like the sun or a tube light, with 0 < i < infinity. And r is reflectance, the fraction of that light the object reflects back, with 0 < r < 1, where 0 means total absorption and 1 means total reflection. Illumination is set by the light source; reflectance is a property of the object.

Typical numbers: Standard textbook values: on a clear sunny day the sun can give about 90,000 lumens per square metre on the earth's surface, a cloudy day about 10,000, a full moon about 0.1, and a typical office about 1,000. Reflectance: black velvet about 0.01, stainless steel 0.65, a flat white wall 0.80, silver-plated metal 0.90 and snow 0.93. Worked: a white wall in an office gives about 1,000 x 0.80 = 800 units; black velvet in the same office gives 1,000 x 0.01 = 10 units. The same white wall in sunlight gives 90,000 x 0.80 = 72,000. The camera's job is to squeeze this huge range into, say, 0 to 255.

Why the model matters: Illumination usually changes slowly across a scene, like a shadow spreading across a page, while reflectance changes quickly at object edges and texture, like ink on paper. That difference lets us separate them. A technique called homomorphic filtering (lesson 12) takes the logarithm, so the product becomes a sum, log f = log i + log r, and then suppresses the slow part to remove uneven lighting while keeping detail. Document scanning apps rely on this idea to fight shadows.

Real-life example 1, photographing a classroom whiteboard: Your phone sees the whiteboard near the window brightly lit and the far end dim. The reflectance of the white board is the same everywhere, but illumination changes, so the far side comes out gray. Black marker has low reflectance everywhere. If the app knows the slow illumination pattern, it can divide it out and make the whole board equally white with sharp black writing. This is the model f = i x r at work.

Real-life example 2, night shots on a phone: At night the illumination i is tiny, so very few photons reach each pixel and random photon arrival makes the image grainy. Phones solve this in a smart way: they take many short frames in a second, align them and average them. As we will see in lesson 04, averaging K noisy images reduces the noise spread by a factor of the square root of K, so 16 frames cut it by 4. That is how night mode gets clean pictures in a dark Dhaka street.

Common mistakes: Thinking the eye sees absolute brightness; it sees relative brightness and adapts. Confusing rods (dim light, no colour, many) with cones (colour, detail, fewer). Thinking a 12 megapixel colour camera measures 36 million colour values; with a Bayer filter it measures 12 million single-colour values and guesses the rest. Mixing up luminance (measurable, perceived energy) and brightness (subjective). Forgetting that reflectance must be between 0 and 1.

What exams ask: Draw and label the eye and explain rods vs cones. Define brightness adaptation and the Weber ratio, and explain Mach bands and simultaneous contrast. Relate wavelength, frequency and energy. Describe single, strip and array sensors. State the illumination-reflectance model with its ranges and give example values.

Recap: The eye focuses light on the retina, where cones give colour and detail in bright light and rods give sensitivity in dim light. The eye adapts over a huge range but sees only a window at a time, and it judges brightness relatively, as Mach bands and simultaneous contrast show. Light is described by wavelength, frequency and energy, and visible light is only 400 to 700 nm. Cameras use sensor strips or arrays, mostly CMOS with a Bayer filter. The image is the product of illumination and reflectance. Next lesson: how this continuous image is turned into a grid of numbers by sampling and quantization.
key_points: Cones (about 6-7 million, mostly in the fovea) see colour and detail in bright light; rods (about 75-150 million) work in dim light without colour.
The eye adapts over roughly 10^10 levels of light, but only a small window at a time; perceived brightness is roughly logarithmic.
Weber ratio = smallest noticeable change divided by background intensity; a smaller ratio means better discrimination.
Mach bands and simultaneous contrast show that perceived brightness is not the same as pixel value.
c = wavelength x frequency and E = h x frequency; visible light spans about 400-700 nm.
Images are captured by single sensors, strips or arrays; phone cameras use CMOS arrays with a Bayer filter (RGGB) and demosaicing.
Image formation model: f(x, y) = i(x, y) x r(x, y), with illumination 0 < i < infinity and reflectance 0 < r < 1.
lessons.tip: Keep a small table of the illumination and reflectance numbers and try products yourself. Seeing that sunlight on snow and moonlight on velvet differ by millions of times makes it obvious why cameras struggle with exposure.
lessons.task: Draw three identical gray squares on paper (same pencil pressure) and colour the area around them black, gray and left white. Ask two friends which square is darkest. Then explain the result using simultaneous contrast.

quiz.q: Which receptors let you see colour and fine detail in bright light?
quiz.explain: Cones, packed in the fovea, are colour-sensitive and each has its own nerve, so they give sharp detail in bright light.

quiz.q: If the Weber ratio is 0.02, what is the smallest noticeable change on a background of 200?
quiz.explain: delta Ic = 0.02 x 200 = 4 units.

quiz.q: A white wall (reflectance 0.8) in an office lit at 1,000 units gives about...
In a Bayer filter, why are there two green pixels in every 2 x 2 block?
options: Red and blue cannot be filtered
The eye is most sensitive to green and it carries most brightness detail
quiz.explain: Human vision is most sensitive in the green range, so doubling green improves perceived sharpness.

quiz.explain: Perceived brightness depends on the surroundings; this effect is simultaneous contrast.

lessons.title: Sampling and Quantization
lessons.content:
Imagine describing the sky at sunset to a friend over the phone, but you are only allowed to talk about a few spots, and for each spot you may only use one of eight colour words. You would have to choose which spots to describe and squeeze each colour into the nearest word. You would lose detail in two different ways: by skipping places, and by rounding colours. That is exactly what a camera does to turn the smooth, continuous world into a digital image. The first loss is called sampling, the second quantization. Getting both right decides how sharp, smooth and large an image is.

Continuous to digital: The scene in front of a camera is continuous: brightness changes smoothly from point to point and can take any value. Sensors produce a continuous voltage that follows this. To store it on a computer we must make it discrete in two directions. Digitizing the coordinates (x, y), that is, measuring only at a grid of positions, is sampling. Digitizing the amplitude, that is, rounding each measured value to one of a fixed set of levels, is quantization. In a sensor array the grid of pixels already does the sampling, and an analog-to-digital converter does the quantization.

A one-line picture: Take one horizontal line across a photo of a white kurta against a dark door. Along the line the true brightness rises smoothly from dark to bright and back. Sampling picks equally spaced points along the line, say every 0.1 mm on the sensor. Quantization takes the brightness at each of those points and replaces it with the nearest allowed level, say one of 8 levels. The result is a staircase: flat steps at sample points, each step at an allowed height. Do this for every line and you have a digital image.

The image as a matrix: After sampling and quantization the image is an M x N array: M rows and N columns. We write f(x, y) with x from 0 to M-1 and y from 0 to N-1. The number of allowed intensity levels is L, and for hardware convenience L is a power of two: L = 2^k, where k is the number of bits per pixel. With k = 8, L = 256 levels, 0 to 255. With k = 1, L = 2: a binary image, black and white only, like a fax.

Storage worked: The number of bits needed is b = M x N x k. For a 1024 x 1024 image with k = 8: b = 1024 x 1024 x 8 = 8,388,608 bits. Divide by 8 to get bytes: 1,048,576 bytes, which is exactly 1 MiB. A colour image with three 8-bit channels needs three times that, 3 MiB. A tiny 32 x 32 binary image needs 32 x 32 x 1 = 1,024 bits, only 128 bytes. A 12 megapixel phone photo, 4000 x 3000 with 3 bytes per pixel, needs 36,000,000 bytes, about 36 MB, before compression. These sums explain why compression (lesson 24) is not optional.

Spatial resolution: Spatial resolution is the smallest detail you can tell apart. Saying "1024 x 1024" alone is not a measure of resolution unless you know how much real space the image covers. A meaningful measure is dots (pixels) per unit distance, like dpi (dots per inch), or line pairs per unit distance. A line pair is one dark line plus one light line next to it. If each line is 0.1 mm wide, one line pair is 0.2 mm, so the pattern has 1 / 0.2 = 5 line pairs per mm. Printing gives a feel: newspapers are often printed around 75 dpi, magazines around 133 dpi, and photo prints around 300 dpi. A 4 x 6 inch print at 300 dpi needs 1200 x 1800 = 2.16 million pixels.

What low spatial resolution does: Keep the size of the picture on screen the same but reduce the number of samples, for example from 1024 x 1024 down to 256 x 256 and then 64 x 64. Each sample now covers a bigger patch of the scene, so fine details merge. Edges become jagged staircases, a look called pixelation or "checkerboard effect", thin lines vanish, and small text becomes unreadable. CCTV footage from an old camera where a number plate is just a few blocks is this problem. No later processing can invent details that sampling never captured; it can only guess.

Intensity resolution: Intensity resolution is the smallest change in brightness you can tell apart, and it is set by k. With 8 bits, the step between levels is tiny compared to the full range. If we reduce the number of levels while keeping the spatial grid, say from 256 to 16 levels, smooth areas like a clear sky or a person's cheek start showing visible bands, as if drawn with a few crayons. These ridges are called false contouring. They usually become visible around 16 levels or fewer in smooth regions. Busy areas full of texture, like a crowd at a cricket match, hide false contours much better.

Quantization worked: Suppose we keep only 8 levels (k = 3) instead of 256. Each new level covers 256 / 8 = 32 old values. A pixel with value 137 falls in band number 137 // 32 = 4, which covers 128 to 159. We can represent it by the start of the band, 128, or by the middle, 144. Using the middle keeps the maximum error to half a step, here 16. The general rule: the larger the step, the larger the quantization error, and the error behaves like noise added to the image. From your DSP course (deep-cse-5-7 lesson 04) you know each extra bit buys about 6 dB of signal-to-quantization-noise ratio; for 8 bits that is about 6.02 x 8 + 1.76 = 49.9 dB.

Which matters more, samples or levels? Experiments by Huang in 1965 showed that it depends on the image content. For images with a lot of detail, such as a crowd, viewers accepted fewer gray levels as long as spatial resolution was kept high. For smooth images with large plain areas, such as a face, more gray levels mattered. This idea, called isopreference, tells engineers they can trade bits for pixels depending on the job. A fingerprint scanner may use high spatial resolution with fewer levels, while a medical X-ray needs many levels (often 10 to 16 bits) to show subtle tissue differences.

Aliasing in 2D: Sampling theory from Signals & Systems (deep-cse-3-7 lesson 19) says that to capture a signal correctly you must sample at more than twice its highest frequency. In images, frequency means how quickly brightness changes across space, measured in cycles per unit distance. A fine pattern of stripes 2 mm apart (one cycle every 2 mm) needs samples closer than 1 mm on the object. If we sample too coarsely, the fine pattern does not just disappear; it shows up disguised as a false, slower pattern. This is aliasing. In images it looks like jagged edges and strange wavy patterns.

Moire patterns: The most famous aliasing effect is the moire pattern. When a newsreader on TV wears a finely striped shirt, the stripes can turn into swirling waves on screen, because the camera's pixel grid is too coarse for the stripes. You see the same when you take a phone photo of a computer screen: the pixel grid of the screen beats against the pixel grid of the camera. Scanning a printed newspaper photo, which is made of a regular grid of halftone dots, also produces moire. The cure is to blur slightly before sampling (an anti-aliasing filter, which many cameras build in), or to sample more densely. After the fact, notch filters in the frequency domain (lesson 12) can remove much of it.

Zooming is not more resolution: When you pinch-zoom a photo, the phone creates a bigger grid by inventing new pixels between old ones. This is interpolation (lesson 05). The image gets bigger but not more detailed; the information was fixed at sampling time. Police shows that "enhance" a blurry CCTV frame into a sharp face are fiction. Modern AI super-resolution can produce believable details, but they are guesses learned from other images, not truth, which is why they must not be used as evidence.

Dynamic range and contrast: The dynamic range of an imaging system is the ratio of the largest measurable intensity to the smallest detectable one. The upper limit is saturation: when a pixel collects so much light that it hits its maximum, everything brighter also reads 255, and detail is lost, like a white sky with no clouds. The lower limit is noise: in very dark areas the random variation is as large as the signal. Image contrast is the difference between the highest and lowest intensity in an image. An image that uses the full 0 to 255 range has high contrast; one squeezed into 100 to 140 looks flat and gray. HDR mode on phones merges several exposures to extend dynamic range.

Choosing M, N and k in practice: For a document scanner reading text, 300 dpi and 8 bits gray are plenty, and the final saved file can even be 1-bit after thresholding. For a medical CT slice, 512 x 512 with 12 bits or more is typical, because doctors care about small differences in tissue density. For a satellite tracking river erosion along the Padma, what matters is metres per pixel on the ground: a 10 m per pixel image cannot show a 3 m wide footpath. Always ask: what is the smallest object, and what is the smallest brightness difference, that I must see?

Real-life example 1, a passport photo kiosk: The government passport form needs a photo of a certain pixel size. A kiosk camera captures a large image, crops the face, and resamples it down to the required size. If it shrinks carelessly without first smoothing, fine patterns in clothing can alias into odd waves. Good software applies a small blur and then samples, which avoids moire and gives a clean, smaller image that meets the size limit for upload.

Real-life example 2, a mobile banking cheque deposit: Some banks let you deposit a cheque by photographing it. The bank's server needs to read the printed amount and the MICR line at the bottom. If you are too far away, each digit covers too few pixels: spatial resolution is too low and recognition fails. If the room is too bright and the paper saturates to 255, faint signatures disappear. That is why the app guides you to fill the frame and avoid glare: it is managing sampling and dynamic range for you.

Common mistakes: Mixing up sampling (where we measure) with quantization (how finely we round). Calling an image "high resolution" because it has many pixels, without saying how much area those pixels cover. Forgetting to divide by 8 when converting bits to bytes, or mixing 1,000 and 1,024 when converting to KB and MB. Believing zoom or interpolation adds real detail. Thinking more gray levels always help; beyond what the sensor's noise allows, extra bits only store noise.

What exams ask: Define sampling and quantization with a diagram of one scan line. Compute storage for given M, N, k. Explain false contouring and the checkerboard effect with an example. Define spatial and intensity resolution, dpi and line pairs. Explain aliasing and moire and how to reduce them. Discuss isopreference curves.

Recap: Sampling turns continuous positions into a grid; quantization turns continuous brightness into L = 2^k levels. Storage is b = M x N x k bits. Too few samples cause pixelation and aliasing such as moire; too few levels cause false contours. Resolution is meaningful only per unit distance. Dynamic range is limited by saturation and noise. Next lesson: once we have the grid, how do pixels relate to their neighbours, and what basic arithmetic can we do with whole images?
key_points: Sampling digitizes coordinates (the grid); quantization digitizes amplitude (the levels).
L = 2^k gray levels; storage b = M x N x k bits (1024 x 1024 x 8 bits = 1 MiB).
Spatial resolution is meaningful per unit distance (dpi, line pairs per mm); too few samples cause pixelation.
Too few gray levels cause false contouring in smooth areas, often visible around 16 levels or fewer.
Sampling below twice the highest spatial frequency causes aliasing, seen as jagged edges and moire patterns.
Zooming by interpolation enlarges an image but cannot add real detail lost at sampling.
Dynamic range is bounded by saturation at the top and noise at the bottom; contrast is the spread of intensities used.
lessons.tip: Do every storage problem in bits first, then divide by 8 for bytes, and write whether you mean 1,000 or 1,024 for KB and MB. Most lost marks in this chapter come from unit slips, not from the idea.
lessons.task: Take a photo of your laptop or TV screen with your phone and look for wavy coloured patterns. Then move closer and further and see how the pattern changes. Write two lines explaining it using sampling and aliasing.

quiz.q: Rounding each measured brightness to one of 16 allowed values is...
quiz.explain: Quantization digitizes amplitude; sampling digitizes position.

quiz.q: How many bytes does a 512 x 512 image with 8 bits per pixel need?
quiz.explain: 512 x 512 x 8 = 2,097,152 bits; divided by 8 that is 262,144 bytes (256 KiB).

quiz.q: Visible ridges in a smooth sky after reducing gray levels are called...
quiz.explain: Too few intensity levels turn smooth gradients into visible steps called false contours.

quiz.q: A striped shirt turns into swirling waves on TV. The cause is...
quiz.explain: The stripes are finer than the pixel grid can capture, so they alias into a false low-frequency pattern (moire).

quiz.q: A 6 x 4 inch print at 300 dpi needs how many pixels?

lessons.title: Pixel Relationships, Distances and Basic Image Operations
lessons.content:
Think of a housing colony in Mirpur laid out as a perfect grid of plots. Every plot has neighbours: the ones that share a wall on the north, south, east and west, and the ones that only touch at a corner. Whether two families count as "neighbours" depends on your rule, and that rule changes everything: who is in the same block, how far it is to walk, where the colony's boundary is. Pixels live in exactly such a grid. Before we filter, segment or measure anything, we need precise rules for who is next to whom, how to measure distance, and what arithmetic we may do with whole images. That is this lesson.

Coordinate convention: In most image processing books and libraries, the origin (0, 0) is the top-left pixel. The first coordinate counts rows going down and the second counts columns going right. So in a 480 x 640 image, the bottom-right pixel is at (479, 639). This is different from school graphs, where y goes up. NumPy and OpenCV index as img[row, col]. Many coding bugs in this course come from swapping these, especially when a function such as a drawing call takes (x, y) as (column, row) while the array uses [row, column]. Always check which one a function expects.

The 4-neighbours: A pixel p at (x, y) has two horizontal and two vertical neighbours: (x+1, y), (x-1, y), (x, y+1) and (x, y-1). This set is called N4(p). Each is at distance 1 from p. Example: for p = (5, 5), N4(p) is (6, 5), (4, 5), (5, 6) and (5, 4). If p is on the image border, some of these fall outside the image, and we must decide what to do about that, a problem that will come back as padding in lesson 08.

Diagonal and 8-neighbours: The four diagonal neighbours are (x+1, y+1), (x+1, y-1), (x-1, y+1) and (x-1, y-1), called ND(p). Together, N4(p) and ND(p) make the 8-neighbours N8(p). For p = (5, 5), ND(p) is (6, 6), (6, 4), (4, 6) and (4, 4). The familiar 3 x 3 window used by so many filters is simply p plus its 8-neighbours.

Adjacency: Neighbours are about position; adjacency also cares about values. Let V be the set of intensity values we consider "on". In a binary image V = {1}; in a gray image V might be {100, 101, ..., 150}, all pixels in a band of brightness. Two pixels p and q with values in V are 4-adjacent if q is in N4(p), and 8-adjacent if q is in N8(p). The rule you choose changes which pixels form one object.

The problem with 8-adjacency: Consider this 3 x 3 binary patch, rows from top: [0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]. The "on" pixels are at (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 1) and (2, 2). With 8-adjacency, the pixel (0, 2) can reach the centre (1, 1) in two ways: directly along the diagonal, or through (0, 1). Two different paths between the same pixels cause trouble for algorithms that trace boundaries or count holes, because the structure has an unwanted loop.

m-adjacency fixes it: Mixed adjacency (m-adjacency) says p and q with values in V are m-adjacent if q is in N4(p), or if q is in ND(p) and the set N4(p) intersected with N4(q) has no pixels whose values are in V. In words: use a diagonal link only when there is no 4-connected way around the corner. In our patch, (0, 2) and (1, 1) are diagonal, but they share the 4-neighbour (0, 1) which is on, so the diagonal link is dropped and only the path through (0, 1) remains. The centre (1, 1) and corner (2, 2) are diagonal and share 4-neighbours (1, 2) and (2, 1), both off, so that diagonal link stays. Now there is exactly one path. Simple, and it removes the ambiguity.

Paths, connectivity and components: A path from p to q is a sequence of pixels, each adjacent to the next, under the chosen adjacency. Its length is the number of steps. If the first and last pixels are the same, it is a closed path. Two pixels are connected in a set S if there is a path between them using only pixels of S. All pixels connected to a given pixel form a connected component. If S has only one component, it is a connected set. Counting the rice grains in a photo, the number of coins on a table, or the characters on a number plate all start by finding connected components (lesson 19 shows the labelling algorithm).

Regions and boundaries: A connected set of pixels is called a region. Two regions are adjacent if their union is connected. The boundary (border, contour) of a region is the set of its pixels that have at least one neighbour outside the region. An interesting catch: with 4-adjacency for the foreground, you should use 8-adjacency for the background, and vice versa, otherwise a diagonal line can both separate and not separate the background, a small paradox. Edges and boundaries are different ideas: a boundary is a property of a region; an edge is a place of sharp intensity change, which we find in lesson 20.

Distance measures: For pixels p = (x, y) and q = (s, t) there are three common distances. Euclidean distance De is the straight-line distance: square root of (x - s)^2 + (y - t)^2. City-block distance D4 is |x - s| + |y - t|, like walking on a grid of streets in Motijheel where you can only go along rows and columns. Chessboard distance D8 is the larger of |x - s| and |y - t|, like a king on a chessboard that can step diagonally at the same cost.

Distances worked: Let p = (2, 3) and q = (5, 7). The differences are 3 and 4. De = square root of (9 + 16) = 5. D4 = 3 + 4 = 7. D8 = max(3, 4) = 4. Always De and D8 are at most D4, and D8 is at most De. The pixels within D4 distance 1 of p are exactly N4(p) plus p, forming a diamond shape; those within D8 distance 1 form a 3 x 3 square, which is N8(p) plus p. D4 and D8 ignore pixel values; if you want the shortest path through only "on" pixels, the answer depends on the adjacency rule, and m-adjacency paths can be longer than simple distances suggest.

Element-wise vs matrix operations: Images are matrices, but most image operations are element-wise, also called array operations: pixel (i, j) of the result depends only on pixel (i, j) of the inputs. Worked: A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]]. The element-wise product is [[5, 12], [21, 32]]. The matrix product, as in linear algebra (deep-cse-2-5 lesson 06), is [[19, 22], [43, 50]], quite different. In NumPy, A * B is element-wise and A @ B is the matrix product. Unless a book says "matrix product", assume element-wise in image processing.

Linear vs nonlinear operators: An operator H is linear if H(a f1 + b f2) = a H(f1) + b H(f2) for any images f1, f2 and numbers a, b. Summing all pixels is linear. Taking the maximum is not. Worked: f1 = [[0, 2], [2, 3]], f2 = [[6, 5], [4, 7]], a = 1, b = -1. Left side: max of f1 - f2 = max of [[-6, -3], [-2, -4]] = -2. Right side: max(f1) - max(f2) = 3 - 7 = -4. Since -2 is not -4, max is nonlinear. Linear operators have a huge theory behind them (convolution, Fourier) which we use in lessons 08 to 12; nonlinear ones like the median filter are often better at keeping edges.

Arithmetic 1, averaging to reduce noise: Suppose you take K photos of the same still scene, each with independent random noise of zero mean and standard deviation sigma. If you average them pixel by pixel, the noise variance falls by a factor K and the standard deviation by the square root of K. Worked: sigma = 20 gray levels and K = 16 frames gives 20 / 4 = 5. Astronomers stack hundreds of frames of faint galaxies this way, and phone night modes do it in a second. It only works if the frames are aligned and the scene does not move.

Arithmetic 2, subtraction to see change: Subtracting two images shows what changed. In digital subtraction angiography (DSA), a doctor takes an X-ray, injects a contrast dye into the blood, and takes another. Subtracting the first from the second removes bones and tissue that did not change, leaving only the blood vessels filled with dye. Security cameras use the same trick: subtract a background image from the current frame, and only moving people or vehicles remain. Satellite change detection, such as new buildings near Purbachal, works the same way on images from two dates.

Arithmetic 3, multiplication and division: Multiplying an image by a mask of 1s and 0s keeps only a region of interest, for example only the face. Dividing an image by an estimate of the illumination pattern corrects shading, like the whiteboard example in lesson 02: if the left side gets half the light, dividing by the light pattern makes both sides equal. Division by zero must be avoided by adding a tiny number to the denominator.

Bringing results back to 0-255: Arithmetic can push values outside the 8-bit range. Subtraction can give -255 to 255, addition up to 510. A standard fix: first shift so the minimum is 0: fm = f - min(f). Then scale to the full range: fs = 255 x fm / max(fm). Worked: differences [-50, 0, 30, 150]. Shift: [0, 50, 80, 200]. Scale: 255 x [0, 50, 80, 200] / 200 = [0, 63.75, 102, 255], rounded to [0, 64, 102, 255]. Another common choice is clipping (saturating): anything below 0 becomes 0, above 255 becomes 255. Watch out: uint8 arithmetic in NumPy wraps around, so 250 + 10 becomes 4, not 260. Convert to a larger type first.

Set and logical operations: For binary images, treat the "on" pixels as a set. Union is OR: pixels on in either image. Intersection is AND: on in both. Complement is NOT: flip on and off. Difference A minus B: on in A but not in B. These are the building blocks of morphology (lessons 18 and 19). For gray images, the union of two images can be defined as the pixel-wise maximum and intersection as the pixel-wise minimum, which is exactly what grayscale morphology uses.

Real-life example 1, counting eggs on a tray: A poultry farm in Gazipur wants to count eggs on trays from a camera. After thresholding, the eggs are white blobs. Using 8-adjacency, two eggs that barely touch at a corner pixel might merge into one component, making the count wrong; using 4-adjacency, they stay separate. Engineers test both and choose the rule that matches reality, and often apply a small erosion (lesson 18) first so touching eggs separate.

Real-life example 2, a shop's CCTV: A small shop in New Market keeps a background image of the empty aisle taken at opening time. Every new frame minus the background gives a difference image. Pixels whose absolute difference exceeds 30 are marked as "changed". Connected components of changed pixels larger than a few hundred pixels are counted as people. Lights switching on change every pixel, so the system slowly updates its background with a running average to adapt.

Common mistakes: Swapping x and y between libraries. Using 8-adjacency for both foreground and background and getting paradoxes. Thinking D4, D8 and De give the same answer. Confusing element-wise and matrix products. Forgetting overflow and underflow with 8-bit integers. Averaging frames that are not aligned, which blurs the scene instead of cleaning it.

What exams ask: Define N4, ND, N8; 4-, 8- and m-adjacency, and show with a small binary grid why m-adjacency removes multiple paths. Compute De, D4 and D8 between two pixels. Find the shortest 4-, 8- or m-path between two pixels for a given V. Prove an operator is linear or nonlinear. Explain image averaging and DSA.

Recap: Pixels sit on a grid with origin at the top-left. N4, ND and N8 define neighbours; adjacency adds a value rule, and m-adjacency removes ambiguous diagonal paths. Paths give connectivity, components, regions and boundaries. De, D4 and D8 measure distance in different ways. Image operations are usually element-wise; linear ones obey superposition. Averaging reduces noise by the square root of K, subtraction reveals change, and results must be rescaled or clipped. Next lesson: moving pixels around, with geometric transformations and interpolation.
key_points: Origin is the top-left pixel; arrays are indexed [row, column].
N4 has 4 edge-sharing neighbours, ND 4 diagonal ones, N8 all 8.
m-adjacency uses a diagonal link only when no shared 4-neighbour is in V, removing ambiguous multiple paths.
For p = (2, 3), q = (5, 7): Euclidean 5, city-block D4 = 7, chessboard D8 = 4.
Image arithmetic is element-wise; an operator is linear if it obeys superposition (sum is linear, max is not).
Averaging K noisy aligned images cuts noise standard deviation by the square root of K; subtraction reveals change (DSA, CCTV).
Rescale results with fm = f - min f and fs = 255 fm / max fm, or clip; beware uint8 wraparound.
lessons.tip: When an adjacency or path question appears, redraw the grid large on paper and literally draw the allowed links with a pencil. Paths that look obvious in your head often break the m-adjacency rule.
lessons.task: On graph paper, mark a 5 x 5 binary pattern shaped like the letter X. Count how many connected components it has using 4-adjacency and then using 8-adjacency. Then pick two pixels and compute their De, D4 and D8 distances.

m-adjacency was introduced mainly to...
options: Remove ambiguous multiple paths that 8-adjacency creates
quiz.explain: With 8-adjacency two pixels can be linked both diagonally and around a corner; m-adjacency keeps only one.

quiz.q: Averaging 25 aligned frames with independent noise of standard deviation 10 leaves noise of about...
quiz.explain: Standard deviation falls by the square root of K: 10 / 5 = 2.

quiz.q: Which operator is nonlinear?
quiz.explain: max(a f1 + b f2) is generally not a max(f1) + b max(f2), as the worked example showed (-2 vs -4).

options: Taking the maximum of two images
Subtracting an image taken before the dye from one taken after

lessons.title: Geometric Transformations and Interpolation
lessons.content:
You photograph a page of your friend's class notes, but the phone was tilted, so the page looks like a trapezium, wider at the bottom. A scanner app turns it into a neat flat rectangle in a blink. Nothing about the ink changed; the app only moved pixels to new places. But moving pixels on a grid is trickier than it sounds, because new positions almost never land exactly on grid points. This lesson covers geometric transformations, which decide where each pixel goes, and interpolation, which decides what value to put there.

Two jobs in one: A geometric transformation of an image has two parts. First, a spatial transformation of coordinates: a rule that says point (x, y) of the input goes to point (x', y') of the output. Second, intensity interpolation: since the computed positions are usually not whole numbers, we must estimate the pixel value at those in-between places. Rotate, resize, straighten, warp: every one of them needs both parts. Getting the first part right but doing the second part badly gives jagged, blocky or blurry results.

Affine transformations: The most common family is the affine transform, which keeps straight lines straight and parallel lines parallel. In homogeneous coordinates (recall deep-cse-5-2 lesson 09), we write a point as (x, y, 1) and multiply by a 3 x 3 matrix whose last row is [0, 0, 1]. The top two rows hold six numbers: four for scaling, rotation and shear, and two for translation. Scaling by cx and cy: x' = cx x, y' = cy y. Rotation by angle theta: x' = x cos theta - y sin theta, y' = x sin theta + y cos theta. Translation: x' = x + tx, y' = y + ty. Shear (slant): x' = x + sv y, y' = y. Combining transforms is just multiplying their matrices, and the order matters, as you saw in graphics.

Rotation worked: Rotate the point (10, 0) by 30 degrees about the origin. cos 30 = 0.866 and sin 30 = 0.5. x' = 10 x 0.866 - 0 x 0.5 = 8.66 and y' = 10 x 0.5 + 0 x 0.866 = 5.0. So the point lands at (8.66, 5.0), which is not on the integer grid. That is the whole reason interpolation exists. Also note: rotating about the image centre, not the corner, means translate the centre to the origin, rotate, and translate back; the three matrices are multiplied into one.

Rotated images get bigger: When you rotate a W x H image by theta, the new bounding box is W |cos theta| + H |sin theta| wide and W |sin theta| + H |cos theta| tall. Worked: a 640 x 480 image rotated 30 degrees needs about 640 x 0.866 + 480 x 0.5 = 794 by 640 x 0.5 + 480 x 0.866 = 736 pixels. If you keep the output 640 x 480, the corners are cut off; if you enlarge it, the empty triangles at the corners must be filled with a background colour such as black.

Forward mapping: The obvious approach is forward mapping: go through each input pixel, compute where it goes, and put its value there. Problem one: several input pixels may land on the same output pixel, and you must decide what to do. Problem two, worse: some output pixels get no input pixel at all, leaving holes. Example: scale a 3 x 3 image by 2 into a 6 x 6 output; input (1, 1) goes to (2, 2), input (1, 2) goes to (2, 4), and output (2, 3) is never written. The enlarged image looks like a sieve.

Inverse mapping: The standard solution is inverse mapping: go through each output pixel, apply the inverse transform to find which input position it came from, and interpolate the input there. Every output pixel gets exactly one value, so there are no holes and no overlaps. Worked: for a 2x enlargement, the inverse is division by 2, so output pixel (5, 7) comes from input position (2.5, 3.5), which sits between four input pixels. For the 30 degree rotation, output point (8.66, 5.0) maps back by rotating -30 degrees to (10, 0). Libraries such as OpenCV's warpAffine use inverse mapping internally.

Nearest-neighbour interpolation: The simplest rule: take the value of the input pixel closest to the computed position. For (2.3, 3.8) that is pixel (2, 4). It is very fast and never creates new values, which matters for label images where each value is a class number and averaging "class 2" and "class 4" into "class 3" would be nonsense. But on photos it produces blocky staircases when enlarging and can break thin lines when shrinking or rotating. Pixel-art games use it on purpose to keep the chunky look.

Bilinear interpolation: Bilinear interpolation uses the four nearest pixels and blends them by distance. Think of it as two straight-line interpolations across, then one down. Worked: four pixels around the target: top-left 10, top-right 20, bottom-left 30, bottom-right 40. The target is 0.6 of the way across and 0.3 of the way down. Top row: 10 + 0.6 x (20 - 10) = 16. Bottom row: 30 + 0.6 x (40 - 30) = 36. Down between them: 16 + 0.3 x (36 - 16) = 22. So the new pixel value is 22. As a formula, bilinear interpolation fits v(x, y) = a x + b y + c x y + d through the four neighbours. It gives smooth results at modest cost and is the default in many apps.

Bicubic interpolation: Bicubic uses the 16 nearest pixels (a 4 x 4 block) and fits a smooth cubic surface, with 16 coefficients. It keeps fine detail better and gives sharper enlargements than bilinear, which is why photo editors like it for resizing. It is slower, and it can overshoot near strong edges, creating thin light or dark halos, because cubic curves can bend above the highest neighbour or below the lowest. Results must then be clipped to 0 to 255.

Comparing the three: Enlarge a photo of a Bangla signboard by 4. Nearest neighbour gives blocky letters with staircase edges. Bilinear gives smooth but slightly soft letters. Bicubic gives the sharpest letters with a little halo around strokes. Speed goes the other way: nearest is fastest, then bilinear, then bicubic. Choose by purpose: masks and labels use nearest; previews and real-time video often use bilinear; final quality resizing uses bicubic or better kernels such as Lanczos.

Zooming and shrinking: Zooming (enlarging) means oversampling: creating more pixels than the original had, using interpolation to fill them. Shrinking means undersampling: keeping fewer pixels. Shrinking has its own danger: if you simply keep every second row and column, fine patterns alias into moire, as you saw in lesson 03. The safe way is to smooth first (for example average 2 x 2 blocks or apply a Gaussian blur, lesson 09) and then sample. Many libraries offer an "area" interpolation mode for shrinking that does exactly this averaging.

Image registration: Often we need to align two images of the same scene, taken at different times, from different angles or by different sensors. This is image registration. Doctors align an MRI and a CT of the same patient; satellite analysts align this year's and last year's images before subtracting them. The usual approach uses tie points (control points): features whose positions are known in both images, such as road crossings or corners of buildings. Each pair gives two equations. An affine transform has six unknowns, so three point pairs are the minimum; in practice we use many more and solve by least squares (deep-cse-2-5 lesson 22), which averages out small errors in picking points.

Perspective (projective) transforms: A tilted page photographed by a phone is not just an affine change: parallel lines of the page meet towards a vanishing point, so a rectangle becomes a general quadrilateral. This needs a projective transform, also called a homography, which in homogeneous coordinates is a full 3 x 3 matrix with 8 free parameters (the ninth is just a scale). Four point pairs, the four corners of the page, are enough to find it. Then inverse mapping with bilinear interpolation produces the flat page. This is exactly the step inside document scanner apps.

The scanner pipeline worked: The app finds the four page corners in the photo, say at (120, 80), (900, 60), (980, 1250) and (60, 1300) in (column, row). It decides on an output size, for example an A4-shaped 1240 x 1754 image. It computes the homography mapping output corners (0, 0), (1239, 0), (1239, 1753) and (0, 1753) back to those four photo corners. For each of the 2.17 million output pixels it applies the matrix, divides by the third homogeneous coordinate, and interpolates bilinearly. The result looks as if it had been scanned flat.

Real-life example 1, Google Maps style imagery: Aerial and satellite photos of Dhaka are taken from different angles and positions. To build a single seamless map, each photo is registered to ground control points with known GPS coordinates and warped so that roads line up across photo boundaries. Bilinear or bicubic interpolation keeps roads smooth instead of jagged.

Real-life example 2, fixing a crooked National ID card scan: A government office receives thousands of NID card photos with small rotations of a few degrees. Before reading the text, software estimates the rotation angle from the direction of the card's long edges, rotates the image back about its centre with inverse mapping and bilinear interpolation, and crops. Text recognition accuracy jumps once lines of text are perfectly horizontal.

Common mistakes: Using forward mapping and getting holes. Rotating about the corner instead of the centre, so the image swings out of frame. Shrinking without smoothing and getting moire. Using bilinear or bicubic on label masks and creating fake class values. Forgetting that bicubic can overshoot past 0 or 255. Mixing (x, y) and (row, column) order when building the matrix, which rotates the wrong way or flips the image. Using only three badly chosen tie points that lie almost in a straight line, which makes the system unstable.

What exams ask: Write the affine matrices for scaling, rotation, translation and shear and compose them. Explain forward vs inverse mapping and why inverse mapping is preferred. Compute a bilinear interpolation value from four neighbours. Compare nearest, bilinear and bicubic. Explain image registration with tie points and how many points an affine or projective transform needs.

Recap: Geometric transformation means mapping coordinates and then interpolating intensities. Affine transforms (scale, rotate, translate, shear) use 3 x 3 homogeneous matrices; projective transforms handle perspective with 8 parameters. Inverse mapping avoids holes. Nearest is fast and blocky, bilinear smooth, bicubic sharpest but slower. Shrink only after smoothing. Registration aligns images using tie points and least squares. Next lesson: instead of moving pixels, we change their values with intensity transformations.
key_points: A geometric transform = spatial mapping of coordinates + intensity interpolation at non-integer positions.
Affine transforms (scale, rotate, translate, shear) use a 3 x 3 homogeneous matrix with 6 parameters; order of composition matters.
Forward mapping leaves holes and overlaps; inverse mapping visits every output pixel and is the standard method.
Nearest-neighbour is fast but blocky; bilinear blends 4 neighbours; bicubic uses 16 and is sharper but slower and can overshoot.
Bilinear worked: corners 10, 20, 30, 40 at 0.6 across and 0.3 down give 16, 36, then 22.
Shrink only after smoothing to avoid aliasing; zooming cannot add real detail.
Registration aligns images with tie points: at least 3 pairs for affine, 4 for projective (homography), solved by least squares.
lessons.tip: For any geometric transform question, first decide the direction: are you mapping input to output or output back to input? Writing the inverse matrix explicitly saves you from half the usual mistakes.
lessons.task: Write a 2 x 2 patch of pixel values on paper, such as 50, 100 / 150, 200. Compute bilinear values at five positions inside it (centre, quarter points). Then do the same with nearest neighbour and compare which looks smoother.

quiz.q: Why is inverse mapping preferred over forward mapping?
options: It is the only way to rotate
Every output pixel gets exactly one value, so there are no holes
quiz.explain: Going from each output pixel back to the input guarantees full coverage without holes or overlaps.

quiz.q: Bilinear interpolation between 10 (top-left), 20 (top-right), 30 (bottom-left), 40 (bottom-right) at the exact centre gives...
quiz.explain: Top row at 0.5: 15, bottom row: 35, halfway down: 25.

quiz.q: Which interpolation should be used to resize a segmentation label mask?
quiz.explain: Nearest-neighbour never creates new values, so class labels stay valid.

quiz.q: How many point pairs are needed at minimum to find a projective (homography) transform?
quiz.explain: A homography has 8 free parameters and each pair gives 2 equations, so 4 pairs.

lessons.title: Intensity Transformations: Negatives, Log, Gamma and Contrast Stretching
lessons.content:
When you drag the brightness slider in a photo app, every pixel in the picture changes at once, and each pixel's new value depends only on its own old value. A pixel of 100 becomes, say, 130, wherever it is and whatever its neighbours are. This is the simplest kind of image processing, called point processing or intensity transformation, and it is surprisingly powerful. With one small function you can make a negative, reveal details hidden in shadows, correct a display, stretch a dull image to full contrast, or pick out only the bright bones in an X-ray.

The idea: Write the input gray level as r and the output as s. An intensity transformation is s = T(r), applied to every pixel. T is just a function from 0..L-1 to 0..L-1, so for 8-bit images it can be stored as a table of 256 entries called a look-up table (LUT). To process a 12 megapixel image, you compute the 256 entries once and then simply look up each pixel, which is extremely fast. Because each output pixel depends on a 1 x 1 neighbourhood, this is the smallest possible spatial operation; lesson 08 grows the neighbourhood.

Reading a transformation curve: Draw r on the horizontal axis and s on the vertical. The straight diagonal line s = r is the identity, changing nothing. Wherever the curve is steeper than the diagonal, it stretches that input range over a bigger output range, increasing contrast there. Wherever it is flatter, it compresses that range, reducing contrast. Curves above the diagonal brighten, curves below darken. Learning to read these curves is the key to this whole lesson, and photo apps literally show you the "Curves" tool for this reason.

Image negative: The negative is s = L - 1 - r. For 8-bit images, s = 255 - r. Worked: r = 30 becomes 225, r = 200 becomes 55, 0 becomes 255. Dark becomes light and light becomes dark. Why bother? The eye is better at seeing gray detail on a light background than in a large dark area. Radiologists sometimes view mammograms as negatives so that small white or gray structures inside dark tissue become easier to inspect. It is also how old film negatives were turned into prints.

Log transformation: The log transform is s = c log(1 + r), where c is a constant. It expands dark values and compresses bright values. The 1 is added so that r = 0 gives log 1 = 0 instead of minus infinity. To map 0..255 to 0..255 with the natural log, c = 255 / ln 256 = about 45.99. Worked: r = 10 gives 45.99 x ln 11 = about 110, and r = 100 gives 45.99 x ln 101 = about 212. So the dark value 10 jumped to 110, while 100 only moved to 212. A dark corner suddenly shows detail, and bright parts squeeze together.

Where log shines, Fourier spectra: The classic use is displaying the Fourier spectrum (lesson 11). Its values can range from 0 to about 1.5 million in a typical image. Scaled linearly into 0..255, only the brightest few points are visible and the rest is black. Applying log10(1 + r) squeezes that range into about 0 to 6.2, and then scaling by 255 / 6.2, about 41, gives a picture where the whole spectrum is visible. The inverse log (exponential) does the opposite, which is rarely needed for display.

Power-law (gamma) transformation: The power-law transform is s = c r^gamma, with r and s normalised to 0..1. With gamma less than 1 the curve rises fast at first, like log, brightening dark areas. With gamma greater than 1 it starts flat and rises late, darkening and stretching bright areas. Unlike the log, you can tune gamma continuously to get a whole family of curves. Gamma = 1 is the identity.

Gamma worked: Take r = 0.2 (about 51 out of 255). With gamma = 0.4: 0.2^0.4 = 0.525, about 134. With gamma = 2.5: 0.2^2.5 = 0.018, about 5. Now r = 0.8 (204): gamma 0.4 gives 0.915, about 233; gamma 2.5 gives 0.572, about 146. So gamma 0.4 lifts dark pixels a lot (51 to 134) and bright pixels a little (204 to 233): good for an underexposed photo. Gamma 2.5 crushes darks (51 to 5) and stretches brights: good for a washed-out, too-bright aerial image where detail is hiding in the highlights.

Gamma correction: Many displays historically respond with roughly a power law: the light they emit is about the input voltage raised to a power near 2.2. Fed a value of 0.5, such a screen shows only 0.5^2.2 = 0.22 of full brightness, so images look too dark. Gamma correction pre-distorts the image with the inverse power, 1/2.2 = 0.45: 0.5^0.45 = 0.73, about 186. After the screen's own power law, the viewer sees 0.5 as intended. This is why standard image files such as sRGB JPEGs store gamma-encoded values, and why doing maths like averaging directly on those values is not physically exact.

Piecewise-linear contrast stretching: Sometimes a simple shape is best. Contrast stretching maps a narrow input range onto the full output range. Choose two control points (r1, s1) and (r2, s2) and connect them with straight lines. The most common case sets r1 to the minimum and r2 to the maximum intensity in the image, s1 = 0 and s2 = 255. Worked: a foggy photo of Cox's Bazar beach only uses values 60 to 160. The stretch is s = (r - 60) x 255 / 100. Then r = 60 becomes 0, r = 160 becomes 255, and r = 100 becomes 102. The dull 100-level range now spans all 256 levels, and the image looks clear.

Thresholding as a limit: If you squeeze r1 and r2 together at a single value m, with s1 = 0 and s2 = 255, the stretch becomes a step: s = 0 if r < m and s = 255 if r >= m. This is thresholding, which turns a gray image into a binary one. A scanned page with dark ink and light paper is a natural candidate. Choosing m well is a whole topic of its own, done in lesson 21 with methods like Otsu's.

Intensity-level slicing: Sometimes you want to highlight a specific band of intensities. Approach one: set all pixels in the band [A, B] to white and everything else to black, giving a binary map of that band. Approach two: brighten pixels in the band but leave others unchanged, so context remains. Worked: in an angiogram, blood vessels with contrast dye fall around 150 to 200. Setting those to 255 while keeping others as they are makes the vessels stand out against the anatomy.

CT windowing, slicing in practice: CT scanners record values in Hounsfield units: about -1000 for air, 0 for water, and several hundred to over a thousand for bone. A screen can only show 256 levels, so doctors choose a "window". A typical soft-tissue window has level (centre) 40 and width 400, so values from 40 - 200 = -160 to 40 + 200 = 240 are stretched linearly onto 0..255; anything below is black, anything above is white. A value of 100 maps to (100 + 160) x 255 / 400, about 166. A bone window uses a much wider range. This is contrast stretching plus clipping, exactly as above, used every day in hospitals.

Bit-plane slicing: An 8-bit pixel is made of 8 bits, so an image can be split into 8 binary images called bit planes, plane 1 holding the least significant bit and plane 8 the most significant. Worked: the pixel 194 is 11000010 in binary, so it contributes 1 to planes 8, 7 and 2 and 0 to the others. The top planes carry the large structure of the image; the bottom planes look like random noise. Keeping only planes 8 to 5 rebuilds 194 as 128 + 64 = 192, almost the same. This shows how many bits are really needed and is a stepping stone to compression, and the lowest planes are where simple steganography hides secret data, because changing them is invisible to the eye.

Choosing a transformation: Is the image dark overall with detail in shadows? Try gamma less than 1 or log. Is it washed out with detail in highlights? Try gamma greater than 1. Does it use only a narrow band of levels? Contrast stretch. Do you need only one object type that has a known brightness range? Slice it. Is the output for a display that already applies gamma? Apply gamma correction. And always remember that a point operation cannot separate two objects that have exactly the same gray level; for that you need neighbourhoods, edges or colour.

Real-life example 1, Facebook profile photo at a wedding: The stage lights make your face bright but the background guests are dark. A gamma of about 0.6 lifts the guests out of the shadows while only slightly brightening your face. Too low a gamma, say 0.3, makes the image look flat and grayish, because it compresses the bright end too much. Photo apps' "Shadows" sliders are essentially local versions of this idea.

Real-life example 2, reading old land records: Land offices in Bangladesh are digitising old khatian and mouza documents. Many scans are yellowed with faded ink, using only values 120 to 210. A contrast stretch maps 120 to 0 and 210 to 255, making ink darker and paper whiter. A gentle gamma above 1 then darkens faded strokes further, and finally a threshold produces clean black-and-white pages for text recognition.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to normalise r to 0..1 before applying a power law, which gives huge numbers. Mixing up which gamma brightens (less than 1) and which darkens (greater than 1). Forgetting to clip after contrast stretching values outside [r1, r2]. Thinking a point operation can add detail; it only re-maps existing levels, and if two areas share one gray level they stay identical. Applying a LUT to a 16-bit image as if it were 8-bit.

What exams ask: Sketch the curves for negative, log, inverse log, nth power and nth root, and explain each use. Compute outputs for given r, c and gamma. Design a piecewise-linear contrast stretch for given control points. Explain gamma correction for displays. Write the bit planes of a given pixel value and explain what the planes show.

Recap: Point processing applies s = T(r) to each pixel and can be stored as a 256-entry LUT. The negative flips intensities. Log and gamma less than 1 brighten darks; gamma greater than 1 stretches brights. Gamma correction pre-compensates display response. Contrast stretching maps a narrow range to the full range, and its limit is thresholding. Intensity slicing highlights a band, CT windowing is an everyday example, and bit-plane slicing shows which bits carry information. Next lesson: choosing T automatically from the image's own histogram.
key_points: Intensity transformation s = T(r) acts on each pixel alone and can be stored as a 256-entry look-up table.
Negative: s = L - 1 - r (30 becomes 225 for 8-bit).
Log s = c log(1 + r) expands darks and compresses brights; ideal for displaying Fourier spectra.
Power law s = c r^gamma: gamma < 1 brightens darks (0.2 to 0.525 for gamma 0.4), gamma > 1 stretches brights.
Gamma correction applies 1/2.2 = 0.45 so a display with gamma 2.2 shows intended brightness.
Contrast stretching maps [r1, r2] to [0, 255]; thresholding is its limit; CT windowing (level 40, width 400) is stretching plus clipping.
Bit-plane slicing splits 8-bit pixels into 8 binary planes; the top planes carry most structure (194 = 11000010).
lessons.tip: Always sketch the transformation curve next to the diagonal s = r before computing anything. Where it is steeper, contrast rises; where flatter, it falls. One sketch answers most theory questions in this chapter.
