lessons.task: Open your phone's photo editor and find the Curves or Tone tool. Make an S-shaped curve and an inverted S, and note what each does to contrast. Then compute by hand the gamma 0.5 and gamma 2 outputs for pixel values 64, 128 and 192.

quiz.q: For an 8-bit image, the negative of pixel value 70 is...
Which transformation is best for showing a Fourier spectrum with values from 0 to over a million?
quiz.explain: The log compresses the huge range so both small and large values become visible.

quiz.q: A normalised pixel 0.2 after gamma = 2.5 becomes about...
quiz.explain: 0.2^2.5 is about 0.018; gamma greater than 1 darkens low values strongly.

quiz.q: A contrast stretch maps 60 to 0 and 160 to 255 linearly. What does 110 become?
Pixel 194 in binary is 11000010. Keeping only the top 4 bit planes gives...
quiz.explain: The top four bits 1100 give 128 + 64 = 192.

lessons.title: Histogram Processing: Equalisation, Matching and Local Enhancement
lessons.content:
Imagine your class teacher wants to know how the whole class did in a maths test without reading all 60 answer scripts. She draws a simple bar chart: how many students got 0-10, how many got 11-20, and so on. One glance tells her if the test was too hard (most bars on the left) or too easy (most bars on the right). An image histogram is exactly that chart, but for pixels. Instead of marks it counts brightness levels, and one glance tells you if a photo is too dark, too bright or flat and dull.

Where this sits: lesson 06 showed point operations s = T(r), where you pick a curve such as a gamma curve and push every pixel through it. The hard part was choosing the curve by hand. This lesson lets the image choose its own curve. By reading the histogram, the computer can build a transformation automatically. We will cover the histogram itself, histogram equalisation with a full worked example, histogram matching (specification), local histogram processing and CLAHE, and finally using simple statistics like mean and variance to enhance only the parts that need it.

What a histogram is: take an image with L possible gray levels, numbered 0 to L-1 (for an 8-bit image L = 256). For each level rk, count how many pixels have exactly that value. Call the count nk. The histogram is the list h(rk) = nk. If you divide every count by the total number of pixels M x N, you get the normalised histogram p(rk) = nk / MN. These numbers add up to 1, so p(rk) is simply the probability that a randomly chosen pixel has level rk. This link to probability (deep-cse-2-6) is the key idea of the whole lesson.

A tiny example: a 4 x 4 image with values 0 0 1 1 / 0 1 1 2 / 1 2 2 3 / 2 3 3 3 has 16 pixels. Counting gives n0 = 3, n1 = 5, n2 = 4, n3 = 4. So p(0) = 3/16, p(1) = 5/16, p(2) = 4/16 and p(3) = 4/16, which add to 16/16 = 1. Notice the histogram throws away position. It does not know where the pixels are, only how many there are of each level. Two completely different images (a checkerboard and a half-black half-white picture) can have the very same histogram.

Reading histogram shapes: a dark image has its bars crowded at the low end (left). A bright, washed-out image has them crowded at the high end (right). A low-contrast image, like a photo taken through fog or a faded old document, has all its bars squeezed into a narrow band in the middle. A high-contrast image spreads its bars across the whole range from 0 to 255. Phone camera apps show a live histogram in pro mode for exactly this reason: a spike pressed against the right wall means highlights are clipped to pure white and detail there is lost forever.

The idea behind equalisation: a picture usually looks best when its pixels use the whole range of levels fairly evenly. So the goal is a transformation that takes a crowded histogram and spreads it out until it is roughly flat. The trick comes from probability. If you pass a random variable through its own cumulative distribution function (CDF), the result is uniformly distributed. For continuous images, s = T(r) = (L-1) times the integral of p(w) from 0 to r gives a perfectly flat output histogram.

The discrete formula: for real digital images we replace the integral by a running sum. sk = (L-1) x (p(r0) + p(r1) + ... + p(rk)). In words: for each level, add up the probabilities of all levels up to and including it, multiply by L-1, and round to the nearest integer. The result is a look-up table. Each old level rk maps to a new level sk. Because the running sum only goes up, the mapping is monotonic: a darker pixel never becomes brighter than a pixel that was brighter before. That keeps the picture looking natural.

Worked example, step 1: take the classic textbook case of a 64 x 64 image (4096 pixels) with 3 bits per pixel, so L = 8 levels from 0 to 7. The counts are n0 = 790, n1 = 1023, n2 = 850, n3 = 656, n4 = 329, n5 = 245, n6 = 122, n7 = 81. These add to 4096. Dividing by 4096 gives p = 0.19, 0.25, 0.21, 0.16, 0.08, 0.06, 0.03, 0.02. Most pixels are in the four darkest levels, so this is a dark image.

Worked example, step 2: multiply the running sums by L-1 = 7. s0 = 7 x 0.193 = 1.35. s1 = 7 x (0.193 + 0.250) = 3.10. Continuing the running sum gives s2 = 4.55, s3 = 5.67, s4 = 6.23, s5 = 6.65, s6 = 6.86 and s7 = 7.00. Rounding to the nearest level gives the look-up table 0 to 1, 1 to 3, 2 to 5, 3 to 6, 4 to 6, 5 to 7, 6 to 7, 7 to 7.

Worked example, step 3, the new histogram: level 1 now has 790 pixels, level 3 has 1023, level 5 has 850, level 6 has 656 + 329 = 985, and level 7 has 245 + 122 + 81 = 448. As fractions that is about 0.19, 0.25, 0.21, 0.24 and 0.11. The dark pile has been pushed up and spread across the range. The output is not perfectly flat, though. Levels 0, 2 and 4 are now empty, and some levels got merged.

Why the result is not flat: equalisation can only move whole groups of pixels. All 1023 pixels at level 1 must go to the same new level, because the method is a point operation and cannot split them. So in the discrete case you never get an exactly flat histogram; you get one that is spread out and roughly uniform. Rounding also merges nearby levels (4, 5, 6 and 7 collapsed into two levels), which can lose a little fine detail. This is a typical exam question: explain why discrete equalisation is only approximately uniform.

Strengths and dangers of equalisation: it is fully automatic, cheap (one pass to count, one pass through a table) and needs no parameter. It works wonders on dim X-rays, foggy CCTV frames and scanned old photos. But it is blind. If an image has a huge flat background, like a dark sky or a black X-ray border, those many pixels dominate the CDF and the method spends most of the output range on the background, often boosting noise. It can also make a pleasant photo look harsh. Use it when you want detail to become visible, not when you want beauty.

Histogram matching (specification): sometimes you do not want a flat histogram but a particular shape, for example to make satellite images taken on two different days look alike, or to match photos from two cameras. Histogram matching transforms an image so its histogram approximates a chosen target. The method uses equalisation twice. First equalise the input: rk to sk. Then compute the equalisation function G of the target histogram: zq to G(zq). Finally, for each sk, find the target level zq whose G(zq) is closest to sk. The chain rk to sk to zq is the answer.

Matching worked: continue the 8-level example. Suppose the target histogram is p(z) = 0, 0, 0, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30, 0.20, 0.15 for z = 0 to 7. Its equalisation values are G = 7 x running sum = 0, 0, 0, 1.05, 2.45, 4.55, 5.95, 7.00, which round to 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7. Our input mapped to s = 1, 3, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7. Now look up each s in G. s = 1 matches G(3) = 1, so z = 3. s = 3 is closest to G(4) = 2, so z = 4. s = 5 gives z = 5, s = 6 gives z = 6, s = 7 gives z = 7. Final table: 0 to 3, 1 to 4, 2 to 5, 3 to 6, 4 to 6, 5 to 7, 6 to 7, 7 to 7.

Global vs local processing: everything so far is global, one table for the whole picture. But a photo of a room with a bright window has a dark corner and a glaring window at the same time. One global curve cannot fix both. Local histogram processing slides a neighbourhood, say 7 x 7, over the image, computes the histogram of just that window, equalises it, and replaces only the centre pixel. Then it moves one pixel and repeats. Details hidden in small dark regions come out clearly, because each area gets its own curve.

CLAHE, the practical version: plain local equalisation is slow and boosts noise badly in flat regions, since a nearly uniform patch has a spiky histogram that equalisation stretches wildly. Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalisation (CLAHE) fixes both problems. It splits the image into tiles, for example an 8 x 8 grid of tiles. In each tile it clips the histogram at a limit and spreads the clipped excess evenly over all bins, which caps how steep the mapping curve can get. Then it blends the tile mappings with bilinear interpolation so no tile borders show. OpenCV offers it as createCLAHE with a clip limit and tile size, and medical and underwater imaging use it a lot.

Histogram statistics: the histogram also gives cheap statistics. The mean intensity is m = sum of rk x p(rk), a measure of average brightness. The variance is sum of (rk - m) squared x p(rk), and its square root, the standard deviation, measures contrast. For the 8-level example the mean is about 2.08 out of 7 (dark) and the variance about 3.0. Higher variance means pixels are spread out, so more contrast. You can compute these for the whole image (global) or for each neighbourhood (local).

Enhancement with local statistics: a classic method brightens only pixels that are in dark, low-contrast areas while leaving the rest alone. For each pixel compute the local mean and local standard deviation in a 3 x 3 window. If the local mean is below a fraction k0 of the global mean (the area is dark) and the local standard deviation is between k1 and k2 times the global one (there is some detail but not a strong edge), multiply the pixel by a constant E, such as 4. Otherwise leave it unchanged. The SEM image of a filament in the Gonzalez and Woods textbook uses exactly this rule to reveal hidden structure without blowing out the bright parts.

Real-life example 1, a chest X-ray at a district hospital: an old film X-ray scanned at a Sylhet clinic looks gray and dim. Step 1, the software computes the histogram and sees most pixels squeezed between levels 60 and 120. Step 2, global equalisation stretches them, but the large black border steals much of the range. Step 3, the technician switches to CLAHE with an 8 x 8 grid and a modest clip limit. Now the rib edges and lung texture are clear and the noise in flat areas stays calm. The doctor zooms in and sees a small shadow that was invisible before. The data did not change; only how levels are spread did.

Real-life example 2, matching drone photos of a char: an NGO flies a drone over a river char near Gaibandha twice, once in the morning and once in the cloudy afternoon, to map erosion. The afternoon photos are darker, so stitching them together shows an ugly line where the brightness jumps. They use histogram matching: the morning mosaic's histogram becomes the target, and every afternoon photo is matched to it. After matching, the two sets blend smoothly and the change-detection step (subtraction, lesson 04) shows real land loss, not lighting differences.

Where students go wrong: first, forgetting to normalise. You must divide counts by MN before the running sum, or your sk values will be huge. Second, forgetting to multiply by L-1 or multiplying by L instead. Third, not rounding, or rounding down instead of to the nearest level. Fourth, thinking equalisation gives a perfectly flat histogram in the discrete case. Fifth, believing two images with the same histogram must look alike. Exams love: equalise a given small histogram and draw the new one, perform matching from a given target, explain why equalisation is not exactly uniform, and compare global equalisation with CLAHE.

Quick checks you can do in your head: the last value s(L-1) must always be exactly L-1, because the running sum of all probabilities is 1. If your table ends anywhere else, you made an arithmetic mistake. The mapping must never go down. And the number of pixels never changes; only the levels move, so the counts in the new histogram must still add to MN, here 790 + 1023 + 850 + 985 + 448 = 4096.

Recap: a histogram counts how many pixels sit at each gray level and, normalised, behaves like a probability distribution. Equalisation uses the running sum (CDF) times L-1 as a look-up table to spread levels out automatically. Matching chains two equalisations to reach any target shape. Local methods and CLAHE handle uneven lighting while controlling noise, and mean and variance let you enhance only where it is needed. Next lesson (08) moves from single-pixel operations to neighbourhood operations: spatial filtering.
key_points: A histogram h(rk) = nk counts pixels at each level; p(rk) = nk/MN makes it a probability distribution.
Histograms ignore position, so very different images can share one histogram.
Equalisation: sk = (L-1) x running sum of p(rj) up to k, rounded; the last value is always L-1.
Discrete equalisation is only roughly flat because whole groups of pixels move together and levels merge.
Histogram matching equalises input and target, then maps each sk to the zq with the closest G(zq).
Local equalisation and CLAHE (tiles, clip limit, bilinear blending) fix uneven lighting without exploding noise.
Local mean and standard deviation let you enhance only dark, low-contrast regions.
lessons.tip: Always do the running-sum table in columns: rk, nk, p(rk), running sum, times L-1, rounded. Check that the last row equals L-1 and that the new counts still add to MN.
lessons.task: Take a 4 x 4 image of your own using only levels 0 to 3 (write 16 numbers on paper). Draw its histogram, equalise it with sk = 3 x running sum, and write the new 4 x 4 image. Does it look more spread out?

quiz.q: For an 8-bit image, what is the normalised histogram value p(rk)?
options: nk divided by the total number of pixels MN
The running sum of all counts
quiz.explain: Dividing each count by MN turns it into the probability that a pixel has level rk.

quiz.q: In histogram equalisation with L levels, the last mapped value s(L-1) is always...
quiz.explain: The running sum of all probabilities is 1, and 1 x (L-1) = L-1.

quiz.q: Why is discrete histogram equalisation usually not perfectly flat?
options: All pixels at one level must move together, and rounding can merge levels
Because colour images have three channels
quiz.explain: A point operation cannot split a group of equal pixels, so bins move as wholes and some merge.

quiz.q: Which technique would you use to make afternoon drone photos look like morning ones?
quiz.explain: Matching reshapes one image's histogram towards a chosen target histogram.

quiz.q: What does the clip limit in CLAHE do?
options: It caps each tile's histogram so contrast and noise are not boosted too much
It sets the number of tiles to one
It converts the image to binary
quiz.explain: Clipping the histogram limits the slope of the mapping, which controls noise amplification in flat areas.

lessons.title: Spatial Filtering Fundamentals: Kernels, Correlation and Convolution
lessons.content:
Think of a neighbourhood tea stall gossip. If you want to know how a new family on your street really is, you do not judge from one person; you ask the people living around them and mix their opinions. Spatial filtering does the same for pixels. To decide the new value of one pixel, it looks at that pixel and its neighbours, mixes their values with fixed weights, and writes the result into the output. Blurring, sharpening and edge finding all come from this single idea.

Where this sits: lessons 06 and 07 changed every pixel on its own, s = T(r). Those point operations cannot remove noise or find edges, because noise and edges are about how a pixel differs from its neighbours. This lesson builds the machinery of neighbourhood processing: kernels, correlation, convolution, padding, output size, separable kernels and the link to the frequency domain. Lesson 09 then uses it for smoothing and lesson 10 for sharpening, so here we focus on how the sliding works, not on which kernel to choose.

The two ingredients: a spatial filter has a neighbourhood, usually a small odd-sized square such as 3 x 3, 5 x 5 or 7 x 7 centred on the pixel, and an operation done on the pixels inside it. If the operation is a weighted sum, the filter is linear. The weights sit in a small matrix called a kernel; older books also call it a mask, template or window. Odd sizes are used so that there is a clear centre pixel. A 3 x 3 kernel has 9 weights, which we label w(-1,-1) up to w(1,1), with w(0,0) at the centre.

How the sliding works: place the kernel centre on pixel (x, y). Multiply each kernel weight by the image pixel under it. Add up all the products. That sum is the output g(x, y). Then slide the kernel one pixel to the right and repeat, row by row, until every pixel has been visited. Written as a formula for a 3 x 3 kernel: g(x, y) = sum over s and t from -1 to 1 of w(s, t) x f(x + s, y + t). The output is written to a new image, never back into the input, otherwise later pixels would use already-changed values.

Correlation: the formula above, where the kernel is placed as it is and multiplied pixel by pixel, is called correlation. It answers the question how much does this patch look like the kernel. That is why correlation is used for template matching: slide a picture of the digit 7 over a scanned form, and the place with the highest correlation is where a 7 is.

Convolution: convolution is almost the same, but the kernel is first rotated by 180 degrees (flipped left-right and top-bottom). The formula becomes g(x, y) = sum of w(s, t) x f(x - s, y - t). This is the same convolution you met in Signals & Systems (deep-cse-3-7 lessons 09-11) and DSP (deep-cse-5-7 lesson 07), just in two dimensions. Convolution has nice maths: it is commutative and associative, so applying kernel A then kernel B equals applying one combined kernel A * B, and it is what the convolution theorem in lesson 11 talks about.

Worked 1D example with an impulse: let f = 0 0 0 1 0 0 0, a single bright point, and the kernel w = 1 2 3 with centre weight 2. Correlation at the pixel just left of the 1 picks up the right-hand weight 3; at the 1 itself it picks 2; just right of it, it picks 1. So correlation outputs 0 0 3 2 1 0 0, a reversed copy of the kernel. Convolution flips the kernel first and outputs 0 0 1 2 3 0 0, an exact copy. This is why the impulse response of a system is its convolution kernel: convolve anything with a single point and you get the kernel back.

Worked 3 x 3 example: take the patch with rows 10 20 30 / 40 50 60 / 70 80 90 and the kernel with rows -1 0 1 / -2 0 2 / -1 0 1. Correlation multiplies matching positions: -10 + 30 - 80 + 120 - 70 + 90 = 80. For convolution, rotate the kernel to 1 0 -1 / 2 0 -2 / 1 0 -1 first; the sum becomes -80. Same size, opposite sign. For symmetric kernels such as the box or Gaussian, the rotation changes nothing, so correlation and convolution give identical results, which is why many people use the words loosely.

Which one do libraries use: many image libraries actually compute correlation even when the function is called filter or conv. For example, OpenCV's filter2D computes correlation, and deep learning frameworks do the same in what they call convolution layers. For symmetric kernels it does not matter. For asymmetric ones, such as a Sobel kernel or a motion-blur kernel, flip the kernel yourself if you need true convolution. In exams, always state which one you are doing.

The border problem: when the kernel centre sits on the first row, part of the kernel hangs outside the image. There are no pixels there. We must invent them, which is called padding. For a kernel of size m x n we need (m-1)/2 extra rows and (n-1)/2 extra columns on each side; a 3 x 3 kernel needs one row and one column all around.

Padding choices: zero padding fills the border with 0. It is simple but makes a dark frame appear around blurred images, because the edge pixels average in black. Replicate padding copies the nearest edge pixel outward, so 5 7 9 at a border becomes 5 5 7 9. Mirror (reflect) padding copies pixels as in a mirror, so 5 7 9 becomes 7 5 7 9 or 5 5 7 9 depending on whether the edge pixel is repeated. Mirror and replicate keep borders looking natural; zero padding is what convolution theory in lesson 11 assumes. For small kernels on big images the choice barely matters, but on a thumbnail it can ruin the edges.

Output size: with padding chosen to keep the size, the output is the same size as the input (often called same mode). Without padding, the kernel only visits positions where it fits fully, so an M x N image filtered with an m x n kernel gives (M - m + 1) x (N - n + 1) pixels (valid mode). A 512 x 512 image with a 5 x 5 kernel in valid mode becomes 508 x 508. Full mode, used in signal theory, gives (M + m - 1) x (N + n - 1), the full overlap. Neural networks in deep-cse-8-1 talk about exactly these three modes.

Normalising kernels: if the weights of a smoothing kernel add up to 1, the average brightness of a flat area stays the same. A 3 x 3 box kernel of all 1s sums to 9, so we multiply it by 1/9. If the weights sum to 0, as in edge and Laplacian kernels, a flat area gives 0 and only changes survive. Such outputs can be negative, so before display you must shift and scale them, for example add 128 or take absolute value and stretch to 0-255. Forgetting this is the most common reason a beginner's edge image looks completely black.

Separable kernels: some 2D kernels are the product of a column vector and a row vector. The 3 x 3 kernel 1 2 1 / 2 4 2 / 1 2 1 equals the column 1 2 1 times the row 1 2 1. Then you can filter every row with 1 2 1, and then every column of the result with 1 2 1, and get the same answer as the 2D kernel. In linear algebra terms (deep-cse-2-5 lesson 25), a separable kernel has matrix rank 1. Box and Gaussian kernels are separable; Laplacian is not.

Why separability saves time: a direct m x m kernel needs m squared multiplications per pixel; the separable version needs 2m. For an 11 x 11 Gaussian that is 121 versus 22, about 5.5 times fewer. On a Full HD photo of 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels, that is about 251 million multiplications versus about 46 million. Phone camera pipelines and real-time video filters rely on this trick constantly.

Linear vs nonlinear filters: linear filters use a weighted sum, so they obey superposition: filtering (a + b) equals filtering a plus filtering b. Nonlinear filters do something else with the neighbourhood, such as taking the median, the maximum or the minimum. You cannot write a median as a kernel. Nonlinear filters (lesson 09 and morphology in lessons 18-19) are often better at keeping edges, but they lose the nice maths of convolution and the frequency domain.

How filters relate to frequency, a preview: the convolution theorem (deep-cse-2-7 lesson 20) says convolution in space equals multiplication in frequency. So every linear spatial filter is also a frequency filter. A kernel that averages, like the box, passes slow changes and kills fast ones: a lowpass filter. A kernel whose weights sum to zero, like the Laplacian, kills flat areas and keeps fast changes: a highpass filter. Lessons 11 and 12 develop this; for now remember that small kernels are cheap in space, while very large blurs are often cheaper in the frequency domain with the FFT.

Real-life example 1, a selfie beauty filter: a phone app wants to smooth skin. It converts the face area to a working image, slides a 7 x 7 Gaussian kernel using the separable trick (14 multiplications per pixel instead of 49), and uses mirror padding at the face border so no dark halo appears. Skin pores are fast changes, so they fade; the big face shape is a slow change and survives. Fancier apps use an edge-preserving filter so eyes and lips stay sharp, but the sliding-window machinery is exactly what you learned here.

Real-life example 2, finding a stamp on a land document: a land office in Rajshahi scans old deeds and wants to find where the official seal appears. A clean picture of the seal is used as a kernel. The program correlates it across the scanned page; most places give a low score, but where the seal is printed the score peaks. Because brightness varies across old paper, they use normalised correlation, which divides by local brightness and contrast, so a faded seal still scores high. The location of the peak is where the seal sits.

Common mistakes: writing the output back into the input image while sliding, so later pixels use already-filtered neighbours. Forgetting to flip the kernel for true convolution with asymmetric kernels. Forgetting the 1/9 normalisation and getting a far too bright result that clips at 255. Displaying a zero-sum filter output without shifting or taking absolute values. Mixing up rows and columns in x, y notation. Exams ask: compute correlation and convolution of a small patch with a given kernel, state the output size for valid mode, show that a kernel is separable and count the saved multiplications, and explain the difference between linear and nonlinear filters.

Recap: spatial filtering slides a kernel over the image; at each position it multiplies weights by pixels and sums them. Correlation uses the kernel as is; convolution rotates it 180 degrees first, and for symmetric kernels the two agree. Padding (zero, replicate, mirror) decides what happens at borders, and the mode decides output size. Separable kernels turn m squared work into 2m. Linear filters connect directly to frequency-domain filtering, and nonlinear ones like the median do things a kernel cannot. Next, lesson 09 puts these tools to work on smoothing.
key_points: A spatial filter = neighbourhood + operation; a linear filter uses a weighted sum given by a kernel.
Correlation uses the kernel as is; convolution rotates it 180 degrees first.
Correlating an impulse gives a flipped kernel; convolving it gives the kernel itself.
For symmetric kernels correlation and convolution give the same result.
Padding (zero, replicate, mirror) fills missing border pixels; valid mode gives (M-m+1) x (N-n+1).
Smoothing kernels sum to 1; edge kernels sum to 0 and can give negative outputs that need scaling.
A separable (rank-1) kernel costs 2m instead of m squared multiplications per pixel.
Linear spatial filters are also frequency filters (convolution theorem); median-type filters are nonlinear.
lessons.tip: When you compute a filter by hand, write the patch and the kernel side by side, flip the kernel if it is convolution, then multiply cell by cell. Ninety percent of exam mistakes are sign errors from a forgotten flip.
lessons.task: Draw a 5 x 5 grid of numbers on paper (put one bright 9 in the middle and 0 elsewhere). Correlate it with the kernel 1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 9 using zero padding. What pattern appears in the output, and how does it compare with the kernel?

quiz.q: What is the difference between correlation and convolution?
options: Convolution rotates the kernel by 180 degrees before sliding
Correlation works only on colour images
There is no difference for any kernel
quiz.explain: Convolution flips the kernel in both directions; correlation does not.

quiz.q: A 512 x 512 image is filtered with a 5 x 5 kernel without padding (valid mode). What is the output size?
Why is a separable 11 x 11 kernel faster?
options: It needs 22 multiplications per pixel instead of 121
quiz.explain: Filtering rows then columns with 1D kernels costs 2m instead of m squared.

quiz.q: An edge kernel whose weights sum to 0 is applied to a perfectly flat gray area. The output is...
quiz.explain: In a flat area every pixel is equal, so the weighted sum is value x 0 = 0.

quiz.q: Which of these is a nonlinear spatial filter?
quiz.explain: The median sorts values and picks the middle; it cannot be written as a weighted sum.

lessons.title: Smoothing Spatial Filters: Box, Gaussian and Median
lessons.content:
Look at a photo of a wedding stage in Dhaka taken at night on a cheap phone. Up close it is full of tiny coloured specks, like sand thrown on the picture. Now squint your eyes. The specks vanish and the stage looks smooth. Squinting blurs, and blurring averages away the specks. Smoothing filters do this squint on purpose, with numbers. They are the first tool anyone reaches for when an image is noisy, and they also prepare images for later steps like thresholding and edge detection.

Where this sits: lesson 08 built the sliding-window machinery. This lesson picks kernels that smooth. We cover the box (mean) filter, weighted averages, the Gaussian filter and how to choose its sigma and size, the unavoidable trade-off between removing noise and keeping detail, and then the nonlinear order-statistic filters: median, max and min. Noise models and more advanced restoration filters come later in lessons 13-15; here we keep to the everyday smoothing filters.

Why smoothing removes noise: random noise makes neighbouring pixels jump up and down independently, while the true scene usually changes slowly. If you average 9 noisy pixels, the true values agree and stay, but the random ups and downs partly cancel. For independent noise with variance sigma squared, the average of n samples has variance sigma squared divided by n. So a 3 x 3 average cuts noise variance by 9 and noise standard deviation by 3. That is the same idea as averaging K images in lesson 04, but done across space instead of across time.

The box (mean) filter: every weight is equal. A 3 x 3 box kernel is all 1s times 1/9, so each output pixel is the plain average of its 3 x 3 neighbourhood. A 5 x 5 box uses 1/25. Bigger boxes smooth more. The box is the simplest smoothing filter and is very fast; with a running-sum trick (also called an integral image) its cost per pixel does not even depend on the kernel size.

Box filter worked: take the patch 100 102 101 / 99 255 100 / 101 98 103. The centre 255 is a white noise speck in a gray area near 100. The sum of the nine values is 1059, and 1059 / 9 = 117.7, so the output is about 118. The speck went from 255 to 118, much better, but notice the problem: it did not go back to about 100. The average got pulled up by the one outlier. Averaging spreads a big spike over its neighbours instead of removing it.

The blur cost, worked in 1D: averaging also blurs edges. Take a sharp edge 10 10 10 200 200 200. A 3-wide mean filter gives, at the two pixels beside the jump, (10 + 10 + 200) / 3 = 73.3 and (10 + 200 + 200) / 3 = 136.7. The single sharp step has become a ramp 10, 73, 137, 200 across two pixels. With a bigger kernel the ramp gets wider. This is the central trade-off of linear smoothing: the same averaging that kills noise also smears every edge and fine line.

Kernel size, worked: try a 5-wide mean on the longer edge 10 10 10 10 200 200 200 200. The four pixels nearest the jump now become (10 x 4 + 200) / 5 = 48, (10 x 3 + 200 x 2) / 5 = 86, (10 x 2 + 200 x 3) / 5 = 124 and (10 + 200 x 4) / 5 = 162. The ramp is now four pixels wide instead of two. Meanwhile the noise standard deviation drops by the square root of 25, that is 5 times, instead of 3 times. More smoothing buys less noise and pays with wider blur; there is no free lunch, only a choice of how much of each you can live with.

Weighted averages: a better idea is to trust the centre pixel more than far neighbours, because nearby pixels are more likely to belong to the same object. A popular 3 x 3 weighted kernel is 1 2 1 / 2 4 2 / 1 2 1 times 1/16: centre weight 4, edge neighbours 2, corners 1, total 16. It blurs a little less than the box for the same size and, as we saw in lesson 08, it is separable into 1 2 1 times 1 2 1.

The Gaussian filter: the weights follow the bell-shaped Gaussian function w(s, t) = K exp(-(s squared + t squared) / (2 sigma squared)). The parameter sigma controls how wide the bell is, which means how strong the blur is. With sigma = 1, a pixel at distance 1 gets weight exp(-0.5) = 0.607 times the centre weight, a diagonal pixel at distance squared 2 gets exp(-1) = 0.368, and a pixel 3 away gets exp(-4.5) = 0.011, about 1 percent. After normalising a 3 x 3 window to sum 1, the centre is 0.204, edge neighbours 0.124 and corners 0.075.

Choosing Gaussian size: since weights beyond about 3 sigma on each side are almost zero, a good kernel size is about 6 sigma, rounded up to the next odd number. For sigma = 1 use 7 x 7; for sigma = 2 use 13 x 13. A kernel much smaller than this chops off the bell and behaves like a box; a much bigger one only wastes time. The Gaussian is separable, so even a 13 x 13 Gaussian costs 26 multiplications per pixel, not 169.

Why Gaussian is the favourite: it has no sharp corners, so it blurs smoothly without the odd artefacts a box can create. Its Fourier transform is also a Gaussian, so in frequency it is a smooth lowpass with no ripples (lesson 12). Applying a Gaussian twice equals one Gaussian with sigma = square root of (sigma1 squared + sigma2 squared), which makes scale-space and image pyramids possible (lesson 23). And repeating a box filter three or four times gives something very close to a Gaussian, a handy fact when only box filtering is fast on a device.

Smoothing for something else: smoothing is often not the goal but a helper. Before thresholding (lesson 21), blurring merges tiny bright and dark dots so they do not become separate blobs. Before edge detection (lesson 20), it stops noise from being mistaken for edges. To find only large objects, a strong blur followed by a threshold removes everything small. Graphics people use the same Gaussian to make soft shadows and the frosted-glass effect behind phone notifications.

Order-statistic filters: now we leave weighted sums. An order-statistic filter sorts the pixel values in the window and picks one by its rank. These are nonlinear; no kernel can express them. The three basic ones are the median (middle value), the max (largest) and the min (smallest).

Median filter worked: take the same patch 100 102 101 / 99 255 100 / 101 98 103. Sorted: 98, 99, 100, 100, 101, 101, 102, 103, 255. With nine values the median is the fifth one, 101. The speck becomes 101, almost exactly the true background, while the mean gave 118. The median simply ignores outliers, because one extreme value can only push itself to the end of the sorted list; it cannot drag the middle.

Median on salt-and-pepper, worked in 1D: the row 50 52 255 51 0 53 50 has a salt pixel (255) and a pepper pixel (0). A 3-wide median at each interior position looks at three neighbours: (50, 52, 255) gives 52, (52, 255, 51) gives 52, (255, 51, 0) gives 51, (51, 0, 53) gives 51, (0, 53, 50) gives 50. Output: 52 52 51 51 50. Both impulses are gone and no value is pulled far from 50. A mean filter would have smeared the 255 and the 0 into their neighbours.

Why the median keeps edges: run a 3-wide median over the edge 10 10 10 200 200 200. At the last 10 the window is (10, 10, 200), median 10. At the first 200 the window is (10, 200, 200), median 200. The output is the same sharp step. A median does not invent new in-between values; it only chooses values already present. So it removes isolated specks yet keeps step edges crisp. Its weakness: it rounds sharp corners and wipes out thin lines narrower than half the window, and if more than half the window is noise, the median itself is noise.

Max and min filters: the max filter picks the largest value in the window. It removes dark pepper dots, because any window containing a normal pixel will choose that, and it makes bright objects grow. The min filter picks the smallest value, removes bright salt dots and makes dark objects grow. Max and min are exactly grayscale dilation and erosion from morphology (lesson 19). Used together, min then max, they remove small bright details while keeping big shapes, an idea called opening.

Picking the right filter: for fine, grainy Gaussian-like noise (low light, sensor heat), use a Gaussian or weighted average. For salt-and-pepper or impulse noise (bad pixels, transmission errors), use the median. For pepper only, a max; for salt only, a min. If edges must stay sharp at any cost, use a median or an edge-preserving filter such as the bilateral filter, which weights neighbours by both distance and similarity of brightness, so it does not average across an edge. Always start with the smallest kernel that works, because every increase in size costs detail.

Real-life example 1, a skin-smoothing selfie mode: a phone camera in a crowded Gulistan market takes a selfie in harsh light. The app first finds the face, then applies a bilateral or Gaussian blur only on skin areas, so pores and blemishes (fast changes) fade, while a mask keeps the eyes, eyebrows and lips untouched. Finally it blends the smoothed skin with the original at about 50 to 70 percent so the face does not look like plastic. Every step is a smoothing filter plus a mask, nothing more mysterious.

Real-life example 2, cleaning a scanned exam answer sheet: a coaching centre in Mymensingh scans thousands of OMR sheets. Old scanners add black and white specks. Step 1, a 3 x 3 median filter removes the specks without blurring the edges of the filled bubbles. Step 2, a mild Gaussian blur evens out the paper texture. Step 3, thresholding (lesson 21) separates filled bubbles from empty ones. Without the median, specks would sometimes be counted as marks and students would get wrong scores. One small filter protects thousands of results.

Common mistakes: using a mean filter on salt-and-pepper noise and wondering why gray blotches remain. Choosing a huge kernel to kill noise and destroying all detail. Forgetting to normalise the kernel, so the image brightens. Picking a Gaussian size too small for its sigma. Assuming the median is a linear filter or trying to write it as a kernel. Exam questions: apply 3 x 3 mean and median filters to a given patch and compare, explain why the median preserves edges, compute Gaussian weights for a given sigma, choose a filter for a given noise type, and explain the noise-versus-blur trade-off.

Recap: smoothing averages away random noise because noise varies independently while the scene varies slowly; an n-pixel average cuts noise variance by n. Box, weighted and Gaussian filters are linear lowpass filters; Gaussian is smooth, separable and sized at about 6 sigma. All linear smoothing blurs edges. Median, max and min are nonlinear order-statistic filters; the median removes impulse noise and keeps step edges, max removes pepper and min removes salt. Next, lesson 10 does the opposite: sharpening.
key_points: Averaging n independent noisy pixels divides noise variance by n, so smoothing reduces random noise.
Box filter: all weights equal (1/9 for 3 x 3); the weighted 1 2 1 / 2 4 2 / 1 2 1 / 16 trusts the centre more.
Gaussian weights exp(-(s^2+t^2)/(2 sigma^2)); kernel size about 6 sigma, odd; it is separable and ripple-free.
Linear smoothing always blurs edges: 10 10 10 200 200 200 becomes 10, 73, 137, 200.
Median sorts and takes the middle: the patch with a 255 speck gives 101 instead of the mean's 118.
The median removes salt-and-pepper noise and keeps step edges, but rounds corners and erases thin lines.
Max filter removes pepper, min filter removes salt; they are grayscale dilation and erosion.
Choose by noise type: Gaussian for grainy noise, median for impulses, bilateral when edges must stay.
lessons.tip: Whenever you compare filters, test them on two things at once: a noise speck and a sharp edge. A good smoothing filter changes the speck a lot and the edge very little.
lessons.task: Write the row 20 22 21 250 23 20 0 22 21 on paper. Apply a 3-wide mean filter and a 3-wide median filter to the interior pixels. Which one removed the 250 and the 0 better, and which one spread them into their neighbours?

quiz.q: A 3 x 3 window has values 98, 99, 100, 100, 101, 101, 102, 103, 255. What does a median filter output?
quiz.explain: Sorted, the fifth of nine values is 101; the outlier 255 is ignored.

quiz.q: Roughly how large should a Gaussian kernel be for sigma = 2?
quiz.explain: Weights beyond 3 sigma on each side are tiny, so about 6 sigma, rounded up to odd, is enough.

quiz.q: Which filter is best for removing salt-and-pepper noise while keeping edges sharp?
quiz.explain: The median ignores extreme values and never creates in-between values across an edge.

quiz.q: Which filter removes only dark pepper dots from an image?
quiz.explain: A max filter picks the brightest value in the window, so isolated dark dots disappear.

quiz.q: Averaging 9 pixels with independent noise of variance 36 gives noise variance of about...
quiz.explain: The variance of an average of n independent samples is the variance divided by n: 36 / 9 = 4.

lessons.title: Sharpening Spatial Filters: Laplacian, Unsharp Masking and Gradients
lessons.content:
Think of how a teacher highlights the important lines in a textbook with a marker. The words do not change, but the borders of the important parts jump out. Sharpening does this to images. It finds the places where brightness changes, the edges and fine details, and makes those changes stronger, so a slightly soft photo of a rickshaw's painted back panel suddenly shows crisp lines and lettering. Smoothing in lesson 09 averaged neighbours; sharpening does the opposite, it measures differences between neighbours and adds them back.

Where this sits: lesson 08 gave the sliding-kernel machinery and lesson 09 used it to blur. This lesson uses it to sharpen. We start from derivatives, because a derivative measures change. We compare first and second derivatives on a worked 1D profile, build the Laplacian kernels, sharpen a small patch by hand, then learn unsharp masking and highboost filtering, use the Sobel gradient for enhancement, and see why sharpening also boosts noise. Edge detection as a segmentation tool is lesson 20; here sharpening is for making images look crisper to a human.

Derivatives on pixels: a digital image has no smooth curve to differentiate, so we use differences between neighbours. The first derivative in x is df/dx = f(x + 1) - f(x). The second derivative is d2f/dx2 = f(x + 1) + f(x - 1) - 2 f(x), which is the difference of two first differences. These are the simplest finite-difference formulas from Numerical Methods (deep-cse-3-4), and they are all a computer needs.

What we want from them: in a flat area both derivatives should be zero, because nothing changes. At the start and end of a gradual ramp, and along it, we want them to say something. At a sudden step we want a strong response. Let us check the two derivatives against these wishes on a real profile.

Worked profile: take the 1D scan line 5 5 5 4 3 2 1 1 1 1 8 8 8. It has a flat part, a downward ramp from 5 to 1, another flat part, and a sudden step from 1 up to 8. The first differences are 0 0 -1 -1 -1 -1 0 0 0 7 0 0. So the first derivative is non-zero all along the ramp (a constant -1) and gives one big 7 at the step.

Second derivative on the same profile: computing f(x + 1) + f(x - 1) - 2 f(x) from the second pixel onwards gives 0 -1 0 0 0 1 0 0 7 -7 0. Now the ramp shows only at its two ends: -1 where the ramp starts and +1 where it ends, and zero along the middle. At the step the second derivative gives +7 then -7, a double response with a sign change in between. That sign change is called a zero crossing, and it marks the exact centre of the edge.

What the comparison teaches: the first derivative makes thick edges, because it fires along the whole ramp. The second derivative makes thin double edges and responds much more strongly to fine detail like thin lines and isolated points, relative to its response on ramps. For sharpening, where we want fine detail to pop, the second derivative is usually preferred. For finding edge direction and strength, as in lesson 20, the first derivative (gradient) is more useful.

The Laplacian: in 2D we add the second derivatives in x and in y. The Laplacian is del2 f = f(x + 1, y) + f(x - 1, y) + f(x, y + 1) + f(x, y - 1) - 4 f(x, y). As a kernel this is 0 1 0 / 1 -4 1 / 0 1 0. It is isotropic for rotations of 90 degrees, meaning it responds the same to edges in any of those directions. Adding the diagonal second derivatives gives the 8-neighbour version 1 1 1 / 1 -8 1 / 1 1 1, which treats diagonals too. Both kernels sum to zero, so flat areas give zero. Many books also use the negated versions with a positive centre; the only thing that changes is the sign in the sharpening formula.

Sharpening with the Laplacian: the rule is g(x, y) = f(x, y) + c x del2 f(x, y), with c = -1 when the centre weight is negative, as in our kernels. In plain words: subtract the Laplacian from the image. In a flat area the Laplacian is zero, so nothing changes. Near an edge the Laplacian is positive on the dark side and negative on the bright side, so subtracting it makes the dark side darker and the bright side brighter. The edge gets a small overshoot on each side, and our eyes read that overshoot as sharpness.

Sharpening worked: take a horizontal edge patch with rows 20 20 20 / 20 20 20 / 100 100 100 and sharpen the centre pixel (value 20) with the 4-neighbour Laplacian. Neighbours up, left and right are 20 and below is 100. Laplacian = 20 + 20 + 20 + 100 - 4 x 20 = 80. Then g = 20 - 80 = -60, which we clip to 0. Now take a pixel of value 100 on the bright side with neighbour 20 above and 100 on the other three sides: Laplacian = 20 + 100 + 100 + 100 - 400 = -80, so g = 100 + 80 = 180. The dark side went from 20 to 0 and the bright side from 100 to 180: a much stronger, crisper edge.

A shortcut kernel: since g = f - del2 f, you can fold both into one kernel: the identity kernel (1 at the centre) minus the Laplacian kernel gives 0 -1 0 / -1 5 -1 / 0 -1 0. Filtering once with this kernel sharpens directly. The 8-neighbour version is -1 -1 -1 / -1 9 -1 / -1 -1 -1. Both sum to 1, so overall brightness stays the same. This is the sharpen kernel you will find in many photo editors.

Unsharp masking: this old trick comes from film photography darkrooms, where a blurred (unsharp) copy of the negative was used as a mask. The digital steps are: 1, blur the image to get f_blur; 2, subtract to get the mask, g_mask = f - f_blur, which contains only the fine detail the blur removed; 3, add the mask back with a weight k: g = f + k x g_mask. With k = 1 it is called unsharp masking; with k greater than 1 it is called highboost filtering, and it sharpens even more. With k less than 1 the sharpening is gentler.

Unsharp masking worked: take the 1D edge 10 10 10 50 50 50 and a 3-wide mean blur. The blurred row is 10 10 23.3 36.7 50 50. The mask is the difference: 0 0 -13.3 13.3 0 0. With k = 1, g = 10 10 -3.3 63.3 50 50, clipped to 10 10 0 63 50 50. With k = 2 (highboost), g = 10 10 -16.7 76.7 50 50. The dark side dips and the bright side rises right at the edge. Too large a k makes visible bright and dark halos along every edge, the tell-tale sign of an over-sharpened photo.

Photo editors expose three knobs for unsharp masking: amount (k), radius (the sigma of the Gaussian blur, which decides how thick the details being boosted are) and threshold (only sharpen where the mask is bigger than some value, so flat noisy areas such as skin or sky are left alone). Knowing what each knob does in terms of f, f_blur and k makes them easy to tune.

Using the gradient for enhancement: the first derivative also sharpens, especially for showing defects and fine structure. The gradient has two parts, gx and gy, and its magnitude M = square root of (gx squared + gy squared) is large where the image changes fast. The Sobel kernels compute them with a little smoothing built in: gx with -1 0 1 / -2 0 2 / -1 0 1 and gy with -1 -2 -1 / 0 0 0 / 1 2 1. Because a square root is costly, the approximation M about |gx| + |gy| is often used.

Sobel worked: on the patch 10 20 30 / 40 50 60 / 70 80 90, lesson 08 showed gx = 80. For gy, the bottom row minus the top row with weights 1 2 1 gives (70 + 160 + 90) - (10 + 40 + 30) = 320 - 80 = 240. The magnitude is the square root of 80 squared plus 240 squared, about 253, and the cheap approximation gives 320. The direction is arctan(240 / 80), about 71.6 degrees, mostly vertical change, since brightness grows much faster going down the patch than going right. Factories use gradient images like this to make scratches on lenses or cracks on tiles stand out for inspection.

Sharpening amplifies noise: noise is a fast change too, so every sharpening method boosts it along with real detail. A Laplacian on a noisy photo can make the grain look like sandpaper. The cure is to combine methods: smooth first, or use the smoothed gradient as a mask so that sharpening is strong only near real edges and weak in flat areas. Gonzalez and Woods show a classic chain on a bone scan: Laplacian sharpening, Sobel gradient, smoothed gradient used as a mask on the Laplacian result, then a power-law stretch. The point of the chain is that no single filter is enough; each fixes the side-effects of another.

Real-life example 1, inside your phone camera: every phone applies sharpening after demosaicing and noise reduction, because the tiny lens and sensor give slightly soft images. The image pipeline runs an unsharp mask with a small radius, a moderate amount and a threshold so that skies and walls stay smooth. Some phones apply stronger sharpening on text and building edges than on faces. If you take a photo of a Bangla shop sign in Old Dhaka and zoom right in, you can often see faint bright halos along the letters: that is the unsharp mask's overshoot.

Real-life example 2, reading a blurred X-ray of a broken wrist: a radiologist in a Khulna hospital receives a slightly soft digital X-ray. The viewer software offers an edge-enhancement slider, which is unsharp masking with adjustable k. At k about 1 the thin fracture line becomes visible against the bone. Pushing k to 3 makes it sharper, but also turns film grain into fake specks that could be mistaken for tiny fragments. So the radiologist uses a moderate k and compares with the original. Sharpening helps the eye but never adds real information.

Common mistakes: adding the Laplacian instead of subtracting it when the centre weight is negative, which blurs instead of sharpening. Forgetting to clip results to 0-255. Expecting sharpening to recover detail that the blur truly destroyed; it only boosts what is left, while true deblurring is restoration (lesson 15). Over-sharpening and creating halos. Exams ask: compute first and second derivatives of a given profile and comment on ramps, steps and zero crossings, apply a Laplacian kernel to a patch and form g = f - del2 f, explain unsharp masking and highboost with k, and compute Sobel gx, gy and magnitude.

Recap: sharpening highlights intensity change using derivatives. The first difference responds along whole ramps; the second difference responds only at ramp ends and gives a zero crossing at steps, so it suits fine detail. The Laplacian kernels 0 1 0 / 1 -4 1 / 0 1 0 and its 8-neighbour version give g = f - del2 f, or the single kernel 0 -1 0 / -1 5 -1 / 0 -1 0. Unsharp masking adds k times (f - blur), highboost uses k greater than 1. The Sobel gradient magnitude shows where change is strong. All sharpening boosts noise, so combine it with smoothing. Next, lesson 11 looks at the same ideas through frequency: the 2D Fourier transform.
key_points: Digital first derivative: f(x+1) - f(x); second derivative: f(x+1) + f(x-1) - 2f(x).
First derivative fires along ramps (thick edges); second fires at ramp ends and gives a zero crossing at a step.
Laplacian kernel 0 1 0 / 1 -4 1 / 0 1 0 (or 8-neighbour 1 1 1 / 1 -8 1 / 1 1 1) sums to zero.
Sharpen with g = f - Laplacian, or the single kernel 0 -1 0 / -1 5 -1 / 0 -1 0.
Unsharp masking: g = f + k(f - blurred f); k = 1 is unsharp masking, k > 1 is highboost.
Sobel gradient: gx, gy, magnitude sqrt(gx^2 + gy^2) or |gx| + |gy|; used to show defects.
Sharpening always amplifies noise; combine with smoothing or use the gradient as a mask.
Too much sharpening creates bright and dark halos along edges.
lessons.tip: Before memorising any sharpening kernel, compute its result on three tiny cases: a flat patch, a ramp and a step. If you know what it does to those three, you understand the filter.
lessons.task: Write the profile 2 2 2 2 6 6 6 3 3 3 on paper. Compute its first and second differences. Mark where the second difference crosses zero. Then sharpen it with g = f - (second difference) and see how the jumps change.

quiz.q: For the profile 1 1 8 8, what is the second derivative f(x+1) + f(x-1) - 2f(x) at the pixel with value 1 next to the step?
quiz.explain: 8 + 1 - 2 x 1 = 7; the next pixel gives 1 + 8 - 16 = -7, a zero crossing.

quiz.q: Using the kernel 0 1 0 / 1 -4 1 / 0 1 0, the sharpening rule is...
quiz.explain: With a negative centre weight, subtracting the Laplacian makes edges stronger.

quiz.q: In unsharp masking g = f + k(f - f_blur), what is it called when k is greater than 1?
quiz.explain: k > 1 adds more than one copy of the detail mask, which is highboost filtering.

quiz.q: Sobel gives gx = 80 and gy = 240 at a pixel. What is the approximate gradient magnitude using |gx| + |gy|?
quiz.explain: |80| + |240| = 320; the exact value sqrt(80^2 + 240^2) is about 253.

quiz.q: Why does sharpening often make a photo look grainier?
options: It converts the image to binary
Noise is also fast change, so it gets boosted with edges
quiz.explain: Derivatives cannot tell real fine detail from noise, so both are amplified.

lessons.title: The 2D Fourier Transform: Images as Waves
lessons.content:
Think about a song played on a harmonium. Your ear hears one sound, but a musician can tell you it is made of a low note, a middle note and a high note played together. A photo is similar. Your eye sees one picture, but mathematically it can be split into many smooth waves of brightness: slow waves that paint the big areas like the sky and walls, and fast waves that draw the fine details like hair, text and noise. The 2D Fourier transform is the tool that does this split, telling you how much of each wave the picture contains.

Where this sits: in Math III (deep-cse-2-7 lessons 19-20) you met the continuous Fourier transform and the convolution theorem, and in DSP (deep-cse-5-7 lessons 15-17) the DFT, FFT and circular convolution for 1D signals. This lesson moves all of that into two dimensions for images. We cover why frequency is a useful view, the 2D DFT and its inverse, spectrum and phase, centring, periodicity and symmetry, the DC term, log display, 2D aliasing, the convolution theorem with its wraparound trap and zero padding, and the speed of the FFT. Lesson 12 then uses this to filter images.

What frequency means in an image: frequency here is how fast brightness changes as you move across the picture. A clear blue sky changes very slowly: low frequency. A brick wall seen from afar repeats every few pixels: middle frequency. A sharp edge, thin text or grainy noise changes from one pixel to the next: high frequency. A 2D wave also has a direction. Stripes that change from left to right have horizontal frequency, stripes that change from top to bottom have vertical frequency, and diagonal stripes have both.

Why bother with this view: some jobs are much easier in frequency. Blurring means removing high frequencies. Sharpening means boosting them. Periodic noise, like the regular stripes from a faulty scanner or the dot pattern of a printed newspaper, shows up as a few bright spots in frequency and can be deleted precisely, while in the image it is spread over every pixel. Compression (lesson 24) keeps the frequencies the eye cares about and drops the rest. And large convolutions become cheap multiplications.

The 1D DFT recap: for M samples f(0) to f(M-1), the DFT is F(u) = sum over x of f(x) exp(-j 2 pi u x / M), for u = 0 to M-1. Each F(u) is a complex number that says how much of a wave with u cycles across the whole signal is present (its size) and where that wave's peaks are (its angle). The inverse puts the waves back together: f(x) = (1/M) sum over u of F(u) exp(j 2 pi u x / M). Nothing is lost; the DFT is just a different, complete description of the same data.

The 2D DFT: for an M x N image, F(u, v) = sum over x from 0 to M-1 and y from 0 to N-1 of f(x, y) exp(-j 2 pi (u x / M + v y / N)). The inverse is f(x, y) = (1/MN) sum over u and v of F(u, v) exp(j 2 pi (u x / M + v y / N)). Here u and v are frequency variables: u counts how many cycles of a wave fit down the rows and v how many fit across the columns. The output F is also an M x N array, one complex number for each wave.

Worked 2 x 2 example: let f have rows 1 2 / 3 4. With M = N = 2, the exponentials are just +1 or -1. F(0, 0) = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. F(0, 1) = (1 - 2) + (3 - 4) = -2, the left-right change. F(1, 0) = (1 + 2) - (3 + 4) = -4, the top-bottom change. F(1, 1) = 1 - 2 - 3 + 4 = 0, the diagonal checkerboard pattern, which is absent. Reading it back: the image is mostly its average, has a bigger change from top to bottom than from left to right, and no checkerboard component. That is a correct description of 1 2 / 3 4.

Worked stripe example: a 4 x 4 image whose every row is 0 2 0 2 has vertical stripes that alternate every pixel, changing from left to right. Its DFT is zero everywhere except two places: F(0, 0) = 16, the sum of all pixels, and F(0, 2) with magnitude 16, which is the wave with 2 cycles across 4 columns, the fastest possible. One clean pattern in the image becomes one bright dot (plus the average) in the spectrum. Bigger picture: a pattern repeating every 8 pixels across a 256-pixel-wide image gives a peak at v = 256 / 8 = 32.

Spectrum and phase: each F(u, v) is complex, so we split it into magnitude |F(u, v)|, called the Fourier spectrum, and angle phi(u, v), called the phase. The power spectrum is |F| squared. The spectrum tells how strong each wave is; the phase tells where the waves are shifted, which decides where edges and shapes sit. When books show a Fourier picture, they nearly always show the spectrum, because phase images look like random noise to a human.

The phase surprise: take two photos, say a face and a rickshaw. Compute both DFTs, then build a new image from the spectrum of the face and the phase of the rickshaw. The result looks like the rickshaw, not the face. Swap them and you see the face. Phase carries most of the structure, meaning where the edges are; spectrum mostly carries how strong things are. This experiment, popularised by Oppenheim and Lim in 1981, is why filters used in image processing are usually zero-phase: they change magnitudes but leave phase alone so that nothing moves.

The DC term: F(0, 0) is the sum of all pixels, exp of 0 being 1. So F(0, 0) = MN times the mean intensity. For the 2 x 2 example that is 4 x 2.5 = 10. For a 512 x 512 image with mean 100 it is 26,214,400. It is called the DC component, from direct current in electronics, because it is the part that does not vary. It is usually by far the largest value in the spectrum.

Log display: a spectrum's values range from 0 up to millions at the DC term, so if you scale it straight to 0-255 you see one bright dot in a black square. The fix is the log transform from lesson 06: display c x log(1 + |F(u, v)|). With the DC value 26,214,400, natural log(1 + 26,214,400) is about 17.08, so c = 255 / 17.08, about 14.9, maps the largest value to 255 while small values become visible.

Centring the spectrum: the raw DFT puts low frequencies at the four corners of the array, which is awkward to look at. Multiplying the image by (-1) to the power (x + y) before the transform shifts F so that F(0, 0) moves to the centre, at (M/2, N/2). This is the frequency shift property: multiplying by a complex exponential in space shifts in frequency, and (-1) to the power (x + y) is exactly exp(j pi (x + y)). In code, NumPy's fftshift does the same rearrangement after the transform. In a centred spectrum, the middle shows slow waves and the outer ring shows fast detail and noise.

Periodicity and symmetry: the DFT treats the image as if it repeats forever in both directions like floor tiles, so F(u, v) = F(u + M, v) = F(u, v + N). For a real image, F(-u, -v) is the complex conjugate of F(u, v), so the spectrum is symmetric about the centre: you only really need half of it. Rotating an image rotates its spectrum by the same angle. And a strong straight edge in the image creates a bright line in the spectrum perpendicular to that edge; you can see this in the spectrum of any photo of buildings.

2D sampling and aliasing: lesson 03 and Signals & Systems (deep-cse-3-7 lesson 19) showed that sampling too coarsely makes fast patterns pretend to be slow ones. In 2D the rule is the same in each direction: a pattern needs at least two samples per cycle. The fastest representable wave has a period of 2 pixels, which is why the stripe example above with period 2 was at the very edge of the spectrum. Fine patterns like a checked shirt photographed from far away exceed this limit and fold back as wavy moire patterns. Smoothing (a lowpass filter) before shrinking an image removes those frequencies and prevents the moire.

The convolution theorem in 2D: convolving f with a kernel h in space equals multiplying their DFTs: f * h has DFT F x H. And the reverse: multiplying in space equals convolving in frequency. This is the bridge between lessons 08-10 and lesson 12. A spatial smoothing kernel has an H that is large near the centre and small outside: a lowpass. A Laplacian kernel has an H that is zero at the centre and grows outward: a highpass.

The wraparound trap and zero padding: because the DFT assumes the image repeats, multiplying F and H gives circular convolution, where the kernel falling off the right side wraps around and mixes in pixels from the left side (deep-cse-5-7 lesson 17). To get the correct linear convolution, pad both arrays with zeros to size P x Q with P at least A + C - 1 and Q at least B + D - 1, where A x B is the image and C x D the kernel. For two 512 x 512 arrays, P must be at least 1023, and in practice 1024 is used because the FFT likes powers of 2. Then crop the result.

Separability and FFT speed: the 2D DFT kernel splits into a row part and a column part, so you can do 1D DFTs on every row, then on every column of the result. A direct 2D DFT of an N x N image needs about N to the power 4 multiply-adds: for N = 512 that is about 68.7 billion. Doing rows then columns with direct 1D DFTs cuts it to 2 N cubed, about 268 million. Using the FFT for each 1D transform cuts it to about N squared log2 of N squared, about 4.7 million for N = 512, roughly 14,500 times faster than the direct method. This speed is why frequency methods are practical at all.

Real-life example 1, spotting a pattern on a fabric roll: a garment factory in Gazipur checks woven cloth with a line camera. A good fabric has a regular weave, which shows up as a neat grid of bright dots in the spectrum. Step 1, the system takes the 2D FFT of each image patch. Step 2, it compares the spectrum with a reference. Step 3, a broken thread or a stain breaks the regularity, spreading energy between the dots. Step 4, the patch is flagged for a worker to check. Checking every thread in the image directly would be slow and fragile; one spectrum comparison does it at once.

Real-life example 2, why a photo of a TV screen shows waves: point your phone at a computer screen in a cyber cafe and snap a picture. Wavy coloured bands appear. The screen's pixel grid is a high-frequency pattern; the camera sensor is another grid. When the two frequencies are close, their difference appears as a slow beat: aliasing, the moire pattern. In the spectrum you would see bright spots far from the centre folding into wrong places. Moving the phone slightly, changing the zoom or blurring slightly before capture (some cameras have an optical low-pass filter) changes or removes the bands.

Common mistakes: forgetting the 1/MN factor in the inverse transform. Expecting the DC term to be the mean instead of MN times the mean. Displaying the raw spectrum without a log. Forgetting to centre and then hunting for the low frequencies in the middle. Treating multiplication of DFTs as linear convolution without padding, which causes wraparound errors near borders. Thinking the spectrum alone describes the image. Exams ask: compute the DFT of a 2 x 2 image, show F(0, 0) = MN times the mean, explain centring with (-1) to the power (x + y), state the convolution theorem and padding size, explain why phase matters, and compare DFT and FFT costs.

Recap: the 2D DFT rewrites an M x N image as a sum of 2D waves, F(u, v), with the inverse rebuilding it exactly. Spectrum shows strength, phase shows position, and phase carries most of the structure. F(0, 0) equals MN times the mean, and spectra are shown with a log and centred using (-1) to the power (x + y). The DFT assumes periodicity, so the convolution theorem gives circular convolution unless you zero-pad to at least A + C - 1. Separability plus the FFT makes it all fast. Next, lesson 12 designs filters directly in this frequency world.
key_points: Image frequency = how fast brightness changes: smooth areas are low, edges, text and noise are high.
2D DFT: F(u,v) = sum f(x,y) exp(-j2pi(ux/M + vy/N)); the inverse has a 1/MN factor.
Worked: 1 2 / 3 4 gives F = 10, -2, -4, 0; F(0,0) = MN x mean is the DC term.
Spectrum |F| shows strength, phase shows position; phase carries most of the visible structure.
Display spectra with c log(1+|F|) and centre them by multiplying f by (-1)^(x+y) (or fftshift).
The DFT assumes the image repeats; real images give a conjugate-symmetric spectrum.
Convolution in space = multiplication in frequency; zero-pad to P >= A + C - 1 to avoid wraparound.
Rows-then-columns plus FFT: about N^2 log2(N^2) operations instead of N^4 (about 14,500 times faster at N = 512).
lessons.tip: Keep a mental picture: the centre of a centred spectrum is the blur, the outer ring is the detail. Every frequency-domain filter is just a choice of which ring to keep or weaken.
lessons.task: Compute by hand the 2D DFT of the 2 x 2 image 5 1 / 5 1 (only plus and minus signs are needed). Which coefficients are zero and why? Then check that F(0,0) equals 4 times the mean.

quiz.q: For an M x N image, the DC term F(0,0) equals...
quiz.explain: With all exponentials equal to 1, F(0,0) is the sum of all pixels, which is MN times the mean.

quiz.q: Why is the Fourier spectrum usually displayed as c log(1 + |F|)?
options: The DC term is so large that other values would look black
quiz.explain: The log compresses the huge range so small coefficients become visible.

quiz.q: Multiplying an image by (-1)^(x+y) before the DFT does what?
options: Moves F(0,0) to the centre of the array
quiz.explain: It shifts the spectrum by M/2 and N/2, so low frequencies appear in the middle.

quiz.q: A 512 x 512 image is filtered by multiplying DFTs with a 512 x 512 filter. To avoid wraparound, P should be at least...
quiz.explain: P >= A + C - 1 = 512 + 512 - 1 = 1023; in practice 1024 is used.

quiz.q: If you combine the spectrum of photo A with the phase of photo B, the result looks most like...
quiz.explain: Phase carries the positions of edges and shapes, so photo B's structure dominates.

lessons.title: Filtering in the Frequency Domain: Lowpass, Highpass, Homomorphic and Notch Filters
lessons.content:
Imagine you are listening to a song on a cheap speaker in a Dhaka bus. You hear a deep bass line, a singer in the middle, and a sharp hiss on top. A music app with an equaliser lets you push the bass down or cut the hiss, without touching each sound wave by hand. You change the song by turning knobs for each band of frequencies. Filtering an image in the frequency domain is exactly this idea, but for pictures. Instead of sliding a kernel over pixels, we take the image apart into its frequencies, turn some of them up or down, and put the image back together.

Where this fits: lesson 11 showed how the 2D DFT turns an image into a spectrum, where the centre holds slow changes (smooth areas) and the edges of the spectrum hold fast changes (edges, fine texture, noise). Lessons 09 and 10 did smoothing and sharpening in the spatial domain with small kernels. This lesson does the same jobs, plus some jobs that are almost impossible in the spatial domain, by multiplying the spectrum with a filter H(u, v). The key fact behind everything here is the convolution theorem: convolving the image with a kernel in space is the same as multiplying their transforms. So a "multiply" in frequency equals a "slide and sum" in space.

What a frequency filter is: A filter H(u, v) is a 2D array the same size as the (padded) spectrum. Each entry is a number, usually between 0 and 1, that says how much of that frequency to keep. 1 means keep fully, 0 means remove, 0.5 means keep half. We multiply each spectrum value F(u, v) by H(u, v) to get G(u, v) = H(u, v) F(u, v), then take the inverse DFT to get the filtered image. Most filters in this lesson are circularly symmetric: they only depend on the distance D(u, v) from the centre of the centred spectrum, not on the direction. This is why we talk about a "cutoff radius" D0.

The step-by-step procedure: Step 1, take the M x N image f(x, y) and pad it with zeros to size P x Q, usually P = 2M and Q = 2N, to avoid wraparound error (lesson 11 explained why circular convolution needs this). Step 2, multiply the padded image by (-1)^(x+y) so the zero frequency moves to the centre of the spectrum. Step 3, compute the DFT F(u, v). Step 4, build a real, symmetric filter H(u, v) of size P x Q, centred at (P/2, Q/2). Step 5, multiply element by element: G = H F. Step 6, take the inverse DFT, keep the real part (tiny imaginary parts are just rounding error), and multiply again by (-1)^(x+y). Step 7, crop the top-left M x N region. That is the final image. Forgetting step 6's real part or step 7's crop are classic lab mistakes.

Measuring distance in the spectrum: For a centred P x Q spectrum, D(u, v) = sqrt((u - P/2)^2 + (v - Q/2)^2). Worked example: a 512 x 512 image padded to 1024 x 1024 has its centre at (512, 512). The point (542, 552) is 30 steps down and 40 steps right, so D = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = sqrt(2500) = 50. Small D means low frequency, large D means high frequency.

Ideal lowpass filter (ILPF): H(u, v) = 1 if D(u, v) <= D0, and 0 if D(u, v) > D0. It is a sharp circular "cookie cutter": everything inside the circle passes untouched, everything outside is thrown away. With D0 = 50, the point at D = 49 is fully kept and the point at D = 51 is fully removed. It sounds perfect, but it has a famous side effect called ringing: around every edge in the blurred image you see faint ripples, like water rings. The reason is the convolution theorem in reverse. A sharp-edged box in frequency corresponds in space to a function shaped like a sinc (in 2D, a circular version of it), which has a main bump plus many smaller positive and negative ripples around it. Convolving the image with that ripply kernel copies the ripples next to every edge. The smaller D0 is, the wider the ripples. So the ideal filter is mainly a teaching tool, not a practical one.

Butterworth lowpass filter (BLPF): H(u, v) = 1 / (1 + (D / D0)^(2n)), where n is the order. At D = D0 the value is always exactly 0.5, whatever n is. Worked with D0 = 50 and n = 2: at D = 25, H = 1 / (1 + 0.5^4) = 1 / 1.0625 = about 0.941; at D = 50, H = 0.5; at D = 100, H = 1 / (1 + 2^4) = 1 / 17 = about 0.059. So the filter falls smoothly instead of jumping. The order n is a knob: n = 1 has no visible ringing, n = 2 has very little and is a common choice, and as n grows large the Butterworth filter approaches the ideal filter and the ringing comes back.

Gaussian lowpass filter (GLPF): H(u, v) = exp(-D^2 / (2 D0^2)). Worked with D0 = 50 (so 2 D0^2 = 5000): at D = 25, H = exp(-625/5000) = about 0.882; at D = 50, H = exp(-0.5) = about 0.607; at D = 100, H = exp(-2) = about 0.135. The great property of the Gaussian is that its inverse transform is also a Gaussian, which is a smooth single bump with no negative ripples. Therefore a Gaussian lowpass filter never produces ringing. The price: for the same D0 it is a little less sharp at cutting high frequencies than a Butterworth of order 2. In practice the Gaussian is the safe default.

Highpass filters: A highpass filter keeps fast changes and removes slow ones, so it sharpens and finds edges. The simplest way to make one is H_hp(u, v) = 1 - H_lp(u, v). So the ideal highpass is 0 inside the circle and 1 outside, the Butterworth highpass is 1 / (1 + (D0 / D)^(2n)), and the Gaussian highpass is 1 - exp(-D^2 / (2 D0^2)). Worked with the Gaussian and D0 = 50: at D = 25, H = 1 - 0.882 = about 0.118; at D = 50, about 0.393; at D = 100, about 0.865. Notice that at D = 0 every highpass filter is 0. The value at the centre, F(0, 0), is the average brightness of the whole image (lesson 11), so removing it makes the average zero. The output looks like a mostly black image with bright edges. That is why we often add the original image back.

The Laplacian in the frequency domain: Lesson 10 used the Laplacian kernel for sharpening. Its frequency version is H(u, v) = -4 pi^2 D^2(u, v). It grows with the square of the distance, so it boosts high frequencies strongly. To sharpen we compute the Laplacian image, scale it to a sensible range, and use g = f - c times Laplacian, the same idea as lesson 10. Scale carefully: normalise f to [0, 1] and the Laplacian to [-1, 1] before combining, or the result overflows.

Unsharp masking and high-frequency emphasis: In lesson 10, unsharp masking was "original plus k times (original minus blurred)". In frequency, original minus lowpass equals highpass, so g = inverse DFT of [1 + k H_hp(u, v)] F(u, v). With k = 1 this is unsharp masking; with k > 1 it is highboost. A more general form is high-frequency emphasis: [k1 + k2 H_hp] F, where k1 (like 0.5) controls how much of the original stays and k2 (like 0.75) controls how much the edges are boosted. Medical X-rays are a classic case: the chest X-ray is low contrast and blurry, high-frequency emphasis makes the bone edges crisp, and then histogram equalisation (lesson 07) brings up the contrast.

Homomorphic filtering: Lesson 02 introduced the image formation model f = i x r, illumination times reflectance. Illumination changes slowly across a scene (a shadow, a window light), so it lives in low frequencies. Reflectance changes quickly at object edges, so it lives in high frequencies. But they are multiplied, and the Fourier transform of a product is not the product of transforms. The trick is to take the logarithm first: ln f = ln i + ln r. Now they are added, so we can filter them separately. Steps: take ln, DFT, multiply by a filter H that is gammaL (less than 1) at low frequencies and gammaH (greater than 1) at high frequencies, inverse DFT, then exp to undo the log.

Homomorphic worked example: take gammaL = 0.5 and gammaH = 2, and imagine the filter perfectly separates the two parts, so the output is roughly i^0.5 x r^2. A pixel in shadow has i = 100 and r = 0.5, giving 50. A pixel in sunlight has i = 400 and the same r = 0.5, giving 200. The ratio between them is 4. After filtering: shadow pixel 10 x 0.25 = 2.5, sunny pixel 20 x 0.25 = 5, ratio only 2. The lighting difference got squeezed. Now two different surfaces under the same light, r = 0.2 and r = 0.8 with i = 100: before, 20 and 80 (ratio 4); after, 10 x 0.04 = 0.4 and 10 x 0.64 = 6.4 (ratio 16). The surface detail got stretched. That is the whole point: compress the lighting range, expand the detail contrast. Afterwards we rescale to 0 to 255. Real filters are smooth (a Gaussian-shaped high-emphasis filter), so the separation is approximate, but the effect is the same.

Notch filters and periodic noise: Some noise is periodic, a repeating pattern of stripes. Mains interference in an old camera, a scanned newspaper photo with its halftone dot grid that causes moire, or the scan lines in a satellite image. A sine pattern in space shows up in the spectrum as a pair of bright spikes placed symmetrically about the centre, at (u0, v0) and at the mirror point. In the spatial domain the stripes are spread over the whole picture and are hard to remove, but in frequency they are just a few bright dots. A notch reject filter puts small "holes" (zeros, or smooth Gaussian dips) exactly at those spike positions and their mirrors, and is 1 everywhere else. Remove the dots, invert, and the stripes vanish while almost everything else stays. A notch pass filter does the opposite: it keeps only those spikes, giving you an image of the noise pattern itself, which helps you check what you are removing.

Spatial or frequency, which is cheaper? For small kernels, spatial filtering wins. A 3 x 3 kernel on a 1024 x 1024 image needs about 9 multiplications per pixel, around 9.4 million in total. The frequency route needs padding to 2048 x 2048, and one 2D FFT of that size costs on the order of N log2 N with N = 2048^2, about 92 million basic operations, and you need a forward and an inverse transform. But for a 101 x 101 kernel, direct spatial filtering costs about 10,201 multiplications per pixel, roughly 10.7 billion in total, and the FFT route becomes far cheaper. Rule of thumb: small kernels, go spatial; large kernels or filters that are naturally defined in frequency (notches, homomorphic), go frequency.

Real-life example 1, a scanned Prothom Alo photo: Suppose you scan an old printed newspaper photo of a cricket match at the Mirpur stadium. Printed photos are made of tiny halftone dots, and the scanner's own pixel grid beats against the dot grid, so you see a wavy moire pattern. Step 1, compute and display the log spectrum (lesson 06's log transform makes it visible). Step 2, you see a few bright, symmetric star-like spikes away from the centre. Step 3, place Butterworth notch reject filters on each spike and its mirror. Step 4, inverse transform. The waves disappear, the players are still there. Tuning the notch radius matters: too small and some pattern remains, too large and you remove real detail.

Real-life example 2, a classroom photo with a bright window: A teacher in a Sylhet school takes a photo of a whiteboard, but one side is lit by a window and the other side is in shadow. Global contrast stretching cannot fix both sides at once. Homomorphic filtering with gammaL around 0.5 and gammaH around 1.5 to 2 pulls the dark and bright sides closer together while keeping the marker writing sharp. Then simple thresholding (lesson 21) can turn the board into clean black-on-white notes.

Common mistakes: Not padding, which makes the edges of the output contaminated by wraparound from the opposite side. Forgetting to centre, so the filter's circle is placed in the corner of an uncentred spectrum and does nothing sensible. Building H with a different size from the padded spectrum. Taking the absolute value instead of the real part after the inverse transform. Expecting an ideal filter to be "best" and being surprised by ringing.
