Applying a highpass filter and thinking the image is broken because the average dropped to zero. For homomorphic filtering, taking ln of zero: add 1 first, ln(1 + f), and undo with exp(...) - 1.

What exams ask: compute ILPF, BLPF and GLPF values at a given D, explain ringing, derive highpass from lowpass, list the filtering steps, explain the homomorphic log trick and why notch spikes come in symmetric pairs.

Recap: Frequency filtering multiplies the spectrum by H(u, v) and inverts. Lowpass blurs, highpass sharpens, and 1 - lowpass gives highpass. Ideal filters ring, Butterworth trades with its order, Gaussian never rings. Homomorphic filtering uses ln to separate illumination from reflectance. Notch filters wipe out periodic noise that is easy to see as spikes in the spectrum. Next, lesson 13 starts image restoration: what noise looks like and how to model it.
key_points: Frequency-domain filtering computes G(u, v) = H(u, v) F(u, v) on a padded, centred spectrum and then takes the real part of the inverse DFT and crops.
D(u, v) is the distance from the spectrum centre; small D means low frequency, large D means high frequency.
The ideal lowpass filter causes ringing because its spatial counterpart is a ripply sinc-like kernel.
Butterworth H = 1 / (1 + (D/D0)^(2n)) is 0.5 at D0; higher order n means sharper cutoff and more ringing.
Gaussian H = exp(-D^2 / (2 D0^2)) never rings because a Gaussian transforms to a Gaussian.
A highpass filter is 1 minus a lowpass; unsharp masking and high-frequency emphasis add a boosted highpass back to the image.
Homomorphic filtering takes ln to separate illumination (low frequency) from reflectance (high frequency), then compresses one and boosts the other.
Notch reject filters remove periodic noise that shows up as symmetric spikes in the spectrum.
lessons.tip: Always look at the log of the spectrum before choosing a filter. If you can see the problem in the spectrum, such as bright spikes or an overly large bright blob, the filter design usually becomes obvious.
lessons.task: On paper, draw a circle for D0 = 50 and compute Butterworth (n = 2) and Gaussian lowpass values at D = 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100. Plot both curves on the same axes and mark where each one crosses 0.5. If you have Python, apply both filters to a photo with NumPy's fft2 and compare the edges for ringing.

quiz.q: For a centred 1024 x 1024 spectrum, what is D at point (542, 552)?
quiz.explain: The centre is (512, 512). The point is 30 and 40 steps away, so D = sqrt(900 + 1600) = 50.

quiz.q: Why does the ideal lowpass filter produce ringing?
options: Its spatial counterpart is a sinc-like kernel with ripples
It amplifies noise at high frequencies
quiz.explain: A sharp box in frequency corresponds to a ripply sinc-like function in space, and convolving with it copies ripples next to edges.

quiz.q: What is the value of any Butterworth lowpass filter at D = D0?
quiz.explain: At D = D0, (D/D0)^(2n) = 1, so H = 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5 for every order n.

quiz.q: In homomorphic filtering, why do we take the logarithm first?
options: To turn the product i x r into a sum so each part can be filtered separately
quiz.explain: The Fourier transform cannot separate a product, but after ln, ln i + ln r is a sum and the filter acts on each term.

quiz.q: A scanned newspaper photo shows a moire pattern. Which filter is the best fit?
options: Notch reject filter at the spectrum spikes
quiz.explain: Periodic patterns appear as symmetric spikes; a notch reject filter removes just those frequencies.

lessons.title: Noise Models and the Image Degradation Model
lessons.content:
Take a photo of your room at night with a phone and zoom in on a dark wall. Instead of a smooth gray, you see tiny coloured speckles that dance from photo to photo. Nobody painted those dots on your wall. They were added by the camera on the way from the light to the file. That unwanted extra is called noise. Before we can remove it, we have to describe it carefully: where it comes from, what values it takes, and how often. That description is called a noise model, and it is the topic of this lesson.

Enhancement vs restoration: Lessons 06 to 12 were mostly about enhancement, which means making an image look better to a human, and "better" is partly a matter of taste. Restoration is different. It tries to recover the original, true image from a damaged one, using a mathematical model of the damage. Because it has a model, it also has a clear goal: get as close to the original as possible. Lessons 13, 14 and 15 form the restoration block: this lesson builds the model and the noise types, lesson 14 removes noise with spatial filters, and lesson 15 undoes blur with inverse and Wiener filters.

The degradation model: The standard model is g(x, y) = h(x, y) * f(x, y) + eta(x, y). Here f is the true image we want, h is the degradation function (for example a blur caused by motion or a bad lens), * means convolution, eta (the Greek letter, written as a word here) is additive noise, and g is what we actually get. In frequency, using the convolution theorem from lesson 11, this becomes G(u, v) = H(u, v) F(u, v) + N(u, v). Read it as a story: the camera first smears the scene with h, then sprinkles noise on top. The model assumes h is linear and position invariant (the same blur everywhere), which is not always true, but works surprisingly often.

Where noise comes from: During capture, image sensors (CCD and CMOS, lesson 02) count photons, and that count is naturally random, especially in low light when there are few photons. Heat inside the sensor creates electrons that look like light (thermal noise), which is why long exposures and hot phones look noisier. The electronics that amplify and digitise the signal add their own noise. During transmission, a faulty channel or a bad memory cell can flip pixels to extreme values. Interference from electrical or mechanical sources can add a repeating pattern. Each source tends to produce a different kind of noise, with a different probability shape.

Describing noise with a PDF: We treat the noise value at each pixel as a random variable and describe it with a probability density function (PDF), recalling Probability & Statistics (deep-cse-2-6). The PDF tells us which noise values are likely. For most models in this lesson we also assume the noise is independent of position and not correlated with the image. A PDF has a mean (average value) and a variance (how spread out it is); the standard deviation sigma is the square root of the variance.

Gaussian noise: The most used model. p(z) = (1 / (sqrt(2 pi) sigma)) exp(-(z - zbar)^2 / (2 sigma^2)), a bell curve centred at the mean zbar. About 68% of values fall within one sigma of the mean and about 95% within two sigma. Worked: if a pixel's true value is 120 and the noise has mean 0 and sigma 10, then about 68% of such pixels will read between 110 and 130, and about 95% between 100 and 140. Gaussian noise comes from electronic circuits and sensor noise caused by poor light or high temperature. It is mathematically friendly, which is one reason it is used even when it is only approximately right.

Rayleigh noise: p(z) = (2/b)(z - a) exp(-(z - a)^2 / b) for z >= a, and 0 below a. Mean = a + sqrt(pi b / 4) and variance = b(4 - pi) / 4. Worked with a = 0 and b = 100: mean = sqrt(25 pi), about 8.86, and variance about 21.46. Its shape is lopsided, leaning to the left with a long tail to the right. It is a good model for noise in range imaging and some radar-type images.

Erlang (gamma) and exponential noise: Erlang noise has p(z) = a^b z^(b-1) exp(-az) / (b - 1)! for z >= 0, with a > 0 and b a positive integer. Mean = b / a and variance = b / a^2. Worked with a = 0.2 and b = 2: mean 10, variance 50. Exponential noise is the special case b = 1: p(z) = a exp(-az), mean 1/a and variance 1/a^2, so a = 0.1 gives mean 10 and variance 100. These appear in laser imaging, where speckle-type effects follow such shapes.

Uniform noise: p(z) = 1 / (b - a) for a <= z <= b, and 0 elsewhere. Every value in the range is equally likely. Mean = (a + b)/2 and variance = (b - a)^2 / 12. Worked with a = -20 and b = 20: mean 0, variance 1600/12, about 133.3, so sigma is about 11.5. Uniform noise is rare as a physical model but useful in simulations, and it is the classic model for quantisation error from lesson 03, where rounding to the nearest level gives an error spread evenly over half a step either side.

Impulse (salt-and-pepper) noise: Here each pixel is either left alone or replaced by an extreme value. With probability Pa it becomes very dark (pepper, often 0), with probability Pb it becomes very bright (salt, often 255), and otherwise it stays as it was. Worked: in a 1000 x 1000 image with Pa = Pb = 0.05, about 50,000 pixels turn black and about 50,000 turn white, so roughly 10% of the image is ruined, while the other 90% is perfect. That "few pixels completely wrong, the rest perfect" nature is why averaging filters handle it badly and the median filter (lesson 09, and lesson 14) handles it so well. Sources include faulty switching, bit errors in transmission, and dead or stuck sensor pixels.

Periodic noise: This noise is a repeating pattern, such as eta(x, y) = A sin(2 pi u0 x / M + 2 pi v0 y / N), coming from electrical or electromechanical interference during capture. It is the only noise type in this lesson that depends on position. In the spatial domain it shows up as stripes or a fine grid. In the frequency domain it shows up as pairs of bright spikes symmetric about the centre, which is exactly why lesson 12 removed it with notch filters. A good habit is to always check the spectrum: if you see such spikes, you have periodic noise.

Seeing the PDF in a histogram: How do you know which noise you have? Take a test image made of a few flat regions, for example three gray levels of a plain chart, add noise, and look at the histogram (lesson 07). Each flat region was a single spike in the clean histogram. With noise, each spike spreads into the shape of the noise PDF: a bell for Gaussian, a lopsided hump for Rayleigh, a flat block for uniform. With salt-and-pepper, the spikes stay sharp but two new spikes appear at 0 and 255. The noise PDF is literally printed on the histogram.

Estimating noise from a flat patch: In real life you rarely know the noise parameters, but you can estimate them. Find a small region of the image that should be constant, like a plain wall, the sky or a blank part of a document. Any variation there must be noise. Worked: suppose ten pixels from a plain wall read 98, 102, 100, 105, 95, 101, 99, 97, 103, 100. The mean is 1000/10 = 100. The squared differences from the mean are 4, 4, 0, 25, 25, 1, 1, 9, 9, 0, which add up to 78, so the variance is 78/10 = 7.8 and sigma is about 2.79. If the histogram of the patch looks like a bell, you would model this as Gaussian noise with sigma near 2.8. For impulse noise you would instead count the fraction of pixels stuck at 0 and at 255 to estimate Pa and Pb. In practice you use a patch of hundreds of pixels, not ten.

Signal-to-noise ratio: To say how noisy an image is in one number we use the signal-to-noise ratio, the power of the signal divided by the power of the noise. Often it is given in decibels: SNR in dB = 10 log10(signal power / noise power). Worked: a region with true value 100 has signal power 100^2 = 10,000; Gaussian noise with sigma = 5 has power 25; the ratio is 400, and 10 log10(400) is about 26 dB. Halving the noise sigma quadruples the ratio and adds about 6 dB. Higher SNR is better. PSNR, which you will meet in lesson 24 on compression, is a close cousin that uses the peak value 255 instead of the actual signal.

The noise-only case: If the only degradation is noise (h does nothing), the model becomes g = f + eta. We cannot simply subtract the noise, because we only know its statistics, not its exact values. So we filter: we use the neighbourhood of each pixel to guess the true value. That is lesson 14. Periodic noise is the exception, since it can be removed in frequency (lesson 12). When there is also blur (h is not identity), we need the deconvolution tools of lesson 15.

Real-life example 1, Dhaka night CCTV: A shop in Mohammadpur records CCTV at night. Few photons reach the sensor, the camera raises its gain, and Gaussian-like noise grows. Step 1, the technician grabs a few frames and picks a patch of plain shutter. Step 2, computes the mean and sigma of that patch, say sigma about 12. Step 3, checks the histogram: bell-shaped, so Gaussian. Step 4, chooses a smoothing or adaptive filter (lesson 14) and, because the camera is fixed, averages several frames of the still background, which reduces noise variance by the number of frames (lesson 04). Knowing the model turned guesswork into a plan.

Real-life example 2, a satellite photo of the Sundarbans: A satellite image received over a noisy link has scattered black and white pixels from bit errors, plus faint diagonal stripes from sensor electronics. The histogram shows extra spikes at 0 and 255 (impulse), and the spectrum shows a pair of bright symmetric points (periodic). So the correct plan is two separate tools: a median-type filter for the impulse noise and a notch filter for the stripes. Using one big blur for both would smear the river channels that the scientists actually want to map.

Common mistakes: Calling every noise "Gaussian" without looking. Mixing up enhancement (look nicer) and restoration (recover the truth). Thinking noise can be subtracted directly; only its statistics are known. Estimating noise from a patch that contains real texture or an edge, which inflates the variance. Forgetting that variance is in squared units while sigma is in gray levels. Ignoring that impulse noise ruins a few pixels totally rather than all pixels a little.

What exams ask: Write the degradation model in space and frequency. Draw the PDF shapes of Gaussian, Rayleigh, Erlang, exponential, uniform and impulse noise, and give their means and variances. Compute mean and variance from a small patch. Explain how periodic noise appears in the spectrum. Match noise types to their physical sources. Compute an SNR in dB.

Recap: Restoration recovers a true image using a model, g = h * f + eta. Noise is described by its PDF: Gaussian (electronics, low light), Rayleigh (range imaging), Erlang and exponential (laser imaging), uniform (quantisation, simulation), impulse (bit errors, faulty pixels) and periodic (interference). Histograms of flat regions reveal the PDF, and flat patches give the parameters. Next, lesson 14 uses this knowledge to choose the right spatial filter for each noise type.
key_points: Restoration recovers the true image with a model of the damage; enhancement only makes it look better.
The degradation model is g = h * f + eta in space, or G = H F + N in frequency.
Gaussian noise: about 68% of values within one sigma and 95% within two sigma; comes from electronics and low light.
Rayleigh, Erlang, exponential and uniform noise each have their own PDF shape, mean and variance (uniform variance = (b - a)^2 / 12).
Salt-and-pepper (impulse) noise ruins a few pixels completely: with Pa = Pb = 0.05 about 10% of pixels turn black or white.
Periodic noise depends on position and shows up as symmetric spike pairs in the spectrum.
Noise parameters are estimated from the mean and variance of a flat patch, whose histogram reveals the PDF shape.
SNR in dB = 10 log10(signal power / noise power); halving the noise sigma adds about 6 dB.
lessons.tip: Whenever you face a noisy image, ask three questions in order: what does the histogram of a flat area look like, are there spikes in the spectrum, and is there blur too? The answers choose your filter for you.
lessons.task: Compute the mean, variance and sigma of these 8 pixel values from a plain wall by hand: 52, 48, 50, 55, 45, 50, 49, 51. Then take a photo of a plain wall in dim light with your phone, zoom in, and describe whether the speckles look like small random changes (Gaussian-like) or isolated black and white dots (impulse-like).

quiz.q: Which equation is the standard degradation model in the spatial domain?
quiz.explain: The image is convolved with the degradation function h, and additive noise eta is added.

quiz.q: For uniform noise between a = -20 and b = 20, what is the variance?
Ten flat-patch pixels have squared deviations from the mean adding up to 78. What is the variance?
quiz.explain: Variance = 78 / 10 = 7.8, and sigma is its square root, about 2.79.

quiz.q: How does periodic noise usually appear in the Fourier spectrum?
options: As a bright DC term only
As pairs of bright spikes symmetric about the centre
It does not appear at all
quiz.explain: A sinusoidal pattern transforms to a pair of impulses placed symmetrically about the origin.

quiz.q: A signal power of 10,000 and noise power of 25 give an SNR of about...
quiz.explain: The ratio is 400, and 10 log10(400) is about 26 dB.

lessons.title: Restoration with Spatial Filters: Mean, Order-Statistic and Adaptive Filters
lessons.content:
Think of a class of 30 students taking a test, and you want to know how well the class really did. If one student fell asleep and scored 0, and another copied from a topper and scored 100, the plain average gets pulled around by those two. A smart teacher might throw out the lowest and highest marks, or just look at the middle student's score. Restoring a noisy image with spatial filters is the same kind of thinking. For each pixel we look at a small window of neighbours and decide, based on what kind of "cheating" the noise does, which kind of average gives the most honest answer.

Where this fits: Lesson 13 described noise types and the model g = f + eta when only noise is present. Lessons 09 and 10 introduced the box (mean) and median filters for enhancement. Here we widen the toolbox to the full restoration family: four mean filters, five order-statistic filters, and two adaptive filters that change their behaviour based on local statistics. Notation: S_xy is the window (say m x n pixels) centred at (x, y), g(s, t) are the noisy values inside it, and the output is our estimate of f at (x, y).

Arithmetic mean filter: The plain average: f = (1 / mn) times the sum of g(s, t) over S_xy. It smooths local variation, so Gaussian or uniform noise shrinks, but it also blurs edges. Worked on a pepper hit: a 3 x 3 window with eight pixels of 100 and one pepper pixel of 0. The average is 800/9, about 88.9, so the dark dot is not removed, only smudged into a gray patch. On a salt hit (eight 100s and one 255), the average is 1055/9, about 117.2, again a smudge.

Geometric mean filter: f = (product of all g(s, t) in S_xy) raised to the power 1/mn. It smooths about as well as the arithmetic mean but tends to keep a little more image detail. Worked on the salt window: the ninth root of 100^8 times 255 is about 111.0, closer to 100 than the arithmetic mean's 117.2. But one zero in the window makes the whole product zero, so a single pepper pixel turns the output black. Geometric mean is a bad choice when there is pepper noise.

Harmonic mean filter: f = mn divided by the sum of 1 / g(s, t). Worked on the salt window: 9 / (8/100 + 1/255) is about 107.2, better still. Large values contribute tiny 1/g terms, so salt gets ignored. But a pepper pixel of 0 means 1/0, so it fails badly on pepper. It also works well on Gaussian noise.

Contraharmonic mean filter: f = (sum of g^(Q+1)) divided by (sum of g^Q), where Q is the order of the filter. This one has a knob. Q = 0 gives the arithmetic mean and Q = -1 gives the harmonic mean. Positive Q weights large values more, so it removes pepper. Negative Q weights small values more, so it removes salt. Worked with the pepper window and Q = 1.5: the zero contributes 0^2.5 = 0 to the top and 0^1.5 = 0 to the bottom, so the result is (8 x 100^2.5) / (8 x 100^1.5) = 100 exactly. Pepper gone. Worked with the salt window and Q = -1.5: the result is about 104.6; with Q = -3 it is about 101.2. The catch: you must know which noise you have. Use the wrong sign and the filter makes things worse, for example positive Q on salt noise brightens everything near the salt. It also cannot handle salt and pepper at the same time.

Order-statistic filters: These sort the pixels in the window and pick based on rank, not on a weighted sum. They are nonlinear. We use one example window for all of them: 10, 12, 11, 255, 13, 0, 12, 11, 14, which contains one salt (255) and one pepper (0) around a true level near 12. Sorted: 0, 10, 11, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 255. For comparison, the arithmetic mean is 338/9, about 37.6, which is badly wrong.

Median filter: Pick the middle value of the sorted list, the 5th of 9: 12. Both impulses are simply ignored because they sit at the ends of the list. The median removes impulse noise very well while keeping edges sharper than a mean filter of the same size, because it always outputs a value that actually exists in the window rather than inventing a mixed gray. If noise is dense, you can apply it twice or use a larger window, at the cost of losing thin lines and corners.

Max and min filters: Max picks the largest value (here 255) and min picks the smallest (here 0). So max filters remove pepper (dark dots) and also find the brightest points; min filters remove salt and find the darkest points. They also grow bright or dark areas, which is why they reappear in lesson 19 as grayscale dilation and erosion.

Midpoint filter: The average of max and min: (0 + 255) / 2 = 127.5 on our window, which is terrible here. Midpoint works best on randomly distributed noise like Gaussian or uniform noise, where the extremes are not wild. It combines order statistics with averaging.

Alpha-trimmed mean filter: Sort the window, delete the d/2 lowest and d/2 highest values, and average the remaining mn - d. With d = 2 on our window we remove 0 and 255 and average 10, 11, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14: 83/7, about 11.86. With d = 0 it is the arithmetic mean; with d = mn - 1 it becomes the median. It shines on mixed noise, for example Gaussian noise plus some salt-and-pepper: trimming removes the impulses and averaging the rest reduces the Gaussian part.

Adaptive local noise reduction filter: The filters above treat every pixel the same. An adaptive filter looks at local statistics and changes its action. Given the overall noise variance sigma_eta^2 (estimated from a flat patch, lesson 13), the local mean m_L and local variance sigma_L^2 in S_xy, the output is f = g - (sigma_eta^2 / sigma_L^2)(g - m_L). The logic: if sigma_eta^2 is zero, there is no noise, return g. If sigma_L^2 is much bigger than sigma_eta^2, the window probably contains an edge, so keep g almost unchanged. If the two variances are about equal, the window is flat plus noise, so return roughly the local mean. Worked: g = 130, m_L = 120, sigma_eta^2 = 100, sigma_L^2 = 400. The ratio is 0.25, so f = 130 - 0.25 x 10 = 127.5. A small correction, because the area has more variation than noise alone would explain. In practice, if the ratio comes out above 1, we clip it to 1 so the output never overshoots the local mean.

Adaptive median filter: The plain median struggles when impulse noise is dense (say more than about 20% of pixels), and a big fixed window blurs detail. The adaptive median grows its window only where needed and replaces a pixel only if it looks like an impulse. Let z_min, z_max, z_med be the min, max and median in S_xy, z_xy the centre value, and S_max the largest allowed window. Stage A: A1 = z_med - z_min and A2 = z_med - z_max. If A1 > 0 and A2 < 0, the median is not itself an impulse, go to stage B. Otherwise grow the window; if it exceeds S_max, output z_med. Stage B: B1 = z_xy - z_min and B2 = z_xy - z_max. If B1 > 0 and B2 < 0, the centre is not an impulse, output z_xy unchanged. Otherwise output z_med.

Adaptive median worked: Use our window with the centre z_xy = 255. Here z_min = 0, z_max = 255, z_med = 12. Stage A: A1 = 12 > 0 and A2 = 12 - 255 < 0, go to B. Stage B: B1 = 255 > 0 but B2 = 255 - 255 = 0, not below zero, so the centre is an impulse; output 12. Now suppose the centre were 13 instead. Then B1 = 13 > 0 and B2 = 13 - 255 < 0, so 13 is kept untouched. That is the beauty of it: unlike the plain median, good pixels are never changed, so fine detail survives. It can clean images with very heavy salt-and-pepper (such as 25% salt and 25% pepper) with S_max = 7 where a 7 x 7 plain median would blur heavily.

Choosing a filter for each noise type: Gaussian or uniform noise: arithmetic or geometric mean, or the adaptive local filter if you want edges kept. Salt only: harmonic or contraharmonic with negative Q, or min. Pepper only: contraharmonic with positive Q, or max. Salt and pepper together: median, or adaptive median when the noise is dense. Gaussian plus impulses: alpha-trimmed mean. Periodic noise: not a spatial job at all, use notch filters (lesson 12). Always check the result: compare a flat patch's variance before and after, and inspect edges by zooming in.

Real-life example 1, a damaged old family photo: A family in Rajshahi scans a 1980s photo full of white specks from dust and black dots from scratches, roughly 10% of pixels. Step 1, the histogram shows spikes at both 0 and 255, so it is salt-and-pepper. Step 2, a 3 x 3 median removes most dots but softens grandfather's moustache slightly. Step 3, switching to an adaptive median with S_max = 7 removes the dots and leaves untouched pixels exactly as they were, so the fine hair stays crisp. Step 4, a light contrast stretch (lesson 06) finishes the job.

Real-life example 2, a low-light hospital ultrasound or camera feed: A rural clinic's camera captures images of a patient's skin rash for a remote doctor in Dhaka. In dim light, the images have Gaussian-like noise with sigma about 8 from a flat patch. A plain 5 x 5 mean would blur the rash borders that the doctor needs. The adaptive local noise reduction filter, given sigma_eta^2 = 64, smooths the flat skin (where local variance is near 64) and leaves the rash border (where local variance is much larger) almost alone.

Common mistakes: Using a mean filter on salt-and-pepper and calling the result clean. Choosing the wrong sign of Q in the contraharmonic filter. Using a geometric or harmonic mean with pepper zeros (product zero, division by zero). Forgetting that order-statistic filters are nonlinear, so they cannot be done with a single convolution or in the frequency domain. Making the window too big, which erases thin lines. Not clipping the ratio in the adaptive local filter.

What exams ask: Apply the arithmetic, geometric, harmonic, contraharmonic, median, max, min, midpoint and alpha-trimmed filters to a given 3 x 3 window by hand. State which Q removes salt and which removes pepper. Explain the adaptive local filter's three cases. Trace the adaptive median's stages A and B on a window. Match filters to noise types.

Recap: Mean filters average (arithmetic, geometric, harmonic, contraharmonic with Q as the salt/pepper knob). Order-statistic filters rank (median for impulses, max and min for one-sided impulses, midpoint for Gaussian or uniform, alpha-trimmed for mixtures). Adaptive filters use local statistics to protect edges and good pixels. Next, lesson 15 tackles the harder case where the image is also blurred, using inverse and Wiener filtering.
key_points: Arithmetic mean blurs impulses into gray smudges; geometric and harmonic means handle salt but fail on pepper zeros.
Contraharmonic mean: positive Q removes pepper, negative Q removes salt; Q = 0 is the arithmetic mean and Q = -1 the harmonic mean.
Order-statistic filters sort the window: median removes salt-and-pepper while keeping edges better than a mean.
Max removes pepper and min removes salt; midpoint suits Gaussian or uniform noise.
Alpha-trimmed mean drops d extreme values and averages the rest, ideal for Gaussian plus impulse noise.
Adaptive local filter: f = g - (sigma_eta^2 / sigma_L^2)(g - m_L), which keeps edges where local variance is high.
Adaptive median grows its window when needed and only replaces pixels that look like impulses, so good pixels stay untouched.
Periodic noise is removed in frequency with notch filters, not with spatial filters.
lessons.tip: Practise every filter on the same small 3 x 3 window until you can do it in your head; the exam loves one window with a salt, a pepper and a question asking which filter wins.
lessons.task: Take the window 20, 22, 21, 255, 23, 0, 22, 21, 24. By hand, compute its arithmetic mean, median, midpoint, max, min and alpha-trimmed mean with d = 2, then decide which one best estimates the true value near 22.

quiz.q: A 3 x 3 window has eight pixels of 100 and one pepper pixel of 0. What does the contraharmonic mean with Q = 1.5 output?
quiz.explain: 0 raised to positive powers is 0, so it contributes nothing; the result is (8 x 100^2.5)/(8 x 100^1.5) = 100.

quiz.q: Which filter is the worst choice for an image with pepper noise?
quiz.explain: A single zero makes the product zero, so the geometric mean outputs black where pepper appears.

quiz.q: For the window 10, 12, 11, 255, 13, 0, 12, 11, 14, what is the alpha-trimmed mean with d = 2?
quiz.explain: Remove 0 and 255, then average the other seven values: 83/7, about 11.86.

quiz.q: Adaptive local filter: g = 130, m_L = 120, sigma_eta^2 = 100, sigma_L^2 = 400. What is the output?

lessons.title: Estimating the Degradation Function, Inverse Filtering and Wiener Filtering
lessons.content:
You are on a rickshaw in Old Dhaka, the road is bumpy, and you snap a photo of a beautiful old building. At home you see it is smeared sideways: every window has a ghostly copy beside it. The details are not lost forever. They were mixed up in a very specific way, like paint spread by a brush moving in one direction. If you know how the brush moved, can you un-spread the paint? This lesson says: often yes, partly, as long as you are careful about noise. This is called deblurring, or deconvolution.

Where this fits: Lesson 13 gave the full model g = h * f + eta, or in frequency G(u, v) = H(u, v) F(u, v) + N(u, v). Lesson 14 handled the case where h does nothing and only noise is present. Now h is a real blur. Restoration then has two jobs: estimate H (what the blur was) and then invert it without letting noise explode. The three classic ways to estimate H are observation, experimentation and mathematical modelling, and the two classic ways to invert are the inverse filter and the Wiener filter, with constrained least squares as a third option.

The point spread function: The function h is called the point spread function (PSF) because it tells you what happens to a single point of light. A perfect camera turns a point into a point. A blurry camera turns it into a small blob, a shaken camera turns it into a short line. Worked in 1D: take a row with a single bright pixel, 0, 0, 90, 0, 0, and blur it by averaging each pixel with its left and right neighbours. The output is 0, 30, 30, 30, 0. That spread pattern, three equal values of one third, is the PSF. Because the system is assumed linear and position invariant, knowing what happens to one point tells you what happens to every image, since every image is just many points added together.

Estimating H by observation: If you have only the blurred photo, look for a small region where the signal is strong and noise is low, for example a sharp dark letter on a white sign. Call this subimage g_s. Then build by hand or by processing your best guess of what that small region should look like unblurred, f_s. The ratio H_s(u, v) = G_s(u, v) / F_s(u, v) gives an estimate of the blur in that region, and because the blur is assumed to be the same everywhere, you use it for the whole image. It is a detective method: rough but often good enough.

Estimating H by experiment: If you have access to the same camera, you can measure the blur directly. Set up the same settings, and photograph a tiny bright dot of light (an approximation of an impulse) on a dark background. The image you get is the PSF itself. In frequency, the transform of an impulse of strength A is just the constant A, so H(u, v) = G(u, v) / A. Optical engineers measure lenses like this, and microscopes are often calibrated by imaging tiny fluorescent beads.

Estimating H by modelling, atmospheric turbulence: Some blurs follow physics. For long-distance imaging through air, Hufnagel and Stanley proposed the model H(u, v) = exp(-k (u^2 + v^2)^(5/6)), where k describes how strong the turbulence is. Textbook examples use k = 0.0025 for severe, 0.001 for mild and 0.00025 for low turbulence. The shape is close to a Gaussian, a smooth lowpass that blurs more as k grows. It matters for telescopes, aerial photos and surveillance cameras looking across hot roads.

Estimating H by modelling, linear motion blur: If the camera (or the object) moves in a straight line during the exposure time T, with total shift a pixels in x and b pixels in y, the model is H(u, v) = (T / (pi(ua + vb))) sin(pi(ua + vb)) e^(-j pi(ua + vb)). You do not need to memorise all of it, but notice the sine: H becomes exactly zero whenever ua + vb is a nonzero whole number. So motion blur does not just weaken some frequencies, it wipes some out completely. This fact will cause trouble for the inverse filter. In spatial terms, a horizontal motion of 10 pixels gives a PSF that is a short horizontal line of 10 equal values, each one tenth.

Inverse filtering: The simplest idea: if G = H F, then F = G / H. So estimate F-hat(u, v) = G(u, v) / H(u, v), then inverse-transform. With noise, though, G = H F + N, so F-hat = F + N / H. The second term is the problem. Wherever H is tiny, dividing the noise by it makes the noise enormous, and wherever H is zero, the division is undefined. Noise is usually spread evenly over all frequencies, while H for blur is small at high frequencies, so the inverse filter turns high-frequency noise into a storm that drowns the image.

Inverse filter worked: Look at two frequencies, each with true value F = 50 and noise N = 1. At a strong frequency, H = 0.8: G = 0.8 x 50 + 1 = 41, and G / H = 41 / 0.8 = 51.25. Close to 50, an error of only 1.25. At a weak frequency, H = 0.02: G = 0.02 x 50 + 1 = 2, and G / H = 2 / 0.02 = 100. The true value is 50 but we get 100, because the noise of 1 was multiplied by 1/0.02 = 50. Across a whole image there are thousands of weak frequencies, and the result is garbage even though the noise was tiny.

The cutoff trick: A practical fix is to apply the inverse filter only near the centre of the spectrum, within some radius, where H is large, and leave other frequencies alone (or multiply by a smooth lowpass like a Butterworth). This limits the damage. The radius is a trade-off: too small and the image stays blurry, too large and noise floods in. You tune it by eye. It works, but it is a hack. The Wiener filter solves the same problem in a principled way.

The Wiener filter: Norbert Wiener developed this idea in the 1940s. Instead of trying to undo H exactly, it looks for the estimate F-hat that minimises the mean squared error between F-hat and the true f. The answer is F-hat = [ (1/H) x |H|^2 / (|H|^2 + S_eta / S_f) ] G, where S_eta is the power spectrum of the noise and S_f the power spectrum of the true image. Read the bracket as two parts: 1/H is the inverse filter, and |H|^2 / (|H|^2 + S_eta/S_f) is a "trust factor" between 0 and 1. Where the signal is strong compared with the noise, the trust factor is near 1 and Wiener behaves like the inverse filter. Where noise dominates, the trust factor goes to 0 and Wiener refuses to amplify. If there is no noise, S_eta = 0 and Wiener becomes exactly the inverse filter.

The constant K approximation: We rarely know S_f, the spectrum of the image we are trying to find. So in practice we replace the ratio S_eta / S_f by a single constant K and tune it. For real H, the filter simplifies to a gain of H / (H^2 + K). Worked with K = 0.001 on the same two frequencies. Strong, H = 0.8: gain = 0.8 / (0.64 + 0.001), about 1.248, so F-hat = 1.248 x 41, about 51.17. Almost the same as the inverse filter. Weak, H = 0.02: gain = 0.02 / (0.0004 + 0.001), about 14.29, so F-hat = 14.29 x 2, about 28.6. The error is about 21.4 instead of 50. Wiener chose to under-recover the weak frequency rather than blow up the noise. Larger K means more caution (smoother, less noisy, a bit blurrier), smaller K means more aggressive deblurring.

Constrained least squares (CLS) filtering: Wiener needs K, or the power spectra, which are hard to know. CLS needs only the noise mean and variance, which you can estimate from a flat patch (lesson 13). Its idea: among all images that are consistent with the observed g and the known noise level, pick the smoothest one, measured by the energy of its Laplacian (lesson 10). The solution in frequency is F-hat = [ H* / (|H|^2 + gamma |P|^2) ] G, where H* is the complex conjugate of H, P is the transform of the Laplacian kernel and gamma is a parameter adjusted until the leftover error matches the noise level. It often gives better results than Wiener with a hand-picked K, especially for strong noise.

Measuring success: Since restoration is objective, we measure it. In simulations we know the true f, so we compute the mean squared error between f and F-hat's inverse, or PSNR (lesson 24). For real photos, a common practice is to blur a known sharp test image with the estimated PSF, add matching noise, restore it, and see which filter settings give the lowest error, then apply those settings to the real photo.

Blind deconvolution and modern methods: When H is completely unknown, blind deconvolution tries to estimate both the image and the PSF together, usually by iterating between them with assumptions like "the PSF is small and non-negative" and "natural images have sparse edges". Astronomers used deconvolution on Hubble Space Telescope images in the early 1990s before its optics were corrected in 1993. Modern phone cameras reduce blur at capture with optical stabilisation, short exposures and burst merging, and some apps also use trained neural networks for deblurring (deep-cse-8-1 and deep-cse-8-3 go there). The classical filters here are still the foundation and the honest baseline.

Real-life example 1, deblurring a shaky phone photo of a shop sign: You photograph a shop sign in Gulistan from a moving bus, and the text is smeared about 12 pixels horizontally. Step 1, find a sharp-cornered letter edge to confirm the blur is horizontal and estimate its length, 12 pixels. Step 2, model the PSF as a horizontal line of 12 equal values, each 1/12. Step 3, estimate noise from a flat patch of the sign background, sigma about 3. Step 4, try the plain inverse filter: the result is covered in stripes and speckles, because the motion blur's H has zeros. Step 5, use Wiener with K = 0.01, then 0.003, then 0.001, and pick the setting where the letters are readable but noise has not exploded. The shop name becomes legible.

Real-life example 2, a traffic camera on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway: A fixed camera looks along a hot road in summer, and the heat makes the air shimmer, softly blurring distant number plates. Engineers photograph a small bright lamp placed at a known distance, which gives the PSF by experiment. They then compare that measured PSF with the turbulence model exp(-k (u^2 + v^2)^(5/6)) to find a matching k. Using a Wiener or CLS filter tuned for that k improves plate readability enough for the recognition step (see the capstone in lesson 26).

Common mistakes: Expecting the inverse filter to work on real, noisy images. Forgetting that motion blur has exact zeros in H. Getting the blur direction or length wrong, which produces ghost copies in the "restored" result. Setting K to zero and being surprised it equals the inverse filter. Forgetting padding and centring from lesson 12, which adds wraparound artefacts at the borders. Thinking deblurring creates detail that was never captured; it can only recover frequencies that survived above the noise.

What exams ask: State the degradation model and the three ways to estimate H. Explain why the inverse filter fails when H is small or zero, with a numeric example like G/H = 2/0.02. Write the Wiener filter, explain each term, and show that it becomes the inverse filter when noise is zero. Compute a Wiener gain with a given K. Describe the motion blur and turbulence models. Compare Wiener and CLS.

Recap: A blur is described by its point spread function h, or H in frequency. Estimate it by observation, experiment or modelling (turbulence, motion). The inverse filter G/H is exact without noise but explodes where H is small. The Wiener filter adds a trust factor that backs off where noise dominates, practical with a constant K. CLS chooses the smoothest image consistent with the noise level. Next, lesson 16 moves from gray to colour: how colour is seen and stored.
key_points: The point spread function h describes what blur does to a single point; for a linear, position-invariant system it describes the whole blur.
H can be estimated by observation (a clean subimage), by experiment (imaging an impulse, H = G/A) or by modelling.
Turbulence is modelled as H = exp(-k (u^2 + v^2)^(5/6)); linear motion blur has a sine term that makes H exactly zero at some frequencies.
Inverse filtering gives F-hat = F + N/H, so noise explodes where H is small: G = 2, H = 0.02 gives 100 instead of 50.
The Wiener filter minimises mean squared error and multiplies the inverse filter by a trust factor |H|^2 / (|H|^2 + S_eta/S_f).
With a constant K the Wiener gain for real H is H / (H^2 + K); K = 0 gives the inverse filter.
Constrained least squares picks the smoothest image consistent with the known noise mean and variance.
lessons.tip: When a formula has a fraction, always ask what happens when the denominator gets tiny. That one habit explains why the inverse filter fails and why Wiener adds K.
lessons.task: Blur the row 0, 0, 0, 120, 0, 0, 0 by averaging each pixel with its two neighbours and write the result. Then compute the Wiener gain H / (H^2 + K) for H = 0.9, 0.3 and 0.05 with K = 0.01 and compare each with the inverse-filter gain 1/H.

quiz.q: A frequency has F = 50, H = 0.02 and N = 1. What does the inverse filter estimate?
quiz.explain: G = 0.02 x 50 + 1 = 2 and G/H = 2/0.02 = 100; the noise was multiplied by 50.

quiz.q: Why does linear motion blur cause special trouble for inverse filtering?
options: It makes H exactly zero at some frequencies
quiz.explain: The sine term in the motion blur model makes H zero where ua + vb is a nonzero whole number, so G/H is undefined there.

quiz.q: What does the Wiener filter become when the noise power is zero?
quiz.explain: With S_eta = 0 the trust factor is 1, leaving only 1/H.

quiz.q: With K = 0.001 and H = 0.8, the Wiener gain H / (H^2 + K) is about...
quiz.explain: 0.8 / (0.64 + 0.001) = 0.8 / 0.641, about 1.248, slightly below the inverse gain 1.25.

quiz.q: How is H estimated by experiment?
options: By imaging a tiny bright dot with the same camera settings
quiz.explain: A small bright dot approximates an impulse, so its image is the PSF and H = G/A.

lessons.title: Colour Fundamentals and Colour Models: RGB, CMYK, HSI, YCbCr and Pseudocolour
lessons.content:
Look at a ripe mango in a Rajshahi market. You say "yellow-orange". Your friend with a phone says the pixel is (200, 100, 50). A printer at a Nilkhet shop says it needs 0% cyan, 50% magenta and 75% yellow ink plus some black. A painter says it is an orange hue, fairly saturated, medium bright. All four are describing the same colour in different "languages". Those languages are colour models, and this lesson teaches you how they work, why each exists and how to translate between them.

Why colour matters in image processing: Gray images (everything so far) carry brightness only. Colour adds two things. First, humans can tell apart thousands of colour shades but only a few dozen gray levels, so colour helps people see. Second, colour is a powerful descriptor for machines: ripe vs unripe fruit, healthy vs diseased leaves, skin vs background, a red traffic light. Colour image processing has two branches: full-colour processing of images taken by colour cameras (lesson 17), and pseudocolour processing, which assigns colours to gray values to make them easier to read (end of this lesson).

Light and colour: Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum (lesson 02), wavelengths from about 400 nm (violet) to about 700 nm (red). An object looks green because it reflects mostly middle wavelengths and absorbs the rest. Light that has a single wavelength is monochromatic; most real light mixes many wavelengths. Three quantities describe a light source: radiance (the total energy it emits), luminance (how much of that energy a viewer actually perceives, which can be very low for infrared even if radiance is high) and brightness (a subjective feeling that cannot be measured exactly).

How the eye sees colour: The retina has three types of cones (lesson 02). S cones respond most to short wavelengths (peak around 420 nm, bluish), M cones to medium (around 534 nm, greenish) and L cones to long (around 564 nm, yellowish-red). S cones are by far the fewest. Every colour you see is your brain's reading of three numbers: how strongly each cone type fired. That is why three numbers are enough to describe a colour for humans, and why every colour model in this lesson uses three components (CMYK uses four for practical printing reasons).

Primary and secondary colours of light: Additive mixing is what happens when lights are combined, as on a screen. The primaries are red, green and blue. Red plus green gives yellow, green plus blue gives cyan, red plus blue gives magenta, and all three together give white. Subtractive mixing is what happens with pigments and inks, where each ink absorbs (subtracts) some light. The primaries of pigment are cyan, magenta and yellow, exactly the secondaries of light. Cyan ink absorbs red, magenta absorbs green and yellow absorbs blue. Mixing all three should absorb everything and give black.

Hue, saturation and brightness: Humans describe colour with three feelings. Hue is the dominant colour as named, red, orange, green. Saturation is the purity, how much white is mixed in: pure red is fully saturated, pink is red with a lot of white, so less saturated. Brightness is how light or dark it is. Hue and saturation together are called chromaticity. Keep these three in mind, because the HSI model below is built on them.

Tristimulus values and the chromaticity diagram: The amounts of red, green and blue (in the CIE standard, called X, Y and Z) needed to match a colour are its tristimulus values. Divide each by their sum to get chromaticity coordinates: x = X / (X + Y + Z), y = Y / (X + Y + Z), and z = 1 - x - y. Because z follows from x and y, any colour's chromaticity can be drawn as a point on a 2D map, the horseshoe-shaped CIE chromaticity diagram. Pure spectral colours lie on the curved edge, and the equal-energy white point is at x = y = 1/3. Key insight: pick any three primaries, mark them on the diagram, and the triangle between them is every colour those primaries can make. No triangle covers the whole horseshoe, which is why no screen or printer can show every colour humans can see. The range a device can show is called its gamut.

The RGB model: Each colour is a point in a cube with red, green and blue axes running from 0 to 1 (or 0 to 255). Black is at the origin (0, 0, 0), white at (1, 1, 1), and the diagonal between them is the gray line, where R = G = B. The other corners are red, green, blue, cyan, magenta and yellow. With 8 bits per channel, a pixel has 24 bits and the number of possible colours is 2^24 = 16,777,216, often called "16.7 million colours". Cameras and screens work in RGB because their sensors and pixels are red, green and blue. But RGB is awkward for humans: if you want "the same colour but a little lighter", all three numbers change.

The CMY and CMYK models: For printing, convert with CMY = 1 - RGB (values in 0 to 1). Worked: our mango (0.8, 0.4, 0.2) in RGB becomes C = 0.2, M = 0.6, Y = 0.8. In practice, equal cyan, magenta and yellow inks give a muddy dark brown, not true black, and black text printed with three inks wastes ink and blurs if the plates are slightly misaligned. So printers add a fourth ink, black (K). One common conversion: K = min(C, M, Y), and then C' = (C - K)/(1 - K), M' = (M - K)/(1 - K), Y' = (Y - K)/(1 - K). For the mango: K = 0.2, C' = 0, M' = 0.4/0.8 = 0.5, Y' = 0.6/0.8 = 0.75. So it prints with no cyan, 50% magenta, 75% yellow and 20% black. Real print shops use colour profiles that are more complex, but this is the core idea.

The HSI model: HSI separates intensity (I) from the colour information (H and S), much like human description. Picture the RGB cube standing on its black corner with the gray line vertical. Intensity is the height along that line. Saturation is the distance from the line. Hue is the angle around it, with red at 0 degrees, green at 120 and blue at 240. The formulas, with R, G, B normalised to 0 to 1: I = (R + G + B) / 3. S = 1 - 3 min(R, G, B) / (R + G + B). For hue, compute theta = arccos( 0.5((R - G) + (R - B)) / sqrt((R - G)^2 + (R - B)(G - B)) ); then H = theta if B <= G, and H = 360 - theta if B > G.

RGB to HSI worked: Take the mango pixel (200, 100, 50). Normalise: R = 0.784, G = 0.392, B = 0.196. Intensity I = (0.784 + 0.392 + 0.196) / 3 = 0.458, about 117 on a 0 to 255 scale. Saturation S = 1 - 3 x 0.196 / 1.373 = 1 - 0.429 = 0.571. Hue: R - G = 0.392, R - B = 0.588, G - B = 0.196. Numerator = 0.5(0.392 + 0.588) = 0.490. Denominator = sqrt(0.392^2 + 0.588 x 0.196) = sqrt(0.154 + 0.115) = sqrt(0.269), about 0.519. Ratio about 0.945, arccos about 19.1 degrees. Since B < G, H = 19.1 degrees, between red (0) and yellow (60), so orange. Result: H about 19 degrees, S about 0.57, I about 0.46, matching the painter's description exactly. The reverse conversion (HSI to RGB) uses a separate formula for each 120-degree sector and is in every textbook.

HSV, a close cousin: Many software libraries use HSV instead of HSI. V (value) is max(R, G, B) instead of the average, and S = (max - min) / max. For the mango, V = 200/255, about 0.784, S = 150/200 = 0.75, and the hue comes out at 20 degrees, close to the HSI value. So be careful: S and the brightness component differ between HSI and HSV, and in OpenCV-style 8-bit images hue is often stored as 0 to 179 (degrees halved) so it fits in one byte. Always check which convention your tool uses.

YCbCr and Lab: Lesson 04 of Multimedia Systems (deep-cse-5-9) covered YCbCr, which splits a pixel into luma Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B and two colour-difference signals Cb and Cr. For the mango, Y = 0.299 x 200 + 0.587 x 100 + 0.114 x 50, about 124.2. JPEG and video use it because the eye is less sensitive to colour detail than to brightness detail. CIE L*a*b* (Lab) is designed so that equal distances roughly match equal perceived differences: L* is lightness, a* runs green to red, b* runs blue to yellow. It is device-independent and used for colour matching in printing, paint and textile factories, where a colour difference number decides whether a dyed batch is accepted.

Why HSI or HSV helps processing: Suppose you want to find all green leaves in a photo. In RGB, a leaf in sunlight might be (90, 200, 60) and in shadow (30, 70, 20), very different triples. In HSI both have a similar hue (green, around 100 to 110 degrees) and only intensity differs. So a rule like "hue between 80 and 140 and saturation above 0.3" finds leaves in sun and shade alike. Separating brightness from colour makes algorithms robust to lighting changes, a theme lesson 17 uses again and again.

Pseudocolour processing: Here the input is a gray image, and we assign colours to gray levels to make differences easier to see. The simplest method is intensity slicing: cut the 0 to 255 range into bands and give each a colour, for example 0 to 84 blue, 85 to 169 green and 170 to 255 red. A more general method uses three transformation functions, one each for R, G and B, often sinusoids with different phases, so each gray level maps to a distinct colour. Pseudocolour is common in thermal cameras (cold blue, hot red), weather radar and rainfall maps, medical images and luggage X-ray scanners, where different material types get different colours.

Real-life example 1, sorting mangoes and tomatoes by ripeness: A packing house in Chapainawabganj sends mangoes down a conveyor past a camera. Step 1, convert each RGB pixel to HSI (or HSV). Step 2, compute the average hue of the fruit's pixels, ignoring the background by a saturation check. Step 3, green unripe fruit has hue near 90 to 110 degrees, ripe yellow-orange fruit near 20 to 50. Step 4, a rule decides the grade. Because the rule uses hue, a shadow from the conveyor rails, which only lowers intensity, does not change the grade.

Real-life example 2, a garment factory colour check: A factory in Gazipur dyes cotton for a foreign buyer who sent a reference swatch. A spectrophotometer or calibrated camera measures both the swatch and the dyed sample, converts them to Lab, and computes the colour difference. If the difference is below the agreed tolerance, the batch ships. In RGB, the same fabric could read differently under different lights or on different cameras, which is why industry uses device-independent Lab.

Common mistakes: Thinking RGB and CMY primaries are the same (they are complements). Forgetting to normalise to 0 to 1 before using the HSI formulas. Forgetting the B > G rule for hue. Treating hue as a normal number: 359 degrees and 1 degree are neighbours, not far apart, so averaging hues needs care. Hue is meaningless when saturation is zero (gray). Mixing HSI and HSV formulas. Assuming a screen can show every colour.

What exams ask: Explain additive vs subtractive primaries. Convert RGB to CMY and CMYK. Convert an RGB pixel to HSI with numbers like the mango example. Draw the RGB cube and mark the gray line. Explain the chromaticity diagram and gamut. Define hue, saturation, brightness. Explain intensity slicing for pseudocolour and give uses.

Recap: Colour comes from three cone types, so three numbers describe it. RGB suits devices, CMY(K) suits printing, HSI and HSV suit human description and robust processing, YCbCr suits compression and Lab suits colour matching. RGB to HSI gives hue as an angle, saturation as purity and intensity as the average. Pseudocolour paints gray levels to reveal differences. Next, lesson 17 processes full-colour images: corrections, white balance, smoothing, sharpening and colour segmentation.
key_points: Visible light runs from about 400 to 700 nm; three cone types (S, M, L) mean three numbers describe any colour for humans.
Additive primaries of light are red, green and blue; subtractive primaries of pigment are cyan, magenta and yellow.
The RGB cube has black at the origin, white at (1, 1, 1) and gray along the diagonal; 24-bit colour gives 16,777,216 colours.
CMY = 1 - RGB; CMYK adds black with K = min(C, M, Y) to get true black and save ink.
HSI: I = (R + G + B)/3, S = 1 - 3 min/(R + G + B), H is an angle from an arccos formula (360 - theta when B > G).
RGB (200, 100, 50) converts to about H = 19 degrees, S = 0.57, I = 0.46: an orange.
Separating intensity from hue makes colour rules robust to shadows and lighting changes.
Pseudocolour assigns colours to gray levels, for example by intensity slicing in thermal and weather images.
lessons.tip: Do one RGB-to-HSI conversion fully by hand with a calculator. Once you have computed theta and checked B against G yourself, the formula stops being scary.
lessons.task: Open a colour picker on your phone or computer (most paint and slide apps have one). Pick a ripe mango or banana photo, read its RGB value, then convert it by hand to CMY, CMYK and HSI. Check your hue by seeing if the app's HSV/HSB view shows a similar hue angle.

quiz.q: Which colours are the primaries of pigments (inks)?
quiz.explain: Each pigment primary absorbs one light primary: cyan absorbs red, magenta absorbs green, yellow absorbs blue.

quiz.q: How many colours can a 24-bit RGB pixel represent?
quiz.explain: 8 bits per channel gives 2^24 = 16,777,216 combinations.

quiz.q: RGB (0.8, 0.4, 0.2) gives CMY (0.2, 0.6, 0.8). With K = min(C, M, Y), what is M'?
For the pixel (200, 100, 50), what is the HSI intensity on a 0 to 1 scale?
Why is HSI often better than RGB for finding green leaves in sun and shade?
options: Hue stays similar while only intensity changes with lighting
quiz.explain: Shadows mostly lower intensity; hue and saturation stay similar, so a hue rule works in both.

lessons.title: Colour Image Processing
lessons.content:
Imagine you sell handmade nakshi kantha online. You snap a photo of a beautiful red and white kantha under the yellow bulb of your room, upload it, and the customer sees a muddy orange cloth on a creamy yellow background. Your cloth did not change. The light did. Fixing that photo, making the red red again, and maybe cutting the kantha out of the background, is exactly what this lesson is about: doing image processing when every pixel carries three numbers instead of one.

Where this sits: lesson 16 gave us the colour models, RGB, CMY, HSI, YCbCr and friends, and the formulas to move between them. This lesson uses those models as tools. We will take almost every gray-level idea from lessons 06 to 12 (intensity curves, histogram equalisation, smoothing, sharpening) and ask a new question each time: should I apply it to each colour channel separately, or to the colour as a whole, or only to brightness? Then we add two truly colour-only tasks: colour slicing and colour segmentation.

Full-colour vs pseudocolour: Pseudocolour, which we met at the end of lesson 16, starts from a gray image and paints false colours on it (a thermal camera showing hot as red). Full-colour processing starts from a real colour image captured by a colour sensor. In full colour, each pixel is a small vector. In RGB it is c = (R, G, B), for example (200, 150, 100), a warm brown. A 1000 x 1000 photo is therefore three 1000 x 1000 grids stacked like three transparent sheets.

Two ways to process: Method one, per-channel: treat R, G and B as three separate gray images, process each with the gray-level tool you already know, then stack them back. Method two, vector-based: treat each pixel as one vector and design the operation for vectors. Here is the useful fact: for operations that are linear and work the same on every channel, both methods give the same answer. Averaging is the classic case. Average the pixels (200, 150, 100) and (100, 50, 0) as vectors and you get (150, 100, 50). Average the R values alone, 200 and 100, and you get 150; G gives 100; B gives 50. Same result. For nonlinear operations (median, histogram equalisation, edge strength) the two methods can disagree, and then we must think.

Colour transformations: The colour version of the point transform s = T(r) from lesson 06 is a set of functions s_i = T_i(r_1, r_2, ..., r_n), one output component per input component. Each output can depend on all inputs. Example: to make an RGB image 30 percent darker, use s_i = 0.7 r_i for i = R, G, B. In HSI the same job is one function: multiply only I by 0.7 and leave H and S alone. Both give the same picture. The RGB version touches three numbers per pixel, the HSI version one, but the HSI version first needs a conversion there and back, which costs more. So the cheapest model depends on the task, not on fashion.

Colour complements: On the colour wheel, the colour directly opposite a hue is its complement: red and cyan, green and magenta, blue and yellow. In RGB with 8 bits, the complement of a pixel is simply 255 minus each channel. Worked: (200, 150, 100) becomes (55, 105, 155), a cool blue-gray. This is the colour version of the image negative from lesson 06, and it is how old film negatives look. Complements help enhance detail hidden in dark regions, and they explain colour correction: to remove too much of a colour you add its complement.

Colour slicing: Sometimes you want only one colour family to stand out, like highlighting every red chilli in a market photo and turning everything else gray. Pick a prototype colour a = (aR, aG, aB). Cube version: a pixel is kept if each channel is within W/2 of the prototype, |rj - aj| <= W/2 for all three; otherwise it is replaced by a neutral gray such as (128, 128, 128). Sphere version: keep the pixel if its Euclidean distance from a is at most a radius R0. The sphere treats all directions of colour difference equally; the cube is cheaper to test because it needs no square roots.

Tone corrections: Before fixing colour, photographers fix tone, meaning the overall brightness spread. A flat image has weak contrast, a high-key image is mostly light (a white sari on a white wall), a low-key image is mostly dark (a night street in Old Dhaka). The fixes are the same curves as lesson 06: an S-shaped curve raises contrast, a curve that bends up brightens shadows. Applied to R, G and B with the same curve, or to I alone, the hue stays roughly the same while the tone changes.

Colour balance: A colour cast is when the whole image leans toward one colour, usually because of the light source. Tungsten bulbs and evening sun make photos yellow-orange; shade and cloudy skies make them bluish; some tube lights add green. Using the colour wheel, a cast is fixed by adding its complement or by reducing the colours that make it. Too yellow means too much red plus green relative to blue, so we either boost blue or pull red and green down.

White balance with the gray-world idea: The gray-world assumption says: in an average real scene, all the colours together should average to a neutral gray. So if the channel averages are unequal, the light is to blame. Worked: suppose a kantha photo has mean R = 150, mean G = 120 and mean B = 90. The overall gray target is (150 + 120 + 90) / 3 = 120. The gains are 120/150 = 0.8 for red, 120/120 = 1 for green and 120/90 = 1.333 for blue. A pixel (200, 150, 100) becomes (200 x 0.8, 150 x 1, 100 x 1.333) = (160, 150, 133). The orange cast shrinks, and values above 255 after scaling are clipped.

When gray-world fails: The assumption breaks when the scene really is mostly one colour: a photo of a green paddy field, a red Pohela Boishakh crowd, a blue sea at Cox's Bazar. Gray-world would push them toward gray and kill the true colour. Alternatives: the white-patch (max-RGB) method assumes the brightest patch is white and scales so it becomes (255, 255, 255); or the user taps a known white or gray object in the photo, which is what the white-balance eyedropper in editing apps does. Phone cameras combine several such cues with learned models.

Histogram equalisation in colour: Doing lesson 07's equalisation on R, G and B separately is a classic mistake. Each channel gets its own mapping, so the ratios between R, G and B change, and the hue changes: a skin tone may turn greenish or purple. The safe way is to convert to a model that separates brightness from colour (HSI, HSV, YCbCr or Lab), equalise only the intensity or luminance channel, and convert back. Worked: the pixel (200, 150, 100) has I = (200 + 150 + 100) / 3 = 150. If equalisation maps I = 150 to 180, H and S stay the same and the colour simply gets brighter without changing its hue.

Colour smoothing: Smoothing is linear, so per-channel smoothing equals vector smoothing. Run the box or Gaussian filter of lesson 09 on R, G and B, or equivalently average the colour vectors in each window. One choice that differs: smoothing only the I channel of HSI blurs brightness but not colour, which gives a slightly different look. Median filtering is nonlinear: a per-channel median can create a new colour that existed in none of the neighbours, because the middle R, the middle G and the middle B may come from three different pixels. Vector median filters avoid this by choosing the neighbour vector with the smallest total distance to the others.

Colour sharpening: The Laplacian of lesson 10 is linear too, so the Laplacian of a colour vector is simply the vector of the Laplacians of each channel. Sharpen R, G and B with the same kernel and the colour image is sharpened. You can also sharpen just I in HSI, which avoids coloured halos along edges, a popular trick in photo apps because halos look worse in colour than in gray.

Segmentation in HSI: Segmentation means separating the pixels we care about, and colour is often the strongest clue. In HSI, hue alone describes the colour family, so we can make a hue mask: pixels with hue between, say, 60 and 140 degrees for greens. But hue is meaningless when saturation is near zero (gray, white, black pixels have no real hue and their hue values jump around with noise). So we also make a saturation mask, say S above 0.2, and multiply the two masks. The result keeps only strongly coloured green pixels.

Segmentation in RGB with distance: Another approach works directly in RGB. Take sample pixels of the colour you want, compute their average a, and keep every pixel z whose distance D(z, a) is at most a threshold D0. Worked with a leaf green a = (60, 140, 50) and D0 = 30: the pixel (70, 150, 45) has distance sqrt(10^2 + 10^2 + 5^2) = sqrt(225) = 15, so it is kept. The pixel (120, 100, 60) has distance sqrt(60^2 + 40^2 + 10^2) = sqrt(5300), about 72.8, so it is rejected. A smarter distance, the Mahalanobis distance, uses the spread of the samples so that directions where the colour naturally varies more are tolerated more. A cheap version uses a box around a, which skips square roots entirely.

Colour edges: Edge detection is lesson 20, but colour adds a twist. Computing the gradient of R, G and B separately and adding the three magnitudes works most of the time. It is not exact, because the three gradients may point in different directions. The vector gradient (Di Zenzo's method) treats the colour as a vector field and finds the direction where the colour vector changes fastest. It catches edges between two colours of the same brightness, like a red flower on a green leaf of equal intensity, which a gray-level detector may miss entirely.

Noise in colour images: Each channel gets its own noise from the sensor, and in low light the blue channel is often the noisiest because sensors are less sensitive to blue. Converting a noisy image to HSI spreads that noise unevenly: intensity, being an average of three channels, becomes less noisy, while hue and saturation can become very noisy, especially for dull, low-saturation pixels. That is one more reason to denoise before converting, or to denoise luminance and chrominance separately as phone cameras do.

Real-life example 1, rice leaf spots: An agriculture student in Mymensingh photographs rice leaves to measure how much area brown spots cover. Step 1, white balance the photo using a gray card placed in the frame. Step 2, convert to HSV. Step 3, build a mask of healthy green (hue roughly 70 to 160 degrees in a 0 to 360 scale, saturation above 0.25). Step 4, build a mask of brown spots (hue roughly 15 to 45 degrees, medium saturation, lower value). Step 5, clean both masks with the morphology of lesson 18. Step 6, the diseased percentage is spot pixels divided by (spot + healthy) pixels. If 6,000 of 48,000 leaf pixels are brown, the damage is 12.5 percent. The exact hue ranges must be tuned on real samples; they change with camera and light.

Real-life example 2, product photos for an online shop: A small Dhaka business photographs 200 shoes a day under mixed tube light. Their pipeline: correct the colour cast with a white-patch method using the white backdrop, raise contrast with an S-curve on luminance only, equalise or stretch luminance if photos are dull, sharpen luminance lightly, then remove the backdrop by RGB distance from the backdrop colour, giving each shoe a clean transparent background. Doing everything on luminance where possible keeps the true shoe colour, which reduces returns from customers who say the colour looked different.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Equalising R, G and B separately and getting strange hues. Forgetting that hue is undefined when saturation is near zero. Assuming the median filter works the same per channel as on vectors. Using gray-world on a scene that is naturally dominated by one colour. Mixing up colour complement (255 minus each channel) with converting to grayscale. Exams ask you to compute an RGB complement, apply a gray-world correction to given means, decide whether a pixel lies inside a colour slicing cube or sphere, compute an RGB Euclidean distance against a threshold, and explain why intensity-only equalisation preserves hue.

Recap: A colour pixel is a vector. Linear operations such as averaging and Laplacian sharpening can be done per channel safely; nonlinear ones need care. Colour complements, slicing, tone curves and colour balance give easy control over the look. Gray-world and white-patch fix colour casts. Equalise and sharpen only the brightness channel to protect hue. Segment by hue plus saturation, or by distance from a sample colour. Next, lesson 18 moves to shapes: mathematical morphology on binary images.
key_points: A colour pixel is a vector such as (R, G, B); processing can be per-channel or vector-based.
For linear operations like averaging and the Laplacian, per-channel and vector results are identical; for median and equalisation they are not.
The RGB complement is 255 minus each channel, e.g. (200, 150, 100) becomes (55, 105, 155).
Colour slicing keeps pixels inside a cube or sphere around a prototype colour and grays out the rest.
Gray-world white balance scales each channel by (overall mean / channel mean).
Equalise or sharpen only intensity or luminance to avoid hue shifts.
Hue is unreliable at low saturation, so hue masks are combined with saturation masks.
RGB distance segmentation keeps pixels within distance D0 of a sample colour.
lessons.tip: Whenever you plan a colour operation, ask one question first: is it linear? If yes, per-channel is safe. If no, think about brightness-only processing.
lessons.task: Take one indoor photo under a yellow bulb. Pick a white object in it and guess its RGB (or read it with any colour-picker app). Compute the gains that would make it (255, 255, 255) and apply them by hand to two other pixels.

quiz.q: What is the RGB complement of the pixel (200, 150, 100) in an 8-bit image?
quiz.explain: Complement means 255 minus each channel: 255-200=55, 255-150=105, 255-100=155.

quiz.q: Why is equalising R, G and B separately usually a bad idea?
options: It changes the ratios between channels, so hues shift
It only works on gray images by law
quiz.explain: Each channel gets a different mapping, so the balance between R, G and B, and therefore the hue, changes. Equalise intensity only.

quiz.q: Channel means are R = 150, G = 120, B = 90. Under gray-world, what gain is applied to blue?
quiz.explain: Overall mean = 120, so the blue gain is 120 / 90, about 1.333.

quiz.q: For which operation do per-channel and vector processing always give the same result?
quiz.explain: Averaging is linear and identical on each channel, so both methods agree; median and equalisation are nonlinear.

quiz.q: With prototype a = (60, 140, 50) and D0 = 30, the pixel (70, 150, 45) has distance 15. What happens?
options: It is rejected because 15 is odd
It is kept, since 15 is at most 30
Distance cannot be computed in RGB
quiz.explain: sqrt(100 + 100 + 25) = 15, which is within the threshold of 30, so the pixel belongs to the green segment.

lessons.title: Morphology I: Erosion, Dilation, Opening and Closing
lessons.content:
Imagine a scanned answer script from an exam hall. After thresholding, the letters are black on white, but there are tiny black specks from dust, some strokes are broken where the pen skipped, and a few letters have small white holes. You do not want to blur anything; you want to fix shapes. Morphology is the toolbox for exactly that. Think of it like pressing a small rubber stamp all over a picture and asking simple yes-or-no questions: does the stamp fit inside the shape here? Does it touch the shape here? From those two questions come all the operations in this lesson.

Where this sits: Lessons 06 to 17 changed brightness and colour. Morphology changes shape. The word comes from biology, the study of the form of living things, and mathematical morphology was developed in the 1960s by Georges Matheron and Jean Serra in France. This lesson covers binary basics: sets, structuring elements, erosion, dilation, opening and closing. Lesson 19 builds real algorithms on top (boundaries, hole filling, labelling, skeletons) and extends everything to grayscale images.

Images as sets: In a binary image every pixel is either 1 (foreground, the object) or 0 (background). Morphology describes the object as a set A: the set of coordinates (row, column) of all foreground pixels. If an image has ones at (1,1), (1,2) and (2,1), then A = {(1,1), (1,2), (2,1)}. Once the image is a set, we can use set operations from lesson 04: union (OR), intersection (AND), complement (NOT, which swaps object and background) and difference. Morphology adds two new operations on top of these.

Structuring element: The structuring element, SE for short, is a small set B that acts as our probe or stamp. It has a chosen origin, usually its centre. Common shapes: a 3 x 3 square (all nine pixels), a cross or plus (centre and its 4-neighbours, five pixels), a disk (a rough circle of some radius), and a line (horizontal, vertical or diagonal). The SE is to morphology what the kernel is to spatial filtering in lesson 08, but it holds no weights, only membership: a pixel is in it or not.

Reflection and translation: Two small definitions are needed. The reflection of B, written B-hat, flips every point through the origin: B-hat = {-b for b in B}. If B = {(0,0), (0,1)}, a pixel and its right neighbour, then B-hat = {(0,0), (0,-1)}, a pixel and its left neighbour. Symmetric SEs such as the square, cross and disk equal their own reflection, which is why most textbook examples do not worry about it. Translation by z moves every point: (B)z = {b + z for b in B}. Putting the SE with its origin at pixel z just means translating it to z.

Erosion, the definition: The erosion of A by B is A eroded by B = {z : (B)z is a subset of A}. In words: slide the SE over every position z; the output pixel at z is 1 only if the whole stamp, placed with its origin at z, lies inside the object. If even one SE pixel falls on background, the output is 0. With a 3 x 3 square SE this is a minimum or logical AND over the 3 x 3 neighbourhood: the output is 1 only if all nine neighbours are 1.

Erosion, worked: Take a 7 x 7 binary image containing a solid 3 x 3 square of ones at rows 1 to 3, columns 1 to 3, plus one isolated speck at (5,5). That is 10 foreground pixels. Erode with the 3 x 3 square SE (pixels outside the image count as 0). At the centre (2,2) all nine neighbours are 1, so the output is 1. At (1,1) the neighbour (0,0) is 0, so the output is 0. The same happens for every other pixel of the square. The speck at (5,5) has eight zero neighbours, so it vanishes. Result: one single pixel at (2,2). Ten pixels shrank to one.

What erosion does: It shrinks objects, peeling roughly one layer of pixels from the boundary for each step of SE radius. Anything thinner than the SE disappears completely: specks, thin lines, hair-like spurs. Thin bridges connecting two blobs break, so one object may become two. A tiny 1D example with SE [1 1 1]: the row 0 1 1 1 0 1 0 erodes to 0 0 1 0 0 0 0. The run of three ones keeps only its middle; the lonely 1 is gone. Erosion is like a hungry ant that eats the outer layer of every shape.

Dilation, the definition: The dilation of A by B is A dilated by B = {z : (B-hat)z intersected with A is not empty}. In words: the output pixel at z is 1 if the reflected SE placed at z touches the object at even one pixel. An easier picture: put a copy of the SE on every foreground pixel and ink everything the copies cover. With a 3 x 3 square this is a maximum or logical OR over the neighbourhood. Worked on the same 7 x 7 image: the 3 x 3 square grows to a 5 x 5 square (25 pixels), the speck grows to a 3 x 3 block (9 pixels), and the two overlap at one pixel (4,4), giving 25 + 9 - 1 = 33 foreground pixels.

What dilation does: It grows objects, fills small holes and cracks, and joins pieces separated by gaps narrower than the SE. The 1D row 0 1 1 1 0 1 0 dilated by [1 1 1] becomes 1 1 1 1 1 1 1: the gap disappeared and the shape spread to the edges. The classic use is repairing broken text: in a low-quality fax, the strokes of a letter may have gaps of one or two pixels; dilation with a small SE reconnects them so the OCR sees whole characters. The danger is that letters also get fatter and may touch each other.

Duality: Erosion and dilation are duals with respect to complement and reflection: the complement of (A eroded by B) equals (complement of A) dilated by B-hat. In plain words: shrinking the object is the same as growing the background, and vice versa. This is handy in practice: if your library only has dilation, you can erode by complementing the image, dilating, and complementing back. It also explains why every statement about erosion has a mirror statement about dilation.

Not inverses: You might guess that dilation undoes erosion. It does not. In the worked example, erosion left only (2,2); the speck at (5,5) was destroyed and no dilation can bring it back, because dilation only grows what still exists. This information loss is not a bug. It is exactly what makes the next two operations so useful: erosion followed by dilation removes small things for good, but rebuilds the big things it shrank.

Opening: The opening of A by B is erosion followed by dilation with the same SE: A opened by B = (A eroded by B) dilated by B. Worked on the 7 x 7 image: erosion gives the single pixel (2,2); dilating it with the 3 x 3 square gives back the full 3 x 3 square at rows 1 to 3, columns 1 to 3. Final count: 9 pixels. The square survived exactly, and the speck is gone. Geometric meaning: roll the SE around inside the object; the opening is the union of all positions where the SE fits completely. Opening smooths outer contours, removes specks and thin protrusions smaller than the SE, and breaks narrow necks.

Closing: The closing of A by B is dilation followed by erosion: A closed by B = (A dilated by B) eroded by B. Worked in 1D with SE [1 1 1]: the row 0 1 1 1 0 1 1 1 0 has a one-pixel gap. Dilation gives all ones, 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1. Erosion then peels the ends (outside the row is 0) and gives 0 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0. The gap is filled and the outer ends are back where they were. Geometric meaning: roll the SE outside the object; whatever it cannot reach becomes object. Closing fills small holes, bridges narrow gaps and smooths inward dents. Note: closing the 7 x 7 image leaves all 10 pixels unchanged; closing does not remove specks, opening does.

Properties worth remembering: Opening is anti-extensive: the result is always a subset of A, it never adds pixels. Closing is extensive: A is always a subset of the result, it never removes pixels. Both are idempotent: opening an already opened image with the same SE changes nothing, and the same for closing.
