And they are duals: the complement of a closing equals the opening of the complement with the reflected SE. These properties are classic exam true-or-false items.

Opening then closing for noise: A noisy binary image with both white specks in the background and black specks inside objects can be cleaned by an opening (removes background specks and thin spurs) followed by a closing (fills the holes inside objects and rejoins small breaks). Gonzalez and Woods use a noisy fingerprint to show this: opening removes the background noise, closing repairs the broken ridges. This combination is a morphological filter, and for binary images it often beats any blurring filter because it keeps edges perfectly sharp.

Choosing the SE: Size matters most. The SE should be bigger than the noise you want to remove and smaller than the features you want to keep. If specks are at most 2 pixels wide and letter strokes are 5 pixels wide, a 3 x 3 opening removes specks and keeps strokes; a 7 x 7 opening would erase the letters too. Shape matters next: a square treats diagonals more strongly than a cross; a disk behaves the same in all directions; a horizontal line SE removes vertical thin things while keeping horizontal ones, useful for finding table lines in a scanned form.

Implementation and cost: For a flat SE on a binary image, erosion is a logical AND and dilation a logical OR over the SE's footprint, so cost is proportional to the number of pixels times the size of the SE. A 3 x 3 square SE can be split into a 1 x 3 line followed by a 3 x 1 line: dilating by the row and then by the column gives the same result as dilating by the square, with 6 checks per pixel instead of 9, and for a 15 x 15 square, 30 instead of 225. In OpenCV the functions are erode, dilate and morphologyEx; in Python's scipy they live in scipy.ndimage.

Real-life example 1, Bangla OCR on a scanned page: A volunteer project digitises old Bangla books. After adaptive thresholding (lesson 21) the page has dust specks and broken strokes. Step 1, opening with a 2 x 2 or 3 x 3 SE removes specks smaller than the SE. Step 2, closing with a short horizontal line SE repairs small breaks in the matra, the horizontal headline that joins Bangla letters in a word, without fattening vertical strokes much. Step 3, the cleaned image goes to character segmentation and recognition. The risk: too large a closing SE joins neighbouring words along the matra, so the SE length is tuned on a few sample pages.

Real-life example 2, counting tablets on a packaging line: A pharmaceutical factory in Gazipur checks that each blister strip has 10 tablets. A camera above the conveyor takes a picture, and thresholding gives white tablets on a dark background. Two tablets lying close may merge into one blob. Step 1, erosion with a disk SE of radius slightly bigger than half the touching neck separates them. Step 2, count connected components (lesson 19). Step 3, if the count is not 10, push the strip off the line. Because only the count matters, the shrinking by erosion does no harm; if area were needed, each separated blob could be dilated back with the same SE.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Thinking dilation undoes erosion (it does not; that is why opening exists). Mixing up opening and closing: opening = erosion first, removes small bright objects; closing = dilation first, fills small dark gaps. Forgetting how pixels outside the image are treated (for erosion, assuming outside is 0 erodes the borders). Ignoring reflection for non-symmetric SEs. Exams give a small binary grid and an SE and ask for the erosion, dilation, opening and closing by hand, ask to prove or state duality, ask which operation removes salt specks or fills holes, and ask about idempotence.

Recap: A binary image is a set; an SE is a small probe with an origin. Erosion keeps the positions where the SE fits inside, shrinking objects and deleting small parts. Dilation keeps positions where the SE touches, growing objects and filling gaps. They are duals but not inverses. Opening (erode then dilate) removes small objects and spurs; closing (dilate then erode) fills small holes and gaps; both are idempotent. Choose the SE by size and shape. Lesson 19 uses these four operations to build boundary extraction, hole filling, labelling, skeletons and grayscale morphology.
key_points: In binary morphology the object is a set of pixel coordinates and the structuring element (SE) is a small probe with an origin.
Erosion keeps z only if the SE placed at z lies entirely inside the object: it shrinks shapes and deletes small parts.
Dilation keeps z if the reflected SE at z touches the object: it grows shapes and fills gaps.
Erosion and dilation are duals (via complement and reflection) but not inverses.
Opening = erosion then dilation; removes specks and spurs smaller than the SE while keeping larger shapes.
Closing = dilation then erosion; fills small holes and bridges narrow gaps.
Opening never adds pixels, closing never removes pixels, and both are idempotent.
The SE must be larger than the noise and smaller than the features you want to keep.
lessons.tip: Draw a small grid on graph paper and cut a 3 x 3 square out of a card as your SE. Physically sliding it over the grid makes erosion and dilation impossible to forget.
lessons.task: On a 7 x 7 grid, draw a 3 x 5 rectangle of ones and one isolated pixel. With a 3 x 3 square SE, compute by hand the erosion, then the opening, and count the pixels after each step.

quiz.q: A 7 x 7 image has a solid 3 x 3 square plus one isolated pixel (10 ones). After erosion with a 3 x 3 square SE, how many ones remain?
quiz.explain: Only the centre of the square has all nine neighbours equal to 1; the edges of the square and the isolated pixel are removed.

quiz.q: Opening is defined as...
options: Erosion followed by dilation with the same SE
quiz.explain: Opening = erode, then dilate. It removes small objects and then restores the size of the surviving ones.

quiz.q: Which operation is best for filling a one-pixel gap in a broken stroke without growing the stroke overall?
quiz.explain: Closing dilates to bridge the gap and then erodes to bring the outer boundary back.

quiz.q: Which statement about opening and closing is TRUE?
options: Applying opening twice with the same SE gives the same result as applying it once
Closing is a subset of the original image
quiz.explain: Opening and closing are idempotent. Opening never adds pixels, and closing never removes them, so it does not delete specks.

quiz.q: Dilating the 1D row 0 1 1 1 0 1 0 with the SE [1 1 1] (origin at centre) gives...
quiz.explain: Every position has at least one 1 within one step, so every output pixel becomes 1. The first option is the erosion instead.

lessons.title: Morphology II: Morphological Algorithms and Grayscale Morphology
lessons.content:
Lesson 18 gave us four tools: erosion, dilation, opening and closing. On their own they clean shapes. Combined cleverly with set operations, they become algorithms that answer real questions: Where exactly is the outline of this object? Which white blobs are separate objects, and how many are there? Can I fill the holes inside these coins? What is the stick-figure skeleton of this letter? And then the big step: everything also works on gray images, where erosion becomes a minimum and dilation a maximum. This lesson is a tour of those recipes, each built from the same two moves.

Where this sits: This is the second half of morphology. Lesson 18 is assumed: sets, the structuring element (SE), erosion, dilation, opening and closing. The results here feed straight into segmentation (lessons 21 and 22, watershed is morphological at heart), into shape description (lesson 25, boundaries and skeletons) and into the capstone plate reader (lesson 26), where connected components isolate the characters.

Hit-or-miss transform: Erosion asks whether the SE fits inside the object, but it ignores the background. Sometimes you need to match an exact pattern of foreground and background, like an isolated pixel, an end point of a line or a particular corner. The hit-or-miss transform uses two SEs: B1 for pixels that must be foreground and B2 for pixels that must be background. The result is (A eroded by B1) intersected with (complement of A eroded by B2). It marks every position where B1 fits in the object and, at the same time, B2 fits in the background. Example: to find isolated pixels, B1 is the single centre pixel and B2 is its eight neighbours. A pixel is reported only if it is 1 and all eight neighbours are 0. Hit-or-miss is the building block of thinning and of many shape detectors.

Boundary extraction: The boundary of a set A is the set minus its erosion: beta(A) = A minus (A eroded by B). Erosion peels one layer; subtracting what is left keeps exactly that peeled layer. Worked: a solid 5 x 5 square has 25 pixels. Eroding with a 3 x 3 square SE leaves the inner 3 x 3 = 9 pixels. The boundary is 25 - 9 = 16 pixels, the outer ring. For a 3 x 3 square, 9 - 1 = 8 pixels. With a 3 x 3 square SE the boundary is exactly one pixel thick. A bigger SE, say 5 x 5, peels two layers at once and gives a boundary 2 pixels wide, which is sometimes wanted for drawing outlines that stay visible after the image is shrunk.

Hole filling: A hole is a background region completely surrounded by foreground, like the white inside of a coin with a dark ring after thresholding. Given one seed point inside each hole, we grow the seed by conditional dilation: start with X0 containing only the seed, then repeat Xk = (X(k-1) dilated by B) intersected with the complement of A, using a cross SE. Each step lets the region grow by one pixel, but the intersection with the complement of A stops it at the walls of the object. When Xk equals X(k-1), the hole is full. The filled object is Xk union A. Without the intersection, the dilation would leak out and fill the whole image, so that one AND is the whole trick. Automatic versions skip the seeds: flood the background from the image border; any background pixel not reached is a hole.

Extracting connected components: The same idea with A itself instead of its complement extracts one object: start from a seed pixel p in the object and repeat Xk = (X(k-1) dilated by B) intersected with A, until nothing changes. Using a 3 x 3 square SE grows through 8-connected neighbours; a cross grows through 4-connected ones (recall adjacency from lesson 04). The final Xk is the full connected component containing p. Repeating from unvisited pixels finds every object, which is how an X-ray inspection system counts bone fragments or a camera counts chicken eggs on a tray.

Connected-component labelling, the two-pass algorithm: In practice a faster algorithm gives each object its own number in two raster scans. Pass 1: scan left to right, top to bottom. For each foreground pixel, look at its already-visited neighbours (for 4-connectivity: up and left). If none is labelled, assign a new label. If one or more are labelled, copy the smallest label, and if two different labels meet, record that they are equivalent. Pass 2: replace every label by the smallest label of its equivalence class, usually tracked with a union-find structure.

Labelling, worked: Take this 4 x 5 image, rows top to bottom: row 0 = 1 1 0 1 0, row 1 = 0 1 0 1 0, row 2 = 0 1 1 1 0, row 3 = 0 0 0 0 1. Pass 1 with 4-connectivity: (0,0) has no labelled neighbour, so label 1; (0,1) left is 1, so 1; (0,3) gets new label 2; (1,1) up is 1, so 1; (1,3) up is 2, so 2; (2,1) up is 1, so 1; (2,2) left is 1, so 1; (2,3) has left 1 and up 2, so it takes 1 and we record 1 equivalent to 2; (3,4) has up (2,4) = 0 and left (3,3) = 0, so new label 3. Pass 2 turns every 2 into 1. Result: two objects, a U shape of 8 pixels and a single pixel. With 8-connectivity, (3,4) touches (2,3) diagonally, so there would be only one object of 9 pixels. Always state the connectivity you use.

Thinning: Thinning removes boundary pixels repeatedly, but only those whose removal does not break the object apart or shorten its ends, until a one-pixel-wide curve remains. Formally, A thinned by B = A minus (hit-or-miss of A with B), applied with a sequence of eight rotated SEs, one for each direction, in rounds until nothing changes. The famous Zhang-Suen algorithm used in OCR is a fast, practical version of the same idea. Thinning turns thick handwritten strokes into thin centre lines so that stroke shape, not pen thickness, is compared.

Skeletons: The skeleton, or medial axis, of a shape is the set of centres of the largest disks that fit inside it, touching the boundary at two or more points. A rectangle's skeleton looks like two Y shapes joined by a central line; a disk's skeleton is its centre. Morphologically, Lantuejoul's formula builds it from erosions and openings: Sk(A) = (A eroded k times by B) minus the opening of that result by B, and the skeleton is the union of all Sk for k = 0 up to the last k before A erodes to nothing. Keeping each Sk and its k lets you rebuild A exactly by dilating Sk k times. Skeletons are sensitive to noise: a single bump on the boundary creates a long extra branch.

Pruning and convex hull: Pruning removes those short parasitic branches from skeletons or thinned characters: find end points with hit-or-miss, delete a few pixels back from each end point, then grow the main branches back by a conditional dilation. The convex hull H of a set is the smallest convex set containing it, like a rubber band stretched around the object. Morphologically it is built by repeated hit-or-miss with four SEs until convergence. The difference H minus A, the convex deficiency, is a useful descriptor: a hand with spread fingers has a large deficiency, a closed fist a small one.

Grayscale morphology, the idea: Now f(x, y) is a gray image. With a flat SE (just a shape, no heights), grayscale erosion at a pixel is the minimum of f over the SE's footprint, and grayscale dilation is the maximum. Opening and closing keep their definitions: opening = erosion then dilation, closing = dilation then erosion. Picture the image as a landscape where brightness is height. Opening rolls the SE under the surface and shaves off bright peaks narrower than the SE. Closing rolls it on top and fills dark valleys narrower than the SE. Non-flat SEs, with their own height values, also exist, but flat ones cover most practical uses.

Grayscale, worked in 1D: Let f = [10, 50, 20, 80, 30] and use a flat SE of width 3 (the window is clipped at the ends). Erosion takes minima: [10, 10, 20, 20, 30]. Dilation takes maxima: [50, 50, 80, 80, 80]. Opening = dilation of the erosion: [10, 20, 20, 30, 30]; the narrow bright spikes 50 and 80 were shaved down. Closing = erosion of the dilation: [50, 50, 50, 80, 80]; the narrow dark dips 10 and 20 were filled up. Notice the spikes are only one sample wide, narrower than the SE, which is exactly why opening removes them.

Morphological gradient: The difference between dilation and erosion, g = (f dilated by b) minus (f eroded by b), is large where intensity changes quickly within the SE and near zero in flat areas. In the example it is [40, 40, 60, 60, 50]. It is an edge-strength image with no direction, cheap to compute and fairly robust, used before watershed segmentation (lesson 22) to turn object borders into ridges.

Top-hat and bottom-hat: The top-hat transform is f minus the opening of f. Because opening removes bright details smaller than the SE but keeps the slowly varying background, the top-hat keeps only those small bright details sitting on a flat zero background. In the example, f minus opening = [0, 30, 0, 50, 0]: exactly the heights of the two spikes above their local background. The bottom-hat (black top-hat) is the closing minus f, and it extracts small dark details: here [40, 0, 30, 0, 50].

Why top-hat fixes uneven lighting: Gonzalez and Woods show an image of rice grains under light that is brighter at the top than at the bottom. A single global threshold (lesson 21) fails: either the dim grains at the bottom vanish or the bright background at the top turns white. Open the image with a disk SE larger than any grain: the grains disappear and what remains is an estimate of the background lighting. The top-hat, image minus that background, leaves grains on a nearly flat dark floor, and now one threshold separates every grain. The same trick works for dark text on a page with a shadow: use the bottom-hat.

Granulometry: Granulometry measures the size distribution of particles without separating them. Open the image with disks of increasing radius 1, 2, 3 and so on, and after each opening add up all pixel values (the surface area). When the radius passes the size of a group of particles, those particles vanish and the sum drops sharply. Plotting the drops against radius gives a histogram of particle sizes. It is used to grade sand and gravel, to measure grain size in rice and pulses, and to study cells.

Reconstruction brief: Morphological reconstruction repeats conditional dilation of a marker image under a mask image until nothing changes, just like hole filling and component extraction in grayscale. Opening by reconstruction removes small objects but restores the exact shapes of the surviving ones, not the SE-rounded versions an ordinary opening gives. It is the cleanest way to delete all objects that touch the image border, for example half-cut cells at the edges of a microscope image.

Real-life example 1, counting red blood cells: A diagnostic lab in Chattogram uses a microscope camera. Step 1, threshold the stained slide so cells are foreground. Step 2, fill holes, since pale cell centres become holes after thresholding. Step 3, remove cells touching the border by reconstruction, because they are only partly visible. Step 4, open with a small disk to remove debris. Step 5, label connected components with 8-connectivity and count them; measure each area, and flag clumps whose area is about twice the median as possible touching cells for erosion or watershed splitting. The count goes straight into the report.

Real-life example 2, finding cracks in a road photo: A city engineer in Dhaka wants a map of cracks from dashcam images. Cracks are thin dark lines on brighter asphalt. Step 1, apply a bottom-hat (closing minus image) with a disk SE wider than any crack: thin dark cracks become bright, while broad shadows and the general road shade are removed. Step 2, threshold. Step 3, remove small components by area. Step 4, thin the remaining blobs to skeletons and measure their length in pixels, converted to metres with the camera calibration. Long skeletons mean long cracks that need repair first.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Forgetting to intersect with the complement of A during hole filling, so the region leaks over the whole image. Not stating 4- or 8-connectivity when labelling, which changes object counts. Confusing top-hat (small bright details) with bottom-hat (small dark details). Choosing a top-hat SE smaller than the objects, which removes the objects too. Exams ask you to extract a boundary by hand, label a small grid with the two-pass method, write the hole-filling iteration, compute grayscale erosion, dilation and top-hat on a short sequence, and explain how top-hat corrects uneven illumination.

Recap: Hit-or-miss matches exact foreground and background patterns. Boundary = A minus its erosion. Hole filling and component extraction are conditional dilations that stop at the object or background. Two-pass labelling numbers objects, with connectivity stated. Thinning, skeletons, pruning and convex hulls describe shape. In grayscale, erosion is min, dilation is max; opening shaves bright peaks, closing fills dark valleys. Morphological gradient finds edges; top-hat and bottom-hat pull out small bright or dark details and fix uneven lighting. Next, lesson 20 detects edges with derivatives, from Sobel to Canny and the Hough transform.
key_points: Hit-or-miss uses one SE for required foreground and one for required background to find exact patterns.
Boundary extraction: beta(A) = A minus (A eroded by B); a 5 x 5 square gives 25 - 9 = 16 boundary pixels.
Hole filling repeats Xk = (X(k-1) dilated by B) AND (complement of A) from a seed until no change.
Two-pass labelling assigns provisional labels, records equivalences, then merges them; 4- vs 8-connectivity changes counts.
Thinning and skeletons reduce shapes to one-pixel-wide lines; pruning removes spurious branches.
Grayscale erosion = local minimum, dilation = local maximum over a flat SE.
Top-hat = f minus opening extracts small bright details and corrects uneven background lighting.
Morphological gradient = dilation minus erosion gives an edge-strength image.
lessons.tip: For every morphological algorithm, ask which set the dilation is allowed to grow into (A or its complement). That one intersection is what stops each algorithm from flooding the image.
lessons.task: Draw the 4 x 5 grid from the labelling example, then change one pixel so that the U shape becomes two separate objects under 4-connectivity but stays one object under 8-connectivity. Run the two-pass algorithm by hand for both cases.

quiz.q: A solid 5 x 5 square is eroded by a 3 x 3 square SE. How many pixels does the boundary A minus erosion contain?
quiz.explain: The erosion leaves the inner 3 x 3 = 9 pixels; 25 - 9 = 16 pixels form the outer ring.

quiz.q: In hole filling, why is each dilation intersected with the complement of A?
options: To stop the growing region at the object's walls so it does not leak out
To convert the image to grayscale
quiz.explain: Without the intersection, repeated dilation would spread over the whole image. The complement of A keeps the growth inside the hole.

quiz.q: With a flat SE of width 3, what is the grayscale erosion of [10, 50, 20, 80, 30] (window clipped at the ends)?
quiz.explain: Erosion takes the minimum in each window: min(10,50)=10, min(10,50,20)=10, 20, 20, min(80,30)=30.

quiz.q: Which transform is best for removing slowly varying uneven illumination before thresholding small bright grains?
quiz.explain: Opening with an SE larger than the grains estimates the background; subtracting it leaves the grains on a flat background.

quiz.q: In the two-pass labelling example, the pixel at (3,4) touches the U shape only diagonally. How many objects are there with 8-connectivity?
quiz.explain: With 8-connectivity diagonal neighbours count, so the single pixel joins the U shape, giving one object of 9 pixels.

lessons.title: Point, Line and Edge Detection: From Sobel to Canny and the Hough Transform
lessons.content:
Look at a children's colouring book. There is no colour yet, only black outlines, and still you instantly recognise the cow, the boat and the mango tree. Outlines carry most of the shape information in a picture. Edge detection is the computer's way of drawing that colouring-book version of a photo: it finds the places where brightness jumps. This lesson starts segmentation, the job of splitting an image into meaningful parts, with the approach based on discontinuities: isolated points, thin lines and edges. Lessons 21 and 22 take the other approach, based on similarity.

Where this sits: Derivatives of images were introduced in lesson 10 for sharpening, and spatial filtering mechanics in lesson 08. Here the same derivatives are used to detect, not to enhance. We go from the simplest detectors (points and lines) to edge models, gradient operators (Roberts, Prewitt, Sobel), the Laplacian of Gaussian, the Canny detector, and finally the Hough transform, which joins edge pixels into whole lines and circles. Colour edges were mentioned in lesson 17; deep-learning edge and contour detectors belong to Computer Vision (deep-cse-8-3).

Three kinds of discontinuity: A point is a single pixel very different from its surroundings, like a star in a night sky or a dead pixel on a sensor. A line is a thin strip, one to a few pixels wide, different from both sides, like a power cable against the sky. An edge is the border between two regions of different brightness, like the side of a white building against a blue sky. Each is found with derivatives, because derivatives are near zero where things are flat and large where they change.

Point detection: The Laplacian kernel with 8 in the centre and -1 at all eight neighbours sums to zero, so on a flat area its response is 0. Worked: a bright pixel of 200 surrounded by eight pixels of 20 gives 8 x 200 - 8 x 20 = 1600 - 160 = 1440. A pixel in a flat region of 20 gives 8 x 20 - 8 x 20 = 0. We mark a point wherever the absolute response exceeds a threshold T, often set to a large fraction, say 90 percent, of the maximum absolute response in the image. This is how a factory camera can spot a tiny pore in a turbine blade X-ray, or an astronomer can list stars.

Line detection: For thin lines we use kernels that respond to a particular direction. The horizontal line kernel has rows -1 -1 -1, 2 2 2, -1 -1 -1. Worked: a horizontal line one pixel thick with value 100 on a background of 10. Centred on the line, the response is (-1 x 10 x 3) + (2 x 100 x 3) + (-1 x 10 x 3) = -30 + 600 - 30 = 540. The vertical kernel (columns -1, 2, -1) on the same spot gives 0, because each of its rows sees -100 + 200 - 100 = 0 or -10 + 20 - 10 = 0. Similar kernels exist for +45 and -45 degrees. Run all four and pick the strongest response to know both where and in which direction a line is.

Edge models: Real edges come in three shapes. A step edge jumps from one level to another in one pixel, which mainly happens in computer-generated images. A ramp edge rises over several pixels, which is what real cameras produce because of lens blur and sampling. A roof edge goes up and down again, like a thin line seen through a blurry lens. Take a ramp profile such as 10, 10, 10, 40, 70, 100, 100, 100. Its first derivative (differences) is 0, 0, 30, 30, 30, 0, 0: nonzero along the whole ramp, so first derivatives give thick edges. Its second derivative is 0, 30, 0, 0, -30, 0: a positive spike at the start of the ramp, a negative one at the end, and a zero crossing in between that marks the edge centre precisely.

The gradient: In 2D the first derivative becomes the gradient vector, made of gx (rate of change along x) and gy (along y). Its magnitude M = sqrt(gx^2 + gy^2) says how strong the edge is, and its direction alpha = atan2(gy, gx) points toward increasing brightness, across the edge. The edge itself runs perpendicular to the gradient. Because square roots are slow, many systems use the approximation |gx| + |gy|. Different kernels estimate gx and gy in different ways.

Roberts, Prewitt and Sobel: Roberts cross-gradient uses 2 x 2 diagonal differences, gx = z9 - z5 and gy = z8 - z6, in a 3 x 3 neighbourhood numbered z1 to z9 row by row. It is tiny, fast and very sensitive to noise. Prewitt uses 3 x 3 kernels: gx = (z7 + z8 + z9) - (z1 + z2 + z3), the bottom row minus the top row, and gy = (z3 + z6 + z9) - (z1 + z4 + z7), the right column minus the left. Sobel is the same but gives the middle row or column a weight of 2: gx = (z7 + 2 z8 + z9) - (z1 + 2 z2 + z3). The weight 2 adds a little smoothing, which makes Sobel less noise-sensitive, and it is the default in most software. Here x runs down the rows, as in Gonzalez and Woods.

Sobel, worked: Take the patch with rows 10 10 10, then 10 10 100, then 10 100 100: a dark top-left and a bright bottom-right corner. gx = (10 + 2 x 100 + 100) - (10 + 2 x 10 + 10) = 310 - 40 = 270. gy = (10 + 2 x 100 + 100) - (10 + 2 x 10 + 10) = 270 as well. Magnitude = sqrt(270^2 + 270^2), about 381.8; the cheap version |gx| + |gy| gives 540. Direction = atan2(270, 270) = 45 degrees, pointing diagonally toward the bright corner, so the edge runs along the other diagonal. Prewitt on the same patch gives gx = 210 - 30 = 180 and gy = 180. Thresholding M, say at 200, marks this pixel as an edge.

Smooth first: Derivatives amplify noise, because noise is exactly a fast change between neighbours. A gradient image of a noisy photo looks like snow. So almost every practical edge detector smooths the image first, usually with a Gaussian (lesson 09), and then differentiates. The trade-off is the classic one: more smoothing means fewer false edges but blurrier, less precisely located edges, and very fine edges may vanish.

Marr-Hildreth and the Laplacian of Gaussian: David Marr and Ellen Hildreth (1980) argued that edges should be found at multiple scales and that zero crossings of the second derivative locate them precisely. Their method: smooth with a Gaussian of chosen sigma, take the Laplacian, and mark zero crossings, places where the result changes sign between neighbours with a big enough jump. Because both steps are linear, they combine into one kernel, the Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG), shaped like an upside-down Mexican hat. A rule of thumb for kernel size is the smallest odd integer at least 6 sigma, so sigma = 2 gives a 13 x 13 kernel. The difference of two Gaussians (DoG) approximates LoG cheaply. Zero crossings form closed contours, which is nice, but they also produce many weak, spaghetti-like edges.

Canny's three goals: In 1986 John Canny defined what a good edge detector should do. Low error rate: find all real edges and no false ones. Good localisation: the marked edge should be as close as possible to the true edge. Single response: one edge should give one line, not a thick band or double lines. He derived that the first derivative of a Gaussian is a near-optimal answer, and built four practical steps around it.

Canny steps 1 and 2: Step 1, smooth the image with a Gaussian of chosen sigma. Step 2, compute the gradient magnitude M and direction alpha at every pixel, for example with Sobel. So far this is just a smoothed Sobel, and the edges are still several pixels thick, because M is high across the whole ramp.

Canny step 3, non-maximum suppression: Thin the thick ridges to one pixel. At each pixel, round the gradient direction to one of four (0, 45, 90 or 135 degrees) and compare M with its two neighbours along that direction, the pixels in front and behind across the edge. Keep the pixel only if it is the largest of the three; otherwise set it to zero. Worked: across an edge the magnitudes are 80, 120, 90. The middle pixel (120) survives; 80 and 90 are suppressed when it is their turn because each has a larger neighbour. Result: a thin line along the ridge top.

Canny step 4, hysteresis thresholding: One threshold is not enough: too high breaks edges into dashes, too low lets noise in. Canny uses two, a high threshold TH and a low threshold TL, with a ratio of about 2:1 or 3:1. Worked with TH = 100 and TL = 40: a pixel of strength 120 is strong and is kept. A pixel of 30 is dropped. A pixel of 60 is weak: it is kept only if it is connected, through other weak pixels, to a strong pixel. So a long faint edge attached to a strong edge survives, while isolated faint noise does not. This is why Canny edges are long, thin and continuous, and why it is still the default edge detector decades later.

Edge linking: Even Canny leaves gaps, and many tasks need whole boundaries or straight lines, not just edge pixels. Local linking joins neighbouring edge pixels whose magnitudes and directions are similar, for example within 25 degrees. Regional linking fits polygons to a set of points along a known region. Global linking with the Hough transform finds straight lines or circles even when their pixels are scattered and broken.

Hough transform, the idea: A straight line could be written y = mx + c, but vertical lines have infinite slope. Hough's trick, in the form by Duda and Hart (1972), uses the normal form rho = x cos(theta) + y sin(theta), where rho is the line's distance from the origin and theta the angle of its normal, with theta from -90 to +90 degrees. Every edge point (x, y) votes for all the (rho, theta) pairs of lines that could pass through it, which in parameter space is a sinusoidal curve. An accumulator array, a grid over (rho, theta), counts the votes. Peaks in the accumulator are lines supported by many points.

Hough, worked with three points: Edge points (1,1), (2,2) and (3,3). At theta = 0 degrees, rho = x, so the votes go to rho = 1, 2 and 3, three different cells. At theta = 90 degrees, rho = y: again 1, 2, 3. At theta = 45 degrees, rho = (x + y) x 0.707, about 1.41, 2.83 and 4.24, still all different. At theta = -45 degrees, rho = 0.707 x - 0.707 y = 0 for all three points. The cell (rho = 0, theta = -45 degrees) gets three votes, the peak. That pair describes the line x - y = 0, which is y = x through all three points. With thousands of edge pixels and some noise, the true lines still stand out as the tallest peaks.

Hough for circles and cost: A circle (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2 has three parameters, so its accumulator is 3D over (a, b, r), costing much more memory and time. Using the gradient direction at each edge point cuts the search, because the centre must lie along that direction. Line Hough cost grows with the number of edge points times the number of theta steps, which is why we run it on Canny output rather than on every pixel. OpenCV offers HoughLines, a faster probabilistic HoughLinesP that returns segments, and HoughCircles.

Real-life example 1, lane lines on the Dhaka-Mawa expressway: A driver-assist prototype takes dashcam frames. Step 1, convert to gray and apply Gaussian blur. Step 2, run Canny, with thresholds tuned on sample frames. Step 3, keep only a trapezoid region in front of the car, since lanes do not appear in the sky. Step 4, run probabilistic Hough to find straight segments, and keep those whose angle is plausible for lanes (not near horizontal). Step 5, average segments on the left and right to get two lane lines and warn if the car drifts across one. Faded paint, rain and the shadows of trucks break this easily, which is why commercial systems add colour cues, tracking over frames and learned models.

Real-life example 2, counting coins and checking pipes: A bank cash counter camera uses Hough circles on Canny edges to find coins on a tray, and the radius found for each circle tells the coin type, provided the camera height is fixed so pixel size is known. In a garments factory in Ashulia, a camera checks that every cutting table's straight fabric edge is parallel to the guide line by detecting both with Hough and comparing their theta values; a difference of more than 1 degree stops the cutter.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Running a gradient on a noisy image without smoothing. Mixing up gradient direction (across the edge) with edge direction (along it). Thinking the Laplacian alone is a good edge detector; it is very noise-sensitive and gives double edges, which is why it is used with a Gaussian or for zero crossings. Using a single threshold in Canny. Using y = mx + c in Hough. Exams ask you to apply Sobel or Prewitt to a 3 x 3 patch and find magnitude and direction, compute point- or line-kernel responses, list and explain Canny's steps, do non-maximum suppression on a small strip, and fill a small Hough accumulator for three points.

Recap: Points, lines and edges are discontinuities, found with derivatives. The Laplacian finds points; directional kernels find lines. First derivatives (Roberts, Prewitt, Sobel) give edge strength and direction; second derivatives give zero crossings that locate edge centres. Smooth before differentiating. Canny combines Gaussian smoothing, gradient, non-maximum suppression and hysteresis thresholds to give thin, continuous edges. The Hough transform turns scattered edge pixels into whole lines and circles by voting in parameter space. Lesson 21 turns to the similarity approach: thresholding.
key_points: Point detection uses a Laplacian kernel; a pixel of 200 among 20s gives a response of 1440, a flat area gives 0.
Directional line kernels respond strongly to thin lines of their own orientation and give about 0 for other directions.
Gradient magnitude M = sqrt(gx^2 + gy^2) measures edge strength; the gradient points across the edge.
Sobel weights the centre row or column by 2, adding smoothing; it is less noise-sensitive than Roberts or Prewitt.
LoG (Marr-Hildreth) smooths with a Gaussian and finds zero crossings of the Laplacian.
Canny: Gaussian smoothing, gradient, non-maximum suppression, then hysteresis with high and low thresholds.
The Hough transform votes in (rho, theta) space using rho = x cos(theta) + y sin(theta); peaks are lines.
lessons.tip: For every detector, draw a 1D intensity profile and its first and second derivatives by hand. Once you see where each curve peaks or crosses zero, all the 2D kernels make sense.
lessons.task: On paper, make a 5 x 5 image with a vertical edge (left two columns 20, right three columns 120). Apply the Sobel gx and gy kernels at the three interior pixels of the middle row and write the magnitude and direction for each.

quiz.q: For the patch with rows 10 10 10 / 10 10 100 / 10 100 100, Sobel gives gx = 270 and gy = 270. What is the gradient direction?
quiz.explain: atan2(270, 270) = 45 degrees: the gradient points diagonally toward the bright corner.

quiz.q: Why does Canny use two thresholds (hysteresis)?
options: To keep weak edge pixels only when they connect to strong ones, giving continuous edges with little noise
Because one threshold is mathematically impossible
quiz.explain: Strong pixels are kept, weak pixels survive only if linked to strong ones, and the rest are dropped.

quiz.q: A pixel of 200 is surrounded by eight pixels of 20. What does the point-detection Laplacian (8 in the centre, -1 around) give?
Edge points (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) all vote for the same Hough cell. Which one?
quiz.explain: rho = 0.707x - 0.707y = 0 for every point when theta = -45 degrees, giving three votes for the line y = x.

quiz.q: What does non-maximum suppression do in Canny?
options: It removes all edges below the high threshold
It keeps a pixel only if its magnitude is the largest among its neighbours along the gradient direction, thinning edges
quiz.explain: It thins thick gradient ridges to one-pixel lines by keeping only local maxima across the edge.

lessons.title: Thresholding: Global, Otsu and Adaptive
lessons.content:
You photograph your handwritten class notes with your phone to send to a friend. The room has one window, so the left side of the page is bright and the right side sits in shadow. Your phone's scanner app turns it into crisp black writing on pure white paper, shadow gone. The heart of that trick is deciding, for every pixel, one thing: is this ink or paper? That yes-or-no decision is thresholding. It sounds like the simplest idea in the whole course, and it is, but doing it well when light is uneven and noise is present takes real thinking.

Where this sits: Lesson 20 segmented images by looking for discontinuities (edges). Thresholding is the first method of the similarity approach: pixels that look alike, in brightness, belong together. It builds on histograms (lesson 07), smoothing (lesson 09), the image formation model f = i x r (lesson 02) and edges (lesson 20). Lesson 22 continues with region growing, clustering and watershed. Thresholding is also a step inside almost every practical pipeline, including the plate reader in lesson 26.

The basic rule: Pick a threshold T. The output is g(x, y) = 1 if f(x, y) > T, and 0 otherwise. Pixels above T become object (or background, depending on the scene) and the rest the opposite. If one T is used for the whole image, it is global thresholding. If T changes from place to place depending on the neighbourhood, it is variable, local or adaptive thresholding. If we use two or more thresholds to split into three or more classes, it is multiple thresholding.

The histogram view: Thresholding is easiest to understand on the histogram. A page of dark ink on white paper gives a bimodal histogram: one hill near low values (ink) and a bigger hill near high values (paper), with a valley between. The best T sits in that valley. The whole difficulty of thresholding is that real valleys are not always deep and clear. Two things fill them in: noise and uneven illumination.

The role of noise: Imagine an ideal image with ink at exactly 40 and paper at exactly 200. The histogram has two thin spikes and any T between them works perfectly. Now add Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of 10: each spike spreads into a hill about 60 levels wide (plus or minus 3 standard deviations), but there is still a clear gap. With a standard deviation of 50, the hills overlap heavily and no single T can separate them without many mistakes. That is why we often smooth first (lesson 09): averaging reduces the noise spread and digs the valley back out.

The role of illumination: From lesson 02, f = i x r, illumination times reflectance. Paper reflects much more than ink, so under even light the two hills are well apart. Under a light that fades from left to right, the paper on the dark side may be darker than the ink on the bright side. The histogram's hills then smear into each other. No global T can fix this, because the right T is different on each side. The cures are: correct the lighting first (the top-hat or bottom-hat of lesson 19, or dividing by an estimate of i), or use variable thresholding.

Basic iterative global thresholding: When the histogram is reasonably bimodal, this simple algorithm finds T automatically. Step 1, start with an initial T, usually the image mean. Step 2, split pixels into G1 (values above T) and G2 (values at or below T). Step 3, compute their means m1 and m2. Step 4, set the new T = (m1 + m2) / 2. Step 5, repeat steps 2 to 4 until T changes by less than a small amount. It is the threshold that sits halfway between the means of the two groups it creates.

Iterative method, worked: Take a tiny 3-bit image of 60 pixels with gray levels 0 to 7 and counts 8, 12, 10, 2, 1, 6, 14, 7. The mean is (0 x 8 + 1 x 12 + 2 x 10 + 3 x 2 + 4 x 1 + 5 x 6 + 6 x 14 + 7 x 7) / 60 = 205 / 60, about 3.417. Split: levels 0 to 3 (32 pixels) have mean 38 / 32 = 1.1875; levels 4 to 7 (28 pixels) have mean 167 / 28, about 5.964. New T = (1.1875 + 5.964) / 2, about 3.576. That still splits between 3 and 4, so the groups and the means do not change and T stays at 3.576. Converged in one step: levels 0 to 3 are background, 4 to 7 are object.

Otsu's method, the idea: Nobuyuki Otsu (1979) gave a cleaner answer that needs only the histogram and no iteration guesswork. Any T splits pixels into two classes. A good T makes the classes as different as possible from each other and as uniform as possible inside. Otsu measures the first with the between-class variance, sigma_B squared, which is large when the two class means are far apart and both classes are well populated. Since total variance = within-class variance + between-class variance and the total is fixed, maximising between-class variance is the same as minimising within-class variance. Otsu simply tries every k and picks the one with the largest sigma_B squared.

Otsu's formulas: From the normalised histogram p_i, for each candidate k compute P1(k), the fraction of pixels at levels 0 to k; m(k), the cumulative mean, sum of i x p_i for i up to k; and the global mean mG. Then sigma_B squared(k) = (mG x P1(k) - m(k))^2 / (P1(k) x (1 - P1(k))). An equivalent form is P1 x P2 x (m1 - m2)^2, where P2 = 1 - P1 and m1, m2 are the class means: it is big when the means differ a lot and both classes have weight. Everything is cumulative sums over the histogram, so for 256 levels it takes a single pass, fast enough for every video frame.

Otsu, worked: Same histogram, 8, 12, 10, 2, 1, 6, 14, 7 over levels 0 to 7, mG = 205 / 60, about 3.417. For k = 2: P1 = 30/60 = 0.5, class means 1.067 and 5.767, sigma_B squared about 5.522. For k = 3: P1 = 32/60, about 0.533, m(k) = 38/60, about 0.633, so sigma_B squared = (3.417 x 0.533 - 0.633)^2 / (0.533 x 0.467), about 5.679. For k = 4: about 5.618. For k = 1: about 3.967; for k = 5: about 4.581. The maximum is at k = 3, so Otsu also says: levels 0 to 3 are one class, 4 to 7 the other. Here both methods agree, which is typical for a clean bimodal histogram.

How good is the split: Otsu gives a bonus number, the separability measure eta = sigma_B squared(k*) / sigma_G squared, where sigma_G squared is the global variance. It is between 0 and 1. For our histogram, sigma_G squared is about 6.376, so eta = 5.679 / 6.376, about 0.89. A value near 1 means the image really is two well separated groups; a value near 0 means thresholding is a poor fit and another method, or preprocessing, is needed.

When Otsu struggles, small objects: If the object is tiny, for example a few dark text lines covering 3 percent of the page, its hill in the histogram is just a bump on the side of the background hill. The between-class variance is then dominated by the background's own spread, and Otsu may cut through the background instead. The same happens when one class has a much larger variance than the other. The next two tricks fix this by reshaping the histogram before Otsu sees it.

Smoothing first: If noise is the problem, a Gaussian or median filter before thresholding narrows both hills and deepens the valley. Gonzalez and Woods show a noisy image where Otsu fails badly on the raw histogram but succeeds after a 5 x 5 averaging filter. The cost is that boundaries are slightly blurred, so the object outline moves by a pixel or so, which is usually acceptable.

Using edges to improve the histogram: Pixels on or near the object's boundary are roughly half object and half background. So: compute the gradient magnitude (lesson 20) or the absolute Laplacian, keep only pixels where it is high, for example in the top 0.5 percent, and build the histogram from those pixels only. That histogram has two hills of similar size, one from each side of the edges, with a deep valley. Run Otsu on it and apply the T to the whole image. This rescues small objects such as cells on a large slide or a few stars in a big sky.

Multiple thresholds: Some images have three or more classes, such as a medical scan with background, soft tissue and bone, or a map with water, vegetation and roads. Otsu's method extends naturally: choose k1 < k2 to maximise the between-class variance of three classes. The search over pairs is slower but still cheap for 256 levels. Beyond three or four classes, thresholds become unstable and clustering (lesson 22) is the better tool.

Variable thresholding by partitioning: The simplest fix for uneven light is to cut the image into tiles, say 4 x 4, small enough that the light is roughly constant inside each, and run Otsu separately in each tile. It works if every tile contains both object and background; a tile of pure paper gets a meaningless threshold, so tiles with low variance are usually marked all-background.

Local thresholding from local statistics: A smoother method computes a threshold for every pixel from its neighbourhood, typically T(x, y) = m(x, y) - C, the local mean minus a small constant. Worked in a shadowed region: a 3 x 3 window has values 58, 60, 62, 59, 30, 57, 60, 61, 28 (two ink pixels on shadowed paper). The mean is 475 / 9, about 52.8; with C = 5, T is about 47.8, so the ink pixels 30 and 28 become black and the paper pixels around 60 stay white. In a bright region: 200, 205, 198, 202, 120, 199, 201, 203, 118 has mean 1646 / 9, about 182.9, so T is about 177.9 and the ink at 120 and 118 is black. A single global T = 100 would have made the shadowed paper at 60 black and the light ink at 120 white: both regions ruined. Niblack's method uses T = m + k x s with the local standard deviation s and k around -0.2; Sauvola's refinement, T = m x (1 + k x (s / R - 1)), behaves better on plain paper, which is why it is popular for documents.

Making it fast: Computing a local mean in a 31 x 31 window at every pixel naively means 961 additions per pixel. An integral image (summed-area table), where each entry holds the sum of all pixels above and to the left, gives the sum of any rectangle with just 4 lookups, so the cost per pixel no longer depends on window size. A box filter of the same size does the same job. For scanned text, Gonzalez and Woods also describe a moving average along zig-zag scan lines, which is even cheaper and works well on thin strokes.

Real-life example 1, a phone document scanner: Step 1, detect the page corners and correct perspective (lessons 05 and 20). Step 2, convert to gray. Step 3, estimate the uneven background, for example by a large-window closing or blur, and divide the image by it, so the paper becomes uniformly bright. Step 4, apply Sauvola or local-mean thresholding with a window about as big as a few text lines. Step 5, remove specks with a small opening (lesson 18). Step 6, save as a compact black-and-white PDF. The window size is the main knob: too small and the inside of thick letters turns white; too large and the shadow comes back.

Real-life example 2, flood maps from radar satellites: During floods in Sylhet and Sunamganj, agencies map water using radar satellites such as Sentinel-1, which see through clouds. Calm water reflects the radar beam away from the satellite, so it appears very dark, while land appears brighter. The histogram of a flooded scene is bimodal, and Otsu's method, often applied tile by tile and on edge-rich tiles to keep the classes balanced, picks the water-land threshold automatically. Comparing the water mask with a dry-season mask gives the newly flooded area, which helps decide where to send relief boats. Speckle noise in radar is strong, so the image is filtered first.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Using a global threshold on unevenly lit images. Forgetting to smooth a noisy image first. Running Otsu when the object is tiny and wondering why it fails. Picking a local window that is smaller than the objects, which hollows out thick strokes. Forgetting that for some scenes the object is darker than the background, so the comparison flips. Exams give a small histogram and ask for the iterative threshold or Otsu's k by computing sigma_B squared, ask to explain the effects of noise and illumination on the histogram, compare global and adaptive thresholding, and ask how edges can improve Otsu.

Recap: Thresholding labels each pixel by comparing it with T. A clear valley in the histogram makes global thresholding easy; noise and uneven lighting fill the valley. The iterative method puts T halfway between class means; Otsu maximises between-class variance using only cumulative sums, and eta tells you how separable the image is. Smoothing and edge-based histograms help Otsu; multiple thresholds split more classes; local thresholds such as mean minus C, Niblack and Sauvola handle shadows, made fast with integral images. Lesson 22 groups pixels into regions with region growing, clustering and watershed.
key_points: Global thresholding: g = 1 if f > T else 0; works when the histogram has a clear valley.
Noise widens histogram hills and uneven illumination smears them, filling the valley.
The basic iterative method sets T = (m1 + m2) / 2 repeatedly until it stops changing.
Otsu picks the k that maximises between-class variance sigma_B squared = (mG P1 - m)^2 / (P1 (1 - P1)).
For counts 8, 12, 10, 2, 1, 6, 14, 7 both methods split between levels 3 and 4; eta is about 0.89.
Smoothing first and histograms built only from high-gradient pixels help Otsu with noise and small objects.
Adaptive thresholds (local mean minus C, Niblack, Sauvola) handle shadows; integral images make them fast.
lessons.tip: Before choosing a threshold method, always look at the histogram. Two clear hills: global or Otsu. Smeared hills: fix the light or go local.
lessons.task: Draw a histogram for a 3-bit image with counts 5, 15, 10, 3, 2, 8, 12, 5. Run the basic iterative method by hand starting from the mean and see where T settles.

quiz.q: In the basic iterative method, how is the new threshold computed?
options: The average of the two class means, (m1 + m2) / 2
quiz.explain: Split at T, compute the two class means, and set T to their midpoint; repeat until it stops changing.

quiz.q: What does Otsu's method maximise?
quiz.explain: Maximising between-class variance is equivalent to minimising within-class variance, because their sum is fixed.

quiz.q: Why does a single global threshold fail on a page photographed with a shadow on one side?
options: Because the histogram has too many gray levels
Because shadowed paper can be darker than ink on the bright side, so no one T separates them
Because Otsu only works on colour images
quiz.explain: Uneven illumination smears the two hills together; the correct T differs from place to place.

quiz.q: A local 3 x 3 window has mean 52.8 and C = 5. With T = mean - C, which pixel becomes black (ink)?
quiz.explain: T is about 47.8; only values below it, such as 30, are classified as ink.

quiz.q: How can edges help Otsu when the object is very small?
options: By removing all edges from the image first
By converting the image to colour
By building the histogram only from high-gradient pixels, which gives two balanced hills
By making the threshold equal to the maximum gradient
quiz.explain: Pixels near edges are about half object and half background, so their histogram is balanced and has a clear valley.

lessons.title: Region-Based Segmentation and Clustering
lessons.content:
Imagine you spill a bottle of red ink on a big sheet of graph paper. The ink starts at one square and spreads to the neighbouring squares, but only where the paper soaks it up in the same way. It stops at a pencil line, where the paper is different. In the end the ink has painted one connected blob. That is exactly the idea behind region growing, the first method of this lesson. Thresholding (lesson 21) looked at each pixel alone and asked "bright or dark?". Region-based segmentation asks a richer question: "which pixels belong together because they are similar AND touching each other?"

Where this sits: Segmentation means splitting an image into meaningful parts: the rice grain and the background, the tumour and the healthy tissue, the road and the field. Lesson 20 found edges (where things change) and lesson 21 used thresholds (how bright a pixel is). This lesson groups pixels into regions directly. We will see region growing, split and merge, k-means clustering of colours, superpixels, the watershed transform, a quick look at graph cuts and active contours, and finally how to measure whether a segmentation is any good with IoU and Dice. Deep learning segmentation is only previewed here; Computer Vision (deep-cse-8-3) covers it properly.

What a good segmentation must satisfy: The textbook definition (Gonzalez and Woods) says: split the image R into regions R1, R2, ..., Rn so that (a) together they cover every pixel, (b) each region is connected, (c) regions do not overlap, (d) every pixel inside one region passes the same similarity test Q, for example "all gray values within 20 of each other", and (e) two neighbouring regions taken together would fail Q, otherwise they should have been one region. Connected here uses the 4- or 8-adjacency from lesson 04. Keep these five rules in mind; every method below is just a different way to satisfy them.

Region growing, the idea: Pick one or more seed pixels you are sure about, for example a pixel in the middle of a crack in an X-ray. Then look at the seed's neighbours. If a neighbour is similar enough to the seed (the similarity rule), add it to the region. Keep checking the neighbours of every newly added pixel. Stop when no new pixel can be added. In pseudo-code: region = {seed}; queue = [seed]; while queue not empty: p = queue.pop(); for each neighbour q of p: if q not in region and |f(q) - f(seed)| <= T: add q to region and to queue. This is the flood fill from Computer Graphics (deep-cse-5-2 lesson 08) with a similarity test instead of an exact colour match.

Region growing, worked: Take this 5 x 5 gray image, written row by row: row 0 = 20 22 25 24 21, row 1 = 23 198 205 30 26, row 2 = 24 201 210 207 28, row 3 = 22 195 60 212 27, row 4 = 25 24 23 26 29. Put the seed at row 2, column 2 (value 210). The rule: accept a 4-neighbour if its value is within 20 of the seed value, so between 190 and 230. From 210 we accept 205 above, 201 on the left and 207 on the right; the pixel below is 60, rejected. From 205 we reach 198. From 201 we reach 195 below it. From 207 we reach 212 below it; 30 above it is rejected. Nothing else qualifies. The region has 7 pixels: 198, 205, 201, 210, 207, 195 and 212. Notice the dark 60 stays out even though it is surrounded by the bright blob. That is a small hole, and the morphology tools of lesson 19 (hole filling) can close it if needed.

Choices inside region growing: You must choose (1) seeds: by hand, by taking the brightest pixels, or by picking pixels in the peaks of the histogram; (2) the similarity test: compare with the seed value, or with the running mean of the region (more stable, the region adapts as it grows), or use colour distance or texture; (3) connectivity: 4 or 8 neighbours; and (4) a stopping rule, sometimes a maximum size. The weakness is leaking: if there is a single weak spot in the border, for example a pixel of value 190 bridging the object and a bright background, the region pours through it and swallows the background. A strict threshold stops leaks but leaves the region full of holes. Good practice is to smooth the image first (lesson 09) so noise does not cause either problem.

Split and merge, the idea: Region growing starts small and grows. Split and merge starts big and cuts. Take the whole image as one region and test it with Q, for example "max minus min is at most 10". If it fails, split it into four equal quadrants. Test each quadrant; split again those that fail. Keep going until every block passes or is a single pixel. The splitting is stored as a quadtree: each node has four children, NW, NE, SW and SE. Then the merge step joins neighbouring blocks whose union still passes Q, because a big uniform area might have been chopped up only because the cut lines fell through it.

Split and merge, a small trace: Think of a 8 x 8 image with a bright 4 x 4 square in the top-left corner on a dark background. The whole image fails Q (it has both 200 and 20). Split into four 4 x 4 quadrants: the top-left one is all 200, it passes; the other three are all 20, they pass. Done after one split, and the merge step joins the three dark quadrants into one background region. If the bright square had been placed at rows 2 to 5 and columns 2 to 5, it would cross all four quadrants, so every quadrant fails and is split again into 2 x 2 blocks; then many small blocks pass, and merging rebuilds the square and the background. The lesson: split creates blocky pieces aligned to the grid, merge repairs that. The cost is low because uniform areas are handled as big blocks.

K-means for segmentation: Here we forget about position for a moment and look only at pixel values, then group similar values into K clusters (recap deep-cse-6-1 lesson 21). Steps: pick K starting centres; assign every pixel to the nearest centre; move each centre to the mean of its pixels; repeat until nothing changes. Each cluster becomes a label, and pixels with the same label are one segment. For colour images every pixel is a point (R, G, B) in 3D and distance is Euclidean; many people use the Lab colour space (lesson 16) because distance there matches human perception better.

K-means, worked: Nine gray pixels: 10, 12, 15, 200, 210, 190, 14, 205, 120. Let K = 2 with a bad start: centres 10 and 15. Assignment: 10 and 12 are nearer to 10; everything else, including 200, is nearer to 15. New centres: mean(10, 12) = 11 and mean(15, 200, 210, 190, 14, 205, 120) = about 136.29. Assign again: the midpoint between 11 and 136.29 is about 73.6, so 10, 12, 15, 14 go to the first cluster and 200, 210, 190, 205, 120 to the second. New centres: 12.75 and 185. Assign once more: nothing moves, so it has converged. Labels: dark object and bright object. The middle value 120 joined the bright group because it is closer to 185 than to 12.75. K-means needs K given, can depend on the starting centres (run it a few times or use k-means++ starts), and ignores space, so two far apart objects of the same colour get the same label. Run connected-component labelling (lesson 19) after it to split them.

Superpixels: An image of 12 megapixels has 12 million pixels, which is a lot of small things to reason about. Superpixels group pixels into a few hundred or thousand small, compact patches that follow edges, like cutting a photo into tiles shaped to the objects. SLIC (Simple Linear Iterative Clustering) is basically k-means where each pixel is described by colour AND position (l, a, b, x, y), and each centre only searches a small window around itself, which makes it fast. A weight decides how much to care about compactness versus colour. Superpixels are not a final answer; they are a cheaper starting point for later steps such as merging, graph cuts or classification.

Watershed, the topographic view: Think of the gradient magnitude image (lesson 20) as a landscape: flat, uniform areas are valleys, and edges are high ridges. Now imagine water coming up from the bottom of every valley, like the Padma rising during monsoon. Each valley fills into its own lake. Where two lakes would meet, we build a dam. When the whole landscape is under water, the dams are the watershed lines, and they lie exactly on the ridges, which are the object borders. Each lake is one region. The beauty is that the boundaries come out closed and connected, unlike plain edge detection which often leaves gaps.

Watershed, the problem and the fix: Real gradient images have many tiny valleys made by noise. Each becomes its own lake, so the result is over-segmentation: hundreds of little regions instead of a few objects. The standard fix is marker-controlled watershed. You first mark where objects definitely are (internal markers, for example found by thresholding and then eroding, or from the distance transform peaks) and where background definitely is (external markers). Water is allowed to rise only from markers, so you get exactly one region per marker. The classic use is splitting touching objects: coins on a table, cells in a microscope slide, or rice grains pressed together, where thresholding alone gives one big blob.

Graph cuts and active contours, the idea only: Graph-cut segmentation treats each pixel as a node in a graph; edges between neighbours carry a weight that is high when the two pixels look similar. Cutting the graph into foreground and background costs the sum of the weights you cut, so the cheapest cut tends to run along real boundaries. With a few user strokes ("this is object, this is background") a min-cut algorithm finds the best split; the well known GrabCut tool in photo editors works on this principle. Active contours (snakes) start with a curve near the object and let it move, pulled by edges and kept smooth by an internal stiffness, until it hugs the boundary. Both are covered more deeply in Computer Vision (deep-cse-8-3).

Measuring quality, IoU and Dice: How do you know a segmentation is good? Compare it with a ground truth mask drawn by a human expert. Let A be the predicted pixels and B the true pixels. Intersection over Union: IoU = |A and B| / |A or B|. Dice coefficient: Dice = 2|A and B| / (|A| + |B|). Worked: the program marks 100 pixels as tumour, the doctor marked 80, and 60 pixels are in both. Union = 100 + 80 - 60 = 120. IoU = 60 / 120 = 0.5. Dice = 2 x 60 / (100 + 80) = 120 / 180 = about 0.667. Both are 1 for a perfect match and 0 for no overlap. Dice is always at least as large as IoU for the same result, so never compare a Dice score of one paper with an IoU score of another.

Why pixel accuracy is a trap: Suppose a tumour covers 1 percent of a scan. A program that says "no tumour anywhere" gets 99 percent of the pixels right, yet it is useless. IoU and Dice ignore the huge correctly labelled background and focus on the object, which is why medical and satellite segmentation papers report them. This is the same idea as precision and recall for imbalanced classes in deep-cse-6-1 lesson 14.

Deep segmentation, a preview: Modern systems train a neural network to output a label for every pixel. Fully convolutional networks and the U-Net (built originally for biomedical images) are the famous families. Semantic segmentation labels classes (all cars are "car"), while instance segmentation also separates each car. They learn their own similarity rules from thousands of labelled examples, which beats hand-tuned thresholds on messy real photos. But the classic methods here are still used for pre-processing, post-processing (cleaning masks with morphology, splitting blobs with watershed) and in small projects with little data or weak hardware.

Real life example 1, rice grain quality check: A rice mill in Dinajpur wants to count broken grains. A phone camera takes a photo of grains on a black tray. Step 1, smooth and threshold (lesson 21) to get a white mask of grains. Step 2, many grains touch each other, so the mask has big blobs. Step 3, compute the distance transform of the mask; the centre of each grain is a local peak. Step 4, use those peaks as markers for watershed on the inverted distance image, which places dams in the narrow necks between touching grains. Step 5, label each region and measure its length; grains shorter than three quarters of the typical length are counted as broken. The mill gets a percentage in seconds instead of counting by hand.

Real life example 2, flood mapping from satellite images: During a flood in Sylhet, an analyst gets a satellite image and wants the flooded area. Water looks dark and smooth in the near-infrared band. Step 1, run SLIC to get a few thousand superpixels so each patch is uniform. Step 2, compute the mean value of each superpixel. Step 3, run k-means with K = 3 on those means (water, vegetation, built-up). Step 4, pick the cluster with the darkest centre as water. Step 5, compare with a manually checked map using IoU; if IoU is about 0.8 the method is trusted for the whole district. Superpixels made it fast and the boundaries follow river banks nicely.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that k-means and thresholding give labels by value only, so separate objects of the same colour share one label until you run connected components. Using a fixed region growing threshold on an unevenly lit image, which makes the region leak on one side and stop early on the other; compare with the running region mean or fix the lighting first. Running watershed on a raw noisy gradient and being surprised by thousands of regions; use markers or smooth first. Reporting only pixel accuracy. Mixing up IoU and Dice.

What exams ask: Apply region growing by hand on a small matrix with a given seed, threshold and connectivity, and list the region pixels. Draw the quadtree for split and merge on an 8 x 8 image. Run two iterations of k-means on a list of values. Explain the flooding idea of watershed, why over-segmentation happens and how markers fix it. Compute IoU and Dice from given counts. State the five conditions of a valid segmentation.

Recap: Region-based segmentation groups pixels that are both similar and connected. Region growing spreads from seeds and can leak; split and merge cuts with a quadtree and then rejoins; k-means clusters values (or colour plus position in SLIC superpixels); watershed floods the gradient landscape and builds dams on edges, using markers to avoid over-segmentation; graph cuts and snakes are the energy-based cousins. Judge results with IoU and Dice. Next, lesson 23 looks at the same image at many scales with pyramids and wavelets.
key_points: A segmentation splits an image into connected, non-overlapping regions that each satisfy a similarity rule.
Region growing adds neighbours similar to the seed (or region mean); it can leak through weak borders.
Split and merge divides failing blocks into quadrants (quadtree), then merges similar neighbours.
K-means groups pixel values or colours into K clusters; run connected components afterwards to separate objects.
SLIC superpixels are k-means on (colour, x, y) with a local search window.
Watershed floods the gradient image and builds dams on ridges; markers prevent over-segmentation.
IoU = overlap / union and Dice = 2 x overlap / (|A| + |B|); both ignore the easy background.
lessons.tip: Do every algorithm here once by hand on a tiny 5 x 5 grid with coloured pencils. When you can predict which pixel joins a region next, the code becomes obvious.
lessons.task: Draw a 6 x 6 grid and fill it with numbers: a bright blob of values near 200 and a dark background near 20, with one bridging pixel of 185. Grow a region from the centre of the blob with threshold 20, first with 4-neighbours and then with 8-neighbours, and see whether it leaks through the bridge.

quiz.q: In region growing, what usually causes 'leaking'?
options: A weak spot in the border where a neighbour is similar enough to pass the test
quiz.explain: If even one border pixel passes the similarity test, the region flows through it into the neighbouring area.

quiz.q: Split and merge stores its splitting steps in which structure?
quiz.explain: Each failing block splits into four quadrants, which is a node with four children: a quadtree.

quiz.q: A program marks 100 pixels, the ground truth has 80, and 60 overlap. What is IoU?
Why does plain watershed on a noisy image give over-segmentation?
options: Every small noise valley becomes its own basin
quiz.explain: Noise creates many tiny local minima; each fills as a separate lake unless markers restrict the sources.

quiz.q: Two separate red balls in a photo get the same k-means label. What fixes this?
options: Run connected-component labelling on the result
quiz.explain: K-means only uses values, so same-colour objects share a label; connected components separates the touching groups.

lessons.title: Wavelets and Multiresolution Processing
lessons.content:
Open Google Maps on your phone and look at Bangladesh. You see the whole country, rivers as thin lines, no buildings. Zoom in to Dhaka and roads appear. Zoom in again to Dhanmondi and you see single houses. The app does not shrink one giant photo every time; it keeps the map at several prepared sizes and gives you the one that fits your zoom. Looking at the same scene at many sizes is called multiresolution, and it is the idea behind this lesson. Small things (a crack in a bone) show up best at fine scale; big things (a whole lake) are easier to spot at coarse scale. A good image tool looks at both.

Where this sits: Lessons 11 and 12 described an image by its frequencies with the Fourier transform. Fourier tells you which frequencies are present, but not where they are, because each sine wave stretches over the whole image. An edge in the top-left corner and an edge in the bottom-right corner both just add high frequencies. Wavelets fix this: they tell you what is happening at which scale AND at which place. In this lesson we build image pyramids, meet subband coding, work the Haar wavelet transform by hand, do a one-level 2D wavelet transform, and use it for denoising. Lesson 24 then uses wavelets inside JPEG 2000.

Why multiresolution, a simple test: Try to find a rickshaw in a 4000 x 3000 photo by sliding a 50 x 50 template over every position. You would need the template to match rickshaws that are near (big) and far (small). Instead of making templates of many sizes, shrink the image several times and slide the same template on each smaller copy. A rickshaw that is 200 pixels tall in the original is 50 pixels tall after shrinking by 4. This trick is used in classic face detectors and in keypoint methods like SIFT (lesson 25).

The Gaussian pyramid: Level 0 is the original image. To build level 1, blur level 0 with a small Gaussian kernel (lesson 09) and then keep every second row and every second column. Repeat for level 2, 3 and so on. Each level has half the width and half the height, so a quarter of the pixels. Why blur first? Throwing away every second pixel without blurring is sampling too slowly, and lesson 03 showed what that causes: aliasing, with fake patterns like moire on a striped shirt. The blur removes the fine detail that the smaller grid cannot hold, exactly like an anti-aliasing filter in front of an ADC (deep-cse-5-7 lesson 03).

Pyramid storage, worked: A 1024 x 1024 image has 1,048,576 pixels. Level 1 is 512 x 512 = 262,144, level 2 is 256 x 256 = 65,536, and so on down to 1 x 1. The total is N^2 x (1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + ...). After three levels the sum is already 1.3125, and the infinite sum is 4/3. So a whole pyramid costs only about 33 percent more memory than the original. Graphics people use the same structure as mipmaps for textures (deep-cse-5-2 lesson 23).

The Laplacian pyramid: The Gaussian pyramid keeps blurrier and blurrier copies. But what information did we lose between two levels? To find out, take level 1, expand it back to the size of level 0 (upsample by inserting zeros and blurring, or by interpolation), and subtract: L0 = G0 - expand(G1). This difference image holds only the detail that level 1 cannot represent: edges and fine texture. Do the same for every level, and keep the smallest Gaussian level at the end. The magic: you can rebuild the original exactly by going backwards, G0 = L0 + expand(G1), and so on. Most Laplacian values are near zero (smooth areas have no detail), so they compress well. Burt and Adelson introduced this in 1983 for image coding, and it is also used for seamless photo blending: blend each frequency band separately and the seam disappears.

Subband coding, the idea: Split a signal into a low-frequency part (the smooth trend) and a high-frequency part (the quick changes) using a lowpass and a highpass filter. Each part now holds only about half of the frequency range, so you can keep every second sample of each without losing information. Two half-length signals have as many samples as the original, so nothing is wasted. With carefully designed filter pairs (perfect reconstruction filter banks) the synthesis side can rebuild the original exactly. Repeat the split on the low part to go one scale coarser. This is the engine inside the discrete wavelet transform.

The Haar wavelet, the simplest of all: Take numbers in pairs. For each pair (a, b) keep the average (a + b) / 2 and the detail (a - b) / 2. The average is the low-frequency part, the detail is the high-frequency part. You can go back: a = average + detail and b = average - detail. Nothing is lost. The Haar wavelet was described by Alfred Haar in 1909, long before the word wavelet existed, and it is still the easiest way to understand everything that follows.

Haar, worked on [9, 7, 3, 5]: Level 1. Pair (9, 7): average 8, detail 1. Pair (3, 5): average 4, detail -1. So we have averages [8, 4] and details [1, -1]. Level 2: work on the averages only. Pair (8, 4): average 6, detail 2. The full transform is [6, 2, 1, -1]: one overall average, one coarse detail, two fine details. Rebuild: 6 + 2 = 8 and 6 - 2 = 4; then 8 + 1 = 9, 8 - 1 = 7, 4 + (-1) = 3, 4 - (-1) = 5. We are back to [9, 7, 3, 5]. Notice the details are small numbers. In a real smooth image most details are close to zero, and small numbers need few bits. That is the whole reason wavelets compress well.

Normalised Haar: The averaging version above is easy to compute by hand, but it changes the energy (sum of squares) of the signal. The textbook orthonormal Haar uses (a + b) / sqrt(2) and (a - b) / sqrt(2) instead. On [9, 7, 3, 5] this gives level 1 approximations about 11.31 and 5.66, details about 1.41 and -1.41, then level 2 approximation 12 and detail 4. Energy check: 81 + 49 + 9 + 25 = 164, and 144 + 16 + 2 + 2 = 164. Same energy, just packed into fewer large numbers. Exams use either version, so read the question and say which one you use.

The 2D wavelet transform, one level: An image is a 2D grid, so we apply the 1D transform to every row and then to every column of the result. Each row splits into a low half and a high half; then each column does the same. The image becomes four quarter-size subbands: LL (low in both directions, a small blurred copy of the image), and three detail subbands that respond to vertical edges, horizontal edges and diagonal detail. Naming like LH and HL differs between books, so always check which direction each one means.

2D Haar on one 2 x 2 block, worked: Take the block with top row 9, 7 and bottom row 3, 5. The LL value is the mean of all four: (9 + 7 + 3 + 5) / 4 = 6. The left-minus-right detail is ((9 - 7) + (3 - 5)) / 4 = 0: no vertical edge, because the left column is not consistently brighter than the right. The top-minus-bottom detail is ((9 + 7) - (3 + 5)) / 4 = 2: a horizontal edge, the top is brighter. The diagonal detail is ((9 - 7) - (3 - 5)) / 4 = 1. Every 2 x 2 block of an 8 x 8 image gives four such numbers, so the result is four 4 x 4 subbands, still 64 numbers in total.

Multi-level decomposition: Now apply the same 2D transform to the LL subband again, and again. After 3 levels you have 3 x 3 + 1 = 10 subbands: a tiny LL at the coarsest level plus three detail subbands at each of the three scales. Fine scales show small details like hair and text strokes; coarse scales show big structures like a face or a building. This is the layout you see in every wavelet textbook picture, a big square split into smaller and smaller squares in the top-left corner.

Beyond Haar: Haar wavelets are blocky, so they create square artefacts when coefficients are removed. Smoother families exist: Daubechies wavelets (Ingrid Daubechies, late 1980s), and the biorthogonal 5/3 and 9/7 wavelets used in JPEG 2000. The 5/3 is reversible with integers, which allows lossless coding; the 9/7 gives better quality for lossy coding. The fast wavelet transform (Mallat's algorithm) costs O(N) for N samples, even faster than the FFT's O(N log N), because each level processes only half the data of the previous one.

Wavelet denoising: Noise is spread over all coefficients as small random values, while real image structure lives in a few large coefficients. So: transform the image, set small detail coefficients to zero, and transform back. Hard thresholding: keep a coefficient if its magnitude is above T, otherwise set it to 0. Soft thresholding: set small ones to 0 and also shrink the kept ones towards zero by T. Worked with [6, 2, 1, -1] and T = 1, hard: the two fine details 1 and -1 become 0, giving [6, 2, 0, 0], which rebuilds to [8, 8, 4, 4]. The tiny wobbles are gone, the big step from 8 to 4 survives. Soft thresholding would also shrink 2 to 1 and give [7, 7, 5, 5], smoother but with a weaker step. Hard keeps edges sharper; soft gives fewer artefacts. Donoho and Johnstone gave the well known universal threshold T = sigma x sqrt(2 ln N), where sigma is the noise level.

Edges and texture: Large detail coefficients appear exactly where edges are, at the scale matching their size, so a wavelet map is a multi-scale edge detector. Texture (cloth weave, leaf veins, rough concrete) creates energy in particular subbands; the energy of each subband is a simple, useful texture feature for classification (lesson 25). Wavelets are also used for image fusion, for example merging a sharp panchromatic satellite image with a blurrier colour one: take details from the sharp image and approximation from the colour image.
