Real life example 1, a zoomable medical slide: A pathology lab in Dhaka scans a tissue slide at very high resolution, around 100,000 x 80,000 pixels. No phone or laptop can load that. The viewer stores the slide as a pyramid of tiles. When the doctor sees the whole slide, the app downloads the coarse level, a few hundred kilobytes. When she zooms on a suspicious spot, only the fine tiles for that small window are fetched. The total storage is just about one third more than the base level, and every zoom feels instant. Map apps work the same way.

Real life example 2, cleaning an old family photo: Your grandmother's 1970s photo is scanned and full of fine grain noise. A simple blur (lesson 09) removes the grain but also softens faces and eyes. Instead: Step 1, compute a 3-level wavelet transform. Step 2, estimate the noise level from the finest diagonal subband, which is mostly noise. Step 3, soft-threshold the detail subbands. Step 4, inverse transform. The grain is reduced while the edges of the eyes and the outline of the sari, which created large coefficients, are kept much better than with the blur.

Common mistakes: Shrinking an image by dropping pixels without blurring first, then wondering about jagged lines and moire. Forgetting the LL band when counting subbands (3 levels give 10, not 9). Thinking the wavelet transform makes data smaller by itself; it does not, the number of coefficients equals the number of pixels, the saving comes later from small coefficients being zeroed or coded cheaply. Mixing up averaging Haar and orthonormal Haar values. Assuming LH always means horizontal edges; books differ.

What exams ask: Compute the Haar transform of a 4- or 8-sample signal and reconstruct it. Apply one level of 2D Haar to a 4 x 4 image. Explain Gaussian and Laplacian pyramids and prove the 4/3 storage bound. Compare Fourier and wavelet transforms (frequency only vs frequency and location). Explain hard vs soft thresholding with a small example. Name the wavelets used in JPEG 2000.

Recap: Multiresolution looks at an image at many sizes. A Gaussian pyramid is blur-and-shrink, costing at most 4/3 of the memory; a Laplacian pyramid keeps the detail lost between levels and rebuilds the image exactly. Subband coding splits signals into low and high halves; the Haar wavelet does it with averages and differences. A 2D level gives LL plus three detail subbands, and repeating on LL gives a multi-scale picture. Small coefficients can be dropped for denoising and compression, which is exactly where lesson 24 picks up.
key_points: Multiresolution analysis looks at an image at several scales; small and large objects show best at different scales.
A Gaussian pyramid blurs then downsamples by 2; total storage is at most 4/3 of the original.
A Laplacian pyramid stores G_i - expand(G_(i+1)) and allows exact reconstruction.
Haar keeps averages and differences of pairs: [9, 7, 3, 5] becomes [6, 2, 1, -1].
One 2D DWT level gives LL plus three detail subbands; 3 levels give 10 subbands.
Unlike Fourier, wavelets tell both scale and location.
Wavelet denoising zeroes or shrinks small detail coefficients (hard vs soft thresholding).
lessons.tip: Practise Haar on paper until you can do an 8-number signal in under two minutes, including reconstruction. Every wavelet question becomes easy once the averages and differences feel automatic.
lessons.task: Write the 8 numbers 10, 12, 14, 16, 40, 42, 20, 18. Do a full 3-level Haar transform with averages and half-differences. Then zero every detail whose magnitude is 1 or less and reconstruct. Which features of the signal survived?

quiz.q: Why blur before downsampling when building a Gaussian pyramid?
options: To prevent aliasing from details the smaller grid cannot hold
To increase the number of pixels
quiz.explain: Dropping samples without removing fine detail first causes aliasing, as in the sampling theorem.

quiz.q: Using averages and half-differences, what is the one-level Haar transform of the pair (10, 6)?
A 3-level 2D wavelet decomposition produces how many subbands?
quiz.explain: Three detail subbands per level times 3 levels, plus the final LL: 3 x 3 + 1 = 10.

quiz.q: What does a wavelet transform tell you that a plain Fourier transform does not?
options: Where in the image a given scale of detail occurs
quiz.explain: Fourier basis functions span the whole image; wavelets are localised, so they give scale and location.

quiz.q: In hard thresholding with T = 1, the coefficient 0.8 becomes...
quiz.explain: Hard thresholding sets every coefficient with magnitude below T to zero and keeps the rest unchanged.

lessons.title: Image Compression
lessons.content:
Think of packing for a trip to your village before Eid. You cannot carry the whole wardrobe, so you fold clothes tightly (nothing lost, just packed better), you leave out things nobody will notice are missing, and you write a short list instead of describing every item. Image compression does exactly these three things with pixels: it packs repeated patterns, it removes details your eyes will not miss, and it uses short codes for common values. This is why you can send fifty photos over a slow mobile connection in Bangladesh without waiting all day.

Where this sits: Multimedia Systems (deep-cse-5-9) already covered entropy, Huffman, LZW, arithmetic coding, the DCT and the full JPEG pipeline step by step (lessons 06-12). Here we look at compression from the image processing point of view: the three kinds of redundancy in images, how to measure compression and quality, the lossless methods built specially for images (run-length for fax, predictive coding in PNG), a quick JPEG recap, and the wavelet-based JPEG 2000 that grows directly out of lesson 23. We finish with practical choices for everyday uploads.

Why compress, worked: A 12 megapixel phone photo is 4000 x 3000 pixels. Each pixel needs 3 bytes (red, green, blue, 8 bits each). Raw size = 4000 x 3000 x 3 = 36,000,000 bytes, about 36 MB. A typical JPEG of that photo is around 3 MB, so the compression ratio C = 36 / 3 = 12, written 12:1. Video is worse: raw 1920 x 1080 colour at 30 frames per second is 1920 x 1080 x 3 x 30 = 186,624,000 bytes, about 187 MB every second. Without compression, a phone could store only a few minutes of video and a 4G connection could not stream it at all.

Measuring compression: Compression ratio C = n1 / n2, where n1 is the size before and n2 after. Relative data redundancy R = 1 - 1/C. For our photo, R = 1 - 1/12 = about 0.917, meaning about 91.7 percent of the raw data was redundant for this purpose. Another way to say the same thing is bits per pixel: 3 MB for 12 million pixels is 24,000,000 bits / 12,000,000 = 2 bits per pixel, compared with 24 bits per pixel raw.

Redundancy 1, coding redundancy: Using 8 bits for every gray value is wasteful if some values appear much more often than others. Suppose an image has only 4 gray levels with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and 0.125. A fixed-length code needs 2 bits per pixel. A variable-length (Huffman) code gives 0 to the most common level, 10 to the next, and 110 and 111 to the rare ones. Average length = 0.5 x 1 + 0.25 x 2 + 0.125 x 3 + 0.125 x 3 = 1.75 bits. Saving 2 down to 1.75 gives C = 2 / 1.75 = about 1.14 and R = 0.125. Shannon's entropy H = - sum p log2 p for these probabilities is also exactly 1.75 bits, so this Huffman code is perfect here: no lossless code can average fewer bits than the entropy.

Redundancy 2, spatial and temporal redundancy: Neighbouring pixels are usually almost equal: a blue sky, a white wall, a black school board. Knowing one pixel you can guess the next very well. Storing every pixel separately ignores this. Methods that exploit it: run-length coding, predictive coding, transforms like the DCT and wavelets that pack the energy into a few coefficients. In video, consecutive frames are nearly identical, which is temporal redundancy, exploited by motion compensation (deep-cse-5-9 lessons 16-17).

Redundancy 3, irrelevant (psychovisual) information: Your eye is less sensitive to fine colour detail than to fine brightness detail, and hardly notices small errors in busy, high-frequency texture. Data the viewer cannot perceive is irrelevant and can be thrown away. This is what makes lossy compression possible: chroma subsampling (lesson 16, YCbCr), coarse quantisation of high-frequency DCT coefficients, and zeroing small wavelet coefficients. Once removed, it is gone forever, which is why it is called lossy.

Fidelity criteria, measuring quality: For lossy methods we must say how close the result is to the original. Objective measures: the mean squared error MSE = average of (f_hat - f)^2 over all pixels, RMSE = square root of MSE, and the peak signal-to-noise ratio PSNR = 10 log10(255^2 / MSE) in decibels for 8-bit images. Subjective measures: ask people to rate images on a scale (excellent, fine, passable, marginal, inferior, unusable) and average the scores. PSNR is easy to compute but does not always agree with people; measures like SSIM (structural similarity) try to match human judgement better.

PSNR, worked: A 2 x 2 original block has values 100, 102, 98, 101. After compression it reads 101, 100, 98, 104. The errors are 1, -2, 0 and 3. MSE = (1 + 4 + 0 + 9) / 4 = 3.5. RMSE = about 1.87 gray levels. PSNR = 10 log10(65025 / 3.5) = about 42.7 dB. For a whole image, an MSE of 25 (RMSE 5) gives about 34.2 dB and an MSE of 100 (RMSE 10) gives about 28.1 dB. As a rough guide, many lossy photos sit roughly between 30 and 40 dB, and higher is better; each halving of RMSE adds about 6 dB.

Run-length coding: Replace a run of identical values by (value, count). A row of 100 pixels with 40 white, 20 black and 40 white becomes (W, 40), (B, 20), (W, 40): three pairs instead of 100 values. Fax machines are the classic user: a fax line at standard resolution has 1728 pixels and is mostly white, so the CCITT Group 3 and Group 4 standards code run lengths with fixed Huffman tables; Group 4 also codes each line relative to the line above. Run-length is useless on noisy photos where every pixel differs from its neighbour: then it can even make the data bigger.

Lossless predictive coding: Predict each pixel from neighbours already coded, and store only the prediction error. Row: 100, 102, 104, 105, 107. Predict each pixel as the one on its left: errors are 100 (first pixel stored as is), 2, 2, 1, 2. The errors are small and cluster around zero, so their histogram is sharp and their entropy low, which Huffman or arithmetic coding then shrinks. The decoder makes the same prediction and adds the error back, so it is exactly lossless. PNG does this: before DEFLATE (LZ77 plus Huffman, deep-cse-5-9 lesson 08), each row is filtered with one of five predictors: None, Sub (left), Up (above), Average (of left and above) and Paeth (picks whichever of left, above or upper-left is closest to a simple estimate).

How much can lossless do? For natural photos, lossless methods usually reach only about 2:1, sometimes a bit better, because camera noise is random and cannot be predicted. For screenshots, diagrams, scanned text and medical images that must not be altered, lossless is the right choice. Typical lossless formats: PNG, lossless WebP, TIFF with LZW, JPEG-LS and lossless JPEG 2000.

Lossy predictive coding, one line: Do the same prediction, but quantise the error before coding (for example round it to a multiple of 4). This is DPCM. The encoder must predict from the reconstructed values, not the originals, otherwise encoder and decoder drift apart. Quantising the errors creates typical artefacts: slope overload on sharp edges and granular noise in flat areas.

Block transform coding and JPEG, recap: Split the image into 8 x 8 blocks, apply the DCT to each so the energy collects in a few low-frequency coefficients, divide each coefficient by a quantisation table entry and round (this is the only lossy step, and it is where the quality setting acts), scan in zig-zag order so the zeros group together, then code with run-length and Huffman. Colour is converted to YCbCr and the chroma channels are usually subsampled 4:2:0. All details are in deep-cse-5-9 lessons 11-12. The weak point: at high compression each 8 x 8 block is coded on its own, so blocks show visible edges, the familiar blocking artefact, plus ringing around sharp edges.

JPEG 2000 and wavelets: JPEG 2000 replaces 8 x 8 DCT blocks with a multi-level wavelet transform of the whole image (or of large tiles), using the 9/7 wavelet for lossy and the integer 5/3 for lossless coding (lesson 23). Coefficients are quantised and then coded bit-plane by bit-plane in small code blocks with an arithmetic coder (the EBCOT method). Results: no blocking artefacts (errors show as gentle blur instead), lossy and lossless in one standard, progressive decoding (a low-resolution or low-quality version arrives first and improves as more bytes come), and region-of-interest coding (a tumour region kept at higher quality). The price is more computation and much weaker browser support, so JPEG 2000 lives mainly in medical imaging (DICOM), digital cinema distribution and archives, not on ordinary websites.

Other formats in one line each: GIF uses LZW on at most 256 colours, fine for tiny animations and logos. WebP and AVIF use video-codec ideas (block prediction plus transforms) and usually beat JPEG in size at similar quality. HEIC (HEVC-based) is the default photo format on many iPhones. The comparison of formats is in deep-cse-5-9 lesson 13.

Real life example 1, sending exam notes on WhatsApp: A student photographs 10 pages of handwritten notes. Each raw photo is 36 MB. Messaging apps typically resize and recompress photos, so each might arrive as a few hundred kilobytes: smaller dimensions and stronger JPEG quantisation. Text can become blurry and blocky. The better path: use a scanner app that thresholds the page (lesson 21) to black and white, then saves a compressed PDF or PNG. A clean binary page has long white runs, so lossless coding shrinks it a lot, and the letters stay sharp.

Real life example 2, a hospital PACS in Chattogram: CT scans are huge, often hundreds of slices of 512 x 512 pixels at 12 to 16 bits per pixel. Radiologists need exact values for diagnosis, so the archive stores them losslessly (lossless JPEG 2000 or JPEG-LS inside DICOM), roughly halving storage. For quick review on a tablet in the ward, the server sends a lossy, lower-resolution version first, which progressive coding makes possible from the same file. Lossy is never used for the copy the diagnosis is based on.

Common mistakes: Saving the same JPEG again and again after small edits: each save quantises again and the quality drops (generation loss); edit in PNG or the original and export to JPEG once. Using JPEG for screenshots and line drawings, which creates ringing around text; use PNG. Thinking a higher PSNR always means a better looking image. Forgetting that converting a JPEG to PNG does not bring back lost detail, it only stops further loss. Mixing up compression ratio and redundancy: C = 4 means R = 0.75, not 0.25.

What exams ask: Define coding, spatial/temporal and psychovisual redundancy with one example each. Compute compression ratio and relative redundancy. Build a Huffman code for given probabilities, find average length and compare with entropy. Run-length code a binary row. Compute MSE, RMSE and PSNR for a small block. Explain lossless predictive coding with a numeric row. Outline the JPEG steps and say which one is lossy. Compare JPEG with JPEG 2000.

Recap: Compression removes three kinds of redundancy: coding (short codes for common values), spatial and temporal (neighbours and frames look alike), and irrelevant information (detail the eye ignores). Lossless methods like Huffman, run-length, LZW and predictive coding in PNG reproduce every bit but rarely beat about 2:1 on photos. Lossy methods like JPEG and JPEG 2000 quantise transform coefficients for ratios of 10:1 or more, judged with MSE, PSNR or human ratings. Lesson 25 now turns from storing images to describing the shapes inside them.
key_points: Raw images are huge: 4000 x 3000 x 3 = 36 MB; compression ratio C = n1/n2 and redundancy R = 1 - 1/C.
Three redundancies: coding, spatial/temporal (inter-pixel) and irrelevant (psychovisual) information.
No lossless code can average fewer bits than the entropy; Huffman reaches it for probabilities like 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8.
PSNR = 10 log10(255^2 / MSE); MSE 25 gives about 34.2 dB.
Run-length coding suits binary pages and fax; predictive coding stores small prediction errors (PNG filters).
JPEG's only lossy step is quantisation of 8 x 8 DCT coefficients; it causes blocking at high compression.
JPEG 2000 uses wavelets: no blocks, lossless and lossy in one, progressive and ROI coding.
lessons.tip: Keep one table of numbers in your notes: raw size, ratio, redundancy, bits per pixel, MSE and PSNR for one example photo. Most compression exam questions are just these five formulas in different orders.
lessons.task: Take one photo on your phone and check its file size and dimensions in the gallery details. Compute the raw size (width x height x 3 bytes), the compression ratio and the bits per pixel. Then send it to yourself on a messaging app, save the received copy and repeat. How much did the app compress it?

quiz.q: An image is 24 MB raw and 3 MB compressed. What is the relative redundancy?
Which redundancy does chroma subsampling exploit?
quiz.explain: Eyes are less sensitive to fine colour detail, so dropping it is not noticed: psychovisual redundancy.

quiz.q: A block has MSE = 100. What is its PSNR for 8-bit data, approximately?
In JPEG, which step actually throws information away?
quiz.explain: The DCT, zig-zag and Huffman are all reversible; rounding after dividing by the quantisation table is lossy.

quiz.q: Why does run-length coding work poorly on a noisy photo?
options: Neighbouring pixels rarely repeat exactly, so runs are length 1
quiz.explain: With noise almost every pixel differs from the next, so each run is one pixel and the pairs can make data bigger.

lessons.title: Representation, Description and Features
lessons.content:
Suppose your friend is on the phone and you must describe a leaf so well that she can pick the same one from a pile of fifty. You would not read out a million pixel values. You would say: "It is long and thin, about three times longer than wide, with jagged edges, a smooth shiny surface and one hole near the tip." That is representation and description: turning a segmented region into a short list of numbers, called features, that capture its shape and surface. Segmentation (lessons 21-22) told us WHERE the object is. This lesson tells us WHAT it looks like, in a form a classifier can use.

Where this sits: This is the bridge from image processing to pattern recognition. Representation means choosing how to store the region: by its boundary (outline) or by its interior pixels. Description means computing numbers from that representation: perimeter, area, compactness, moments, texture measures and so on. Good descriptors are insensitive to things that should not matter, like where the object is (translation), how it is turned (rotation) and how big it appears (scale). Pattern Recognition (deep-cse-6-12) then classifies these feature vectors, and Computer Vision (deep-cse-8-3) goes deeper into keypoints and learned features.

Boundary following: Before describing a boundary, we need its pixels in order, walking around the object. The Moore boundary tracing algorithm starts at the top-left-most object pixel, looks at the 8 neighbours in a fixed clockwise order starting from the background pixel it came from, steps to the first object pixel it finds, and repeats until it returns to the start. The result is an ordered list of boundary points, which every descriptor below uses. A simpler unordered boundary comes from morphology (lesson 19): A minus (A eroded by B).

Freeman chain codes: Instead of storing every boundary coordinate, store only the direction of each step. With 4-direction codes, 0 means right, 1 up, 2 left, 3 down. With 8-direction codes the diagonals are added, numbered 0 to 7 counterclockwise starting from right. Worked: a rectangle of 3 steps wide and 2 steps tall, traced clockwise from its top-left corner, goes right, right, right, down, down, left, left, left, up, up, giving the code 0003322211. Ten small numbers, each needing only 2 bits, instead of ten (x, y) pairs. Real boundaries are noisy, so the boundary is usually resampled on a coarser grid first, otherwise one jagged pixel changes the code.

Making chain codes invariant: The code above depends on where we start and on how the object is turned. Start point: treat the code as circular and rotate it until it forms the smallest integer. Rotation: use the first difference, which counts how many steps (counterclockwise, mod 4) the direction changes between consecutive codes. For 0003322211 treated circularly: the first element compares 0 with the last code 1 and gives (0 - 1) mod 4 = 3; then 0 to 0 gives 0, 0 to 0 gives 0, 0 to 3 gives 3, and so on, producing 3003030030. Turning the rectangle by 90 degrees adds 1 to every code, but the differences stay the same. The rotation of the first difference with the smallest value, here 0030300303, is called the shape number.

Polygon approximation: A boundary of 2,000 pixels can often be described by a polygon of 10 corners with little error. The splitting method: join the two farthest points with a line; find the boundary point farthest from that line; if its distance is above a tolerance, make it a new vertex and split recursively; otherwise stop. This is the same idea as the Ramer-Douglas-Peucker algorithm used to simplify roads in map apps. The minimum perimeter polygon is a more exact textbook method that fits the tightest polygon inside a strip of cells around the boundary.

Signatures: A signature turns a 2D boundary into a 1D function, usually the distance from the centroid to the boundary as a function of angle, r(theta). A circle of radius R gives a flat line at R. A square of half-side a gives a wave that swings between a (at the middle of each side) and a x sqrt(2), about 1.41a (at the corners), with four bumps. Rotating the object only shifts the signature sideways; dividing by the maximum makes it scale-invariant. Signatures are easy to compare but can break when the shape is not star-shaped, because a ray from the centroid may hit the boundary more than once.

Simple boundary descriptors: Perimeter (length of the boundary; with 8-direction chain codes, count horizontal and vertical steps as 1 and diagonal steps as sqrt(2)). Diameter: the largest distance between two boundary points; the line joining them is the major axis, and the perpendicular extent is the minor axis. Their ratio is the eccentricity (or elongation): a grain of rice has a high ratio, a lentil a low one. Curvature: the rate of change of slope along the boundary; points of high curvature are corners, which are useful landmarks.

Fourier descriptors: Write each boundary point as a complex number s(k) = x(k) + j y(k), for k = 0 to K - 1, and take its 1D DFT (lesson 11). The coefficients a(u) are the Fourier descriptors. Low-frequency coefficients describe the overall shape; high-frequency ones describe fine wiggles and noise. Keep only the first few, inverse transform, and you get a smooth version of the shape: with very few coefficients, any shape looks like an ellipse. Invariance is cheap: translation only changes a(0), rotation multiplies all coefficients by the same phase factor, scaling multiplies all by the same number, so magnitudes divided by |a(1)| ignore position, rotation, scale and starting point.

Regional descriptors, the basics: Area A is the number of pixels in the region. Centroid is the mean row and mean column. Worked: a region with pixels at (row, column) = (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 1) has area 5 and centroid (0.8, 0.6). Mean and standard deviation of gray levels inside the region describe its brightness. Bounding box and extent (area divided by bounding box area) say how well the region fills its box.

Compactness (circularity): A popular shape number is 4 pi A / P^2, where P is the perimeter. It equals 1 for a perfect circle, which encloses the most area for a given perimeter, and is smaller for every other shape. Worked: a 10 x 10 square has A = 100 and P = 40, so 4 pi x 100 / 1600 = about 0.785. A 5 x 10 rectangle has A = 50, P = 30, giving about 0.698. A long thin crack or a star scores much lower. It does not change with size, position or rotation, which is why it is used to separate round fruits from elongated ones. On a pixel grid the perimeter is only approximate, so even a digital circle scores slightly off 1.

Topological descriptors and the Euler number: Some properties survive any stretching without tearing: the number of connected components C and the number of holes H. The Euler number is E = C - H. The letter A has one component and one hole: E = 0. The letter B has one component and two holes: E = -1. The letter i has two components (the dot and the stem) and no hole: E = 2. The digit 8 has E = -1 and the digit 0 has E = 0. In OCR this quickly narrows down which characters are possible, and it does not care about font size or slant.

Moments: The (p, q) moment of a region is m_pq = sum over pixels of x^p y^q f(x, y). m_00 is the area (for a binary region), m_10 / m_00 and m_01 / m_00 give the centroid. Central moments mu_pq use coordinates measured from the centroid, which removes translation; dividing by a power of mu_00 removes scale. In 1962 M. K. Hu combined second- and third-order normalised central moments into seven invariant moments that do not change under translation, scaling and rotation (one also flips sign under mirroring). They are compact shape features for simple recognition tasks such as identifying printed symbols or industrial parts.

Texture, statistical: Texture describes the surface pattern: smooth, coarse, regular. The simplest descriptors use the histogram of the region: mean, variance (a measure of contrast), the third moment (skewness of the histogram), uniformity (sum of p squared, maximal for a constant region) and entropy (randomness). They say how varied the values are, but not how they are arranged, so a checkerboard and random noise with the same histogram look the same to them.

Texture, the co-occurrence matrix (GLCM): To capture arrangement, count how often a pixel with value i has a neighbour with value j at a given offset, for example one step to the right. Worked on a 4 x 4 image with three levels, rows: 0 0 1 1 / 0 0 1 1 / 0 2 2 2 / 2 2 2 2. With the offset "right neighbour" there are 12 pairs: (0,0) appears 2 times, (0,1) 2, (0,2) 1, (1,1) 2 and (2,2) 5. Divide by 12 to get probabilities. Contrast = sum p(i,j) (i - j)^2 = (2 x 1 + 1 x 4) / 12 = 0.5. Energy (uniformity) = sum p^2 = (4 + 4 + 1 + 4 + 25) / 144 = about 0.264. Homogeneity = sum p / (1 + |i - j|) = about 0.861. A smooth surface gives low contrast and high homogeneity; a rough one the opposite. Haralick introduced these features in 1973.

Principal components for features: When you have many features, some are correlated and redundant. PCA (deep-cse-2-5 lesson 25) rotates the feature space so the first axis carries the most variance, and you can keep only the top few. In images, PCA also normalises orientation: the main eigenvector of the pixel coordinates of a region points along its long axis, so you can rotate every object to a standard pose before comparing. Eigenfaces, an early face recognition method, applied PCA to whole face images.

Keypoint features: So far we described whole regions. Many modern tasks instead find small distinctive points. The Harris corner detector (Harris and Stephens, 1988) looks for points where the image changes strongly when a small window is shifted in any direction, which happens at corners but not along straight edges. SIFT (David Lowe) finds keypoints at many scales using a difference-of-Gaussians pyramid (lesson 23), assigns each a main orientation, and builds a 128-number descriptor from gradient-direction histograms in a 4 x 4 grid of cells with 8 directions each. HOG (Dalal and Triggs, 2005) divides a window into cells, makes a histogram of gradient directions in each, and was a landmark for pedestrian detection. Deep networks now learn such features themselves (deep-cse-8-1).

Real life example 1, sorting mangoes in Rajshahi: A packing house photographs mangoes on a conveyor. Segment each mango from the dark belt by thresholding. Then compute features: area (size grade), major and minor axis ratio (shape: round vs elongated variety), compactness, mean hue inside the region (ripeness, colour lesson 17), and GLCM contrast on the skin (spots and scars make it rough). A simple classifier on these five numbers sends each mango to export, local market or juice. Because the features ignore position and rotation, the mango can lie any way on the belt.

Real life example 2, reading digits on a bKash-style bill photo: After thresholding and connected component labelling, each digit is one region. The Euler number immediately separates groups: 0, 6 and 9 have one hole, 8 has two, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7 have none (4 depends on the font). Within a group, compactness, the aspect ratio of the bounding box and a few Hu moments break the ties. This hand-crafted pipeline is fast enough for a cheap phone; a trained network is more accurate on messy handwriting, which is exactly the trade-off in lesson 26.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that chain codes change with the starting point and rotation unless you normalise them. Computing perimeter on a pixel grid as the number of boundary pixels and expecting a circle's compactness to be exactly 1. Using texture histograms and wondering why a checkerboard and noise look the same; use GLCM. Forgetting to fix the GLCM offset and symmetry convention, so numbers differ between tools. Mixing up moments with invariant moments: raw moments change with position.

What exams ask: Write the 4- or 8-direction chain code of a given boundary, its first difference and shape number. Sketch the signature of a circle and a square. Compute area, centroid, perimeter and compactness of a small region. Find the Euler number of letters or digits. Build a GLCM for a tiny image and compute contrast or energy. Explain Fourier descriptors and which coefficient changes under translation. Describe Harris, SIFT or HOG in a few lines.

Recap: A region is represented by its boundary or its interior and described by numbers. Chain codes, polygons, signatures and Fourier descriptors summarise boundaries; area, centroid, compactness, Euler number and moments summarise regions; histogram statistics and the co-occurrence matrix describe texture; PCA tidies feature vectors; Harris, SIFT and HOG describe local keypoints. Lesson 26 now puts the whole course together in one working system: a licence plate reader.
key_points: Representation stores a region by boundary or interior; description turns it into features invariant to position, rotation and scale.
Freeman chain codes store step directions; the first difference gives rotation invariance and the shape number fixes the start point.
Signatures (distance vs angle) and Fourier descriptors summarise boundaries; low Fourier coefficients give the overall shape.
Compactness 4 pi A / P^2 is 1 for a circle and about 0.785 for a square.
Euler number E = components - holes: A = 0, B = -1, i = 2.
Moments give area and centroid; Hu's seven moments are invariant to translation, scale and rotation.
GLCM counts value pairs at an offset; contrast, energy and homogeneity describe texture.
Harris finds corners, SIFT gives 128-number scale-invariant descriptors, HOG uses gradient-direction histograms.
lessons.tip: Make a small table with columns circle, square, long rectangle, letter B, and fill in area, perimeter, compactness and Euler number for each. Seeing which feature separates which shapes is the real skill of this lesson.
lessons.task: On squared paper draw a simple shape of about 15 cells, like an L or a T. Write its 4-direction chain code going clockwise, then its first difference and shape number. Count its area and perimeter in cell units and compute 4 pi A / P^2.

quiz.q: What does the first difference of a chain code achieve?
options: It makes the code invariant to rotation by multiples of 90 (or 45) degrees
quiz.explain: Rotation adds the same number to every direction code, so the differences between consecutive codes stay the same.

quiz.q: What is the compactness 4 pi A / P^2 of a 10 x 10 square?
The Euler number of the letter B is...
quiz.explain: B has 1 component and 2 holes, so E = 1 - 2 = -1.

quiz.q: Which texture description can tell a checkerboard from random noise with the same histogram?
quiz.explain: Histogram statistics ignore arrangement; the GLCM counts neighbouring value pairs, which differ greatly between the two.

quiz.q: In Fourier descriptors, translating the object changes which coefficient?
quiz.explain: Adding a constant to every boundary point only changes the DC term a(0).

lessons.title: Capstone: A Licence Plate Reader, and Course Wrap-Up
lessons.content:
Picture the toll plaza at the entrance of a big bridge at rush hour. Cars, buses and trucks queue up, and every second a vehicle waits costs fuel and patience. Now imagine a camera that reads each licence plate as the car rolls through, matches it to a prepaid account and lifts the barrier without anyone touching cash. In this capstone we design such a system for an invented company, "PlatePath", at a Dhaka toll plaza. Almost every lesson of this course appears in it, and seeing them work together is the best revision you can do.

Requirements first: Before any pixels, write down what the system must do. Functional: detect the plate of each vehicle in the lane, read the full registration (city name, vehicle class letter and the number), and send the text to the billing server. Performance targets for our design: process a frame in under 100 milliseconds, read at least 95 percent of plates correctly in daylight and 90 percent at night, and flag uncertain reads for a human operator instead of guessing. Constraints: outdoor cameras, rain, dust, headlights at night, dirty or bent plates, and an affordable embedded computer in a roadside cabinet. Writing numbers like these early tells you later whether the system is good enough.

Understanding the plate: Bangladeshi registration plates are written in Bangla script, usually on two lines. The top line holds the registration area, such as ঢাকা মেট্রো (Dhaka Metro), and a Bangla letter for the vehicle class, such as গ. The bottom line holds a two-digit and a four-digit number in Bangla digits, like ১২-৩৪৫৬. This is harder than many textbook examples built for Latin characters: Bangla letters have joined headstrokes (matra) that connect letters into one blob, some digits look alike (১ and ৯ differ only in small details, and ৪ looks like an English 8), and both lines must be read correctly. Our pipeline must respect these facts.

Stage 1, capture: The camera points at the lane at a fixed angle. Motion blur is the first enemy. Worked: a car moving at 20 km per hour travels 20 / 3.6 = about 5.56 metres per second. With an exposure of 1/250 second, it moves about 22 millimetres during the exposure. If one pixel covers about 2 millimetres of the plate, that is about 11 pixels of blur, which smears every digit. With an exposure of 1/1000 second the blur drops to about 2.8 pixels, which the later steps can tolerate. Short exposures need more light, so PlatePath uses an infrared flash at night; plates reflect it strongly, and it does not dazzle drivers. Short exposure also raises sensor noise, so the next stages must handle noise (lessons 13-14).

Stage 2, intensity correction: Night frames are dark: suppose the mean gray value around the plate is only 40 out of 255. A gamma transform s = 255 x (r / 255)^gamma with gamma = 0.5 (lesson 06) lifts a pixel of value 40 to 255 x sqrt(40 / 255) = about 101, while bright pixels change much less, so dark details open up without blowing out the white areas. Instead of a fixed gamma, PlatePath can measure the mean brightness and choose gamma per frame. For uneven light, such as one headlight shining on half the plate, local methods like CLAHE (lesson 07) work better than one global curve.

Stage 3, grayscale and denoising: Colour helps only a little for plate reading, so convert to gray: a weighted sum like 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B. Rain and dust create small bright and dark specks, close to salt-and-pepper noise, so a 3 x 3 median filter (lessons 09 and 14) removes them while keeping the sharp edges of characters. A Gaussian blur would also reduce noise but soften those edges, which would hurt the later edge and threshold steps. Choosing the filter by noise type is exactly the judgment lesson 14 practised.

Stage 4, finding the plate: The plate is a rectangle full of sharp vertical character strokes on a light background. Approach A, edges and morphology: compute the horizontal gradient with a Sobel kernel (lesson 20), which responds strongly to vertical strokes; threshold it; then apply a morphological closing with a wide, short structuring element (lesson 18), for example 17 x 3, which joins neighbouring strokes into one solid block. Label connected components (lesson 19) and keep candidates whose width-to-height ratio, area and fill extent fit a plate. Approach B, a trained detector, for example a small neural network or a HOG-based classifier (lesson 25), scans the image and outputs plate boxes. Approach A needs no training data; approach B copes better with clutter such as bumper stickers and shop signs. PlatePath starts with A because it is cheap and explainable, and keeps B as an upgrade.

Rejecting false candidates: Many things look like plates: grilles, stickers, text on trucks. Simple rules remove most: the candidate must lie in the lower part of the vehicle region, its aspect ratio must fall in a range chosen from real samples, and it must contain several separate dark components of similar height after thresholding (characters). Each rule is cheap, and together they cut false alarms sharply. Whatever still passes goes to the next stage, which will reject it if no characters are found.

Stage 5, geometric correction: The camera looks down at an angle, so the rectangle appears as a slanted quadrilateral. Find its four corners (intersections of the strongest boundary lines from a Hough transform, lesson 20, or corners of the fitted polygon, lesson 25). A perspective (projective) transform maps those four points to the corners of a standard rectangle, say 400 x 200 pixels. Four point pairs give eight equations, exactly enough for the eight unknowns of the homography. Use inverse mapping with bilinear interpolation (lesson 05) so the output has no holes. Now every plate has the same size and orientation, which makes everything after this easier.

Stage 6, binarisation: Turn the plate into black characters on white. A single global Otsu threshold (lesson 21) works on evenly lit plates, but shadows and headlight hot spots make one part brighter than another. Adaptive thresholding compares each pixel with the mean of its local window, say 25 x 25 pixels, minus a small constant, so each area gets its own threshold. A small morphological opening removes leftover specks, and a closing repairs small breaks in strokes, being careful not to merge neighbouring characters.

Stage 7, separating lines and characters: Split the two lines using the horizontal projection: sum the black pixels in every row; the gap between the lines shows up as a valley near zero. For the digit line, a vertical projection shows gaps between digits, and connected-component labelling gives each digit as its own region. The top line is harder: the headstroke joins Bangla letters into one component, so segmenting individual letters needs care. A practical trick: the registration area name comes from a fixed list of districts and metro areas, so instead of cutting letters you can recognise the whole word image by matching against the list. The class letter is a single character and is easier to isolate.

Stage 8, features and recognition, option A, template matching: Resize each digit to a fixed size, say 32 x 32, and compare it with stored templates of the ten Bangla digits using normalised cross-correlation, which gives a score between -1 and 1 and ignores overall brightness. The highest score wins. It is simple and needs only ten clean templates per font, but it fails when the font differs, the digit is tilted or partly dirty.

Stage 8, option B, features plus classifier: Compute features such as the Euler number (lesson 25), which separates digits with closed loops from those without, aspect ratio, zoning (the fraction of black pixels in each cell of a 4 x 4 grid) and HOG, and feed them to a classifier such as an SVM or k-nearest neighbours (deep-cse-6-1). Option C, a small convolutional neural network trained on thousands of real plate crops, learns its own features and is usually the most accurate today, at the cost of collecting and labelling data (deep-cse-8-1). PlatePath ships option B first and collects every human-corrected read as training data for option C later.

Using context to fix errors: Recognition gives each character a score, not just a label. Plate grammar helps: the bottom line must be exactly two digits, a dash and four digits; the top line must be a valid area name and a valid class letter. If the classifier says the third character is the letter ক with 51 percent and the digit ৯ with 49 percent, grammar says that position must be a digit, so ৯ wins. If the best full reading is still below a confidence threshold, the system sends the image to an operator. This is cheaper than a wrong charge on someone's account.

Evaluation, worked: Test on 1,000 labelled images collected over a week, day and night, not used for tuning. Suppose the plate is found in 970 of them: detection rate 97 percent. In 912 images every character on the plate is read correctly: end-to-end accuracy 912 / 1000 = 91.2 percent, and 912 / 970 = about 94.0 percent of detected plates. Digit-level accuracy looks much better: 970 plates x 6 digits = 5,820 digits with, say, 70 wrong, so about 98.8 percent of digits are right. This is why you must report plate-level accuracy: one wrong digit is a wrong car. For localisation, IoU of the predicted plate box with the hand-drawn box (lesson 22), counted correct above 0.5, is the usual rule.

Failure analysis: Sort the 88 failures by cause, because each cause has a different fix. Night glare and overexposed plates: adjust infrared flash power and exposure. Motion blur from fast cars: shorter exposure, or deblurring with a known motion length (Wiener filter, lesson 15). Rain streaks: median filtering and taking the best of several frames, since each car appears in many frames. Dirty, bent or non-standard decorative plates: no image trick fixes these fully; send them to an operator. Confusing digit pairs: add more training samples of those pairs. Tracking which cause dominates tells you where to spend effort next.

Making it fast enough: A 1920 x 1080 frame has about 2 million pixels. Doing everything on the full frame is wasteful, so PlatePath first runs cheap steps on a downscaled copy (half or quarter size, a pyramid level from lesson 23) to find candidates, then crops only the plate region at full resolution for correction and recognition. Separable filters (lesson 08) cut the cost of blurs, and integral images make local means for adaptive thresholding constant-time per pixel. Processing only every second frame is enough when a car stays in view for over a second.

Privacy and responsibility: A plate reader records where cars go, which is sensitive personal data. PlatePath stores only what billing needs, deletes images of correctly charged vehicles after a short period, restricts who can search the records and logs every access. Bangladesh's own laws and policies on data and digital security apply, and Professional Ethics and Cyber Law (deep-cse-6-6) discusses these questions. Good engineering includes deciding what not to keep.

Real life connection 1, the same pipeline elsewhere: Parking garages in shopping malls use the same stages to record entry and exit times. Traffic police use them to detect vehicles in bus lanes or running red lights. Change the target from plates to meter displays, and the pipeline reads electricity meters from photos taken by meter readers, a task utility companies care about.

Real life connection 2, document scanning: The pipeline of PlatePath is almost identical to a phone scanner app: find the page (edges plus Hough), correct its perspective, adaptive threshold for uneven light, clean with morphology, segment lines and characters with projections, and recognise them with OCR. If you can build one, you can build the other.

Course recap: You started with an image as a grid of numbers f(x, y) formed by light and sampled into pixels. You learned pixel relationships and geometric warps; point operations and histograms for contrast; spatial filters for smoothing and sharpening; the 2D Fourier transform and frequency filters; noise models, restoration, inverse and Wiener filters; colour models and colour processing; binary and grayscale morphology; edge detection, Hough, thresholding and region segmentation; wavelets and pyramids; compression; and finally description and features. The licence plate reader used nearly all of them.

What next: Pattern Recognition (deep-cse-6-12) studies the classifiers that turn features into decisions, with probability and statistics. Computer Vision (deep-cse-8-3) moves to 3D, cameras, motion, tracking, keypoint matching and learned detection and segmentation. Deep Learning (deep-cse-8-1) explains the convolutional networks that now learn filters like the ones you designed by hand here. A good first project: install Python with OpenCV and NumPy, take photos with your phone, and rebuild the pipeline of this lesson step by step, printing the intermediate image after every stage.
key_points: Write measurable requirements first: speed per frame, accuracy by day and night, and when to defer to a human.
Short exposure fights motion blur: at 20 km/h and 1/250 s a car moves about 22 mm, around 11 pixels at 2 mm per pixel.
Gamma correction lifts dark night frames; median filtering removes rain and dust specks while keeping edges.
Plate localisation: horizontal Sobel, threshold, wide closing, connected components and shape rules, or a trained detector.
Perspective correction maps four corners to a standard rectangle with inverse mapping and bilinear interpolation.
Adaptive thresholding, projections and connected components separate lines and characters; Bangla headstrokes need special care.
Recognition by template matching, features plus a classifier, or a CNN; plate grammar and confidence thresholds fix or flag errors.
Report plate-level accuracy (912/1000 = 91.2%), not just digit accuracy, and analyse failures by cause.
lessons.tip: Build the pipeline one stage at a time and save the output image of every stage. When something fails, you can see exactly which stage broke instead of guessing.
lessons.task: Take a photo of a printed page or a car plate in a parking lot (only your own or a public sign, respecting privacy). On paper, write the 8 stages of this lesson and, for each, name the method you would use for that specific photo and one way it could fail.

quiz.q: A car moves at 20 km/h and the exposure is 1/1000 s. With 2 mm per pixel, how much motion blur is there?
quiz.explain: 20/3.6 = 5.56 m/s; in 1/1000 s that is 5.56 mm, divided by 2 mm per pixel is about 2.8 pixels.

quiz.q: Why is a wide, short structuring element used in a closing during plate localisation?
options: To join neighbouring vertical character strokes into one solid plate block
quiz.explain: Closing with a wide element fills the horizontal gaps between strokes, so the plate becomes one connected component.

quiz.q: How many point correspondences are needed to compute a perspective (projective) transform?
quiz.explain: A homography has 8 unknowns; each point pair gives 2 equations, so 4 pairs are needed.

quiz.q: A plate system reads 98.8% of digits correctly but only 91.2% of plates. Which number matters for billing?
options: Digit accuracy, because it is higher
Plate-level accuracy, because one wrong digit charges the wrong car
quiz.explain: A single wrong character gives a different registration, so plate-level (end-to-end) accuracy is what counts.

quiz.q: Why prefer adaptive thresholding over one global threshold for plates at night?
options: Headlight hot spots and shadows make different parts need different thresholds
quiz.explain: Uneven lighting shifts the local brightness; comparing each pixel with its local mean handles it.
